events.title: Global economy to slow less than expected in 2026 as AI boom offsets war hit: IMF
events.summary: Growth is seen slowing to 3.1% this year from 3.5%, but better than the IMF's 3% July estimate, aided by AI investment and fiscal support. Inflation is expected to rise to 4.7% this year, driven by higher energy costs and an AI investment boom, and then ease to 4.1% in 2027. The IMF now expects the Strait of Hormuz to reopen in March 2027, with conditions returning to a pre-war state by October 2027. BANGKOK — The International Monetary Fund has raised its forecast for global economic growth this year as the AI-driven investment boom helps offset some of the impact from surging energy costs. The IMF expects the global economy to grow at 3.1% in 2026, up from the 3% projected in July , but slower than the 3.5% rate last year. For 2027, it kept the forecast unchanged at 3.4%. The UN agency expects inflation at 4.1% in 2027, above the 3.9% it projected in July – when it estimated the Strait of Hormuz would reopen by mid-July, with conditions broadly returning to pre-war levels by March 2027. For the current year, it maintained its 4.7% outlook. The IMF now estimates that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March next year and return to pre-war state by October. Gulf crude exports averaged 88% of pre-conflict levels in September as traffic picked up, the international body said. The report was released at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, where finance ministers and central bank governors from the fund's 191 members are meeting to discuss geopolitical tensions, mounting public debt and artificial intelligence. AI-related investment gave the global economy a "demand impulse" that helped activity in the first half of the year hold up better than expected, despite the Middle East war and trade tensions, the IMF said. Financial markets also stayed largely calm, which the fund said may partly reflect "AI-related exuberance." For now, "use of buffers and adaptability have helped economies weather the negative shocks," the IMF said, citing measures such as diversifying fuel sources, tapping strategic reserves that have contained the energy-market turmoil unleashed by the Middle East war. But that cushion is "rapidly narrowing" in the near term, it said. Global oil reserves are being drawn down by about 2.7 million barrels a day, nearing levels that could trigger sharp price moves, and energy constraints could impair the AI-led momentum. The growing unease over governments' fiscal health also adds to the headwinds. Overall growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. Thirty-two economies now account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April. Countries that have limited exposure to the war-led supply shock and are catering to the AI-led demand are holding up or strengthening. Taiwan is forecast to grow 10.7% this year and South Korea 3.3%, up from 1.1% in 2025 on semiconductor demand. The U.S. is projected to expand 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by private consumption, fiscal policy and tech investment. Energy importers outside that tech supply chain face higher import bills, weaker real incomes and less fiscal room. The euro zone is estimated to eke out just 1.1% growth this year amid higher energy costs and weak consumer confidence. The Middle East and Central Asia is projected to contract 0.3% this year, with Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit declines before double-digit rebounds in 2027. China is forecast to grow 4.5% this year and 4.0% in 2027, with higher oil prices and structural headwinds weighing on activity. Second-quarter growth of 4.3% was weaker than expected as sluggish consumption and property strains outweighed robust exports. "The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength," the IMF said. While AI has underpinned resilience, the investment boom is also adding to inflationary pressures and financial fragility, the IMF said. "This is a large, front-loaded demand shock" that sees massive investment pouring into sectors such as semiconductors, data centers, and power generation, before any broad productivity gains have materialized, it said in the report. A potential reassessment of AI-related profitability and productivity prospects could see excessive investment pull back and force a sharp correction in equities. The IMF warned that in a scenario where AI productivity gains fail to materialize, U.S. equities could fall 20% and global growth could end up 1.1% below its baseline estimates by 2028, with Asia 1.7% lower. Advanced-economy benchmark yields have climbed to multidecade highs as resurgent inflation, the expected path of policy rates and fiscal concerns push up borrowing costs, the IMF said. Technology firms borrowing to finance AI investment are adding to the pressure. Public debt in advanced economies is projected to reach 115% of GDP by 2031, from 108% in 2025.

events.title: SK Hynix, SoftBank shares plunge as tech stocks in Asia track Wall Street sell-off
events.summary: Asian technology stocks tumbled Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into regional markets. Asian technology stocks fell Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into regional markets, with worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition denting sentiment. In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.8%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 6.75%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 5.65%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell 4.94%, Disco lost 4.69% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.64%. The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , which reported progress on a new chip structure. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates.

events.title: UK growth upgraded but energy prices and rates to bite in 2027
events.summary: The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit growth in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said. The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027. Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain". Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget. Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October. Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money. But in its economic forecast, the IMF projected that the UK would have a sharp fall in borrowing and the lowest annual rate of borrowing of all G7 countries - the group of the world's most advanced economies - over the next five years. The UK is estimated to have the lowest annual deficit - the difference between what the government spends and brings in through taxes in a year - by 2031, suggesting it thinks public spending will be cut in coming years. The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economies to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels. The reversal of downgrades to economic forecasts made at the start of the US-Iran, mean the UK is expected to have the second fasted growing economy in the G7 along with Germany. But growth is estimated to slow in 2027 to 1.2% due to higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weighing on household spending and business investment. Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience". When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks. Economists have suggested Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget. On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to make "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes". "The challenge of continuing to bring down borrowing must be paired with the pressing need for fresh cost of living support to help families facing a difficult winter ahead," the think tank said. Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it". Burnham has pledged to create "good growth in every postcode" as part of his plans to giving nations and regions more control, but his strategy has faced criticism inside his own party. The IMF said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices, with inflation expected to average 3.3% this year and remain above the Bank of England's 2% target in 2027 at 2.8%. The Bank itself has predicted inflation could rise above 4% at the beginning of next year - making it more likely that interest rates will rise. Healey is expected to meet with other finance ministers at the IMF's annual meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, on Tuesday to discuss how the economic impact of the Middle East and European conflicts could be limited. The IMF said the global economy had shown a "remarkable capacity to absorb shocks" not just from the current Middle East conflict, but also from the Covid pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine. events.title: IMF cuts 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies due to prolonged Hormuz closure
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has significantly lowered its 2026 projections for economies across the Gulf due to the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz , and pushed back its forecast on the waterway's reopening. In its latest World Economic Outlook , released on Tuesday, the IMF also slashed its forecasts for the broader region. The Middle East and North Africa economy is estimated to contract by 2 per cent this year, a downward revision of 3.1 percentage points from its April projections. It is the only region expected to record an economic contraction this year. The IMF maintained its 2026 forecast for global growth at 3.1 per cent and lifted its projection for 2027 from to 3.4 per cent. “This is the net result of two main forces that are shaping the outlook,” IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told reporters, referring to the negative supply shock from the Iran war and the positive demand shock from the AI infrastructure boom. The fund said the global economy had so far been able to withstand the impact from the Iran war energy shock due to a combination of factors including supply adjustment, a drawdown of inventories, lower energy intensity, and households and companies adapting to higher prices. The latest forecasts come as Saudi Arabia vowed to press on with bringing its oil supplies to market despite escalating attacks on the kingdom in recent days by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have declined in recent days after tanker attacks reached their highest weekly count this year on October 9. One tanker crossed the waterway on Saturday, down from eight the day before, data from analytics firm Kpler showed. Confirmed total Hormuz clearance stands at roughly 11.9 million barrels per day, or about 30 per cent below its pre-war baseline, Kpler data showed, although daily readings have swung wildly. Energy supply disruptions from the Iran war are the latest in a round of shocks the global economy has weathered in recent years. These have included the 2025 tariffs row, Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Covid-19 pandemic and the global tightening cycle that followed. “The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” Ms Tenreyro said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and rebuilding supply-side resilience.” The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits Silvana Tenreyro, IMF chief economist The fund said the economic outlook is highly uneven across countries, reflecting differences in their exposure to commodities, AI-related activity and borrowing costs. Overall GDP growth in the US is forecast to be 2.3 per cent, compared to 1.1 per cent for the euro area, 1.3 per cent for the UK, 0.7 per cent in Japan and 1.1 per cent in Canada. Growth in China, which is classified as an emerging economy, is forecast to slow to 4.5 per cent growth in 2026, compared to 7 per cent for India and 3.6 per cent for Pakistan. Gulf outlook The IMF projects the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, conditional on the normalisation of shipping routes and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. The new projections for the Middle East 's second-largest economy reflect a downgrade of 7 percentage points for 2026 and an upgrade of 2.4 percentage points for 2027 compared to the fund's April forecast. Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3, 16.7 and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. The fund also lowered its forecasts for Saudi Arabia , but expects the decline to be less sharp compared to Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar because of its diversified export routes. The fund expects Saudi Arabia to slow from a positive growth rate of 4.6 per cent last year to a 3.3 per cent contraction this year. Oman is the only GCC member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. The latest forecast assumes the gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will resume in March 2027, with a return to prewar conditions by October. It also notes that uncertainty is assumed to remain elevated throughout next year. Under these conditions, oil exporters are expected to see economic activity rebound next year, similar to the UAE. Overall GDP growth in Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar would expand by 13.9, 17.1 and 18.8, respectively, the fund said. Saudi Arabia's economic activity would accelerate at a 7.9 per cent pace. The kingdom's ministry of finance last week said its economy was forecast to grow by 12.8 per cent next year. Other oil exporters also faced downgrades for 2026 including Iraq at minus 16 per cent and Iran at minus 7.6 per cent, with the latter also impacted by enhanced sanctions and a US naval blockade. Meanwhile, the fund said importers in the region were expected to remain relatively resilient. Egypt's economy is forecast to expand by a 5.1 per cent pace in 2026, more than 8 percentage points lower than the IMF's April forecast. Morocco's economy is set grow by 4.5 per cent and Jordan's by 2.7 per cent. The fund did not submit projections for Lebanon. Conflict and AI boom lift inflation The fund said that while the Iran war and AI buildout were driving growth in opposite directions, both were adding to inflationary pressures. Global headline inflation is set to increase to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, a cumulative upwards projection of 0.7 percentage points. Ms Tenreyro said this was driving up borrowing costs in advanced economies at a time when public debt was already high. The US Federal Reserve and other central banks in advanced economies have already begun raising interest rates or are expected to this quarter. “This interaction of high debt and high financing costs, in turn, has heightened fiscal concerns and risks,” Ms Tenreyro said. Global bonds have been under significant pressure in recent weeks over fears of higher energy prices, higher-for-longer interest rates and concerns over unchecked government spending. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury , a benchmark for global borrowing costs, has recently traded at its highest level since 2002. Bonds in Japan, France, Germany and the UK have also recently hit multi-decade highs. Pimco, a global investment management firm, warned last week the yield on the 10-Year Treasury could hit 6 per cent for the first time since 2000.

events.title: Bumble shares soar after report dating firm in $1bn takeover talks
events.summary: Published 13 October 2026, 02:36 BST Technology holding company Ithaca could announce a deal to buy the Texas-based firm as early as this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. The jump in Bumble's shares pushed its stock market valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after listing on the Nasdaq in 2021 . Bumble is one of the world's most downloaded dating apps, operating in a crowded market where growth has slowed. The BBC has contacted Bumble and Ithaca for comment. Bumble was launched in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, who was also a co-founder of dating app giant Tinder. Wolfe Herd built Bumble's brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches. It recently abandoned that rule , prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals. "Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August. Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates. Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating. Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services. Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021. According a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier. Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers , book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner. events.title: Ethiopia’s Tigray war: Where do the UAE and Saudi Arabia stand?
events.summary: The Tigray conflict puts the UAE’s backing of Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia’s diplomatic role under scrutiny. Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – As renewed fighting in Ethiopia’s Tigray region threatens to destabilise the Horn of Africa, public backing by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of Ethiopia’s federal government and Saudi Arabia’s record of regional diplomacy are drawing scrutiny. Both Gulf powers have strategic interests in the Horn of Africa, but their roles differ. The UAE has publicly backed Ethiopia’s government while Saudi Arabia has previously helped broker an Ethiopia-Eritrea rapprochement and was reported to have offered to mediate between the two countries in 2025. The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended a war between Ethiopia’s federal government and Tigrayan forces. As tensions with Eritrea add to the risks of a wider confrontation, the positions of Abu Dhabi and Riyadh offer a window into the interests of external powers in the crisis. The UAE: Clear alignment, unproven leverage On September 25, the UAE condemned attacks by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allied armed groups against Ethiopian federal forces, the seizure of airports in Tigray and the escalation in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara. Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan, the UAE minister of state, expressed solidarity with Ethiopia’s government and people, reaffirmed support for the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and called for an end to hostilities, the protection of civilians and adherence to the Pretoria Agreement. The statement made Abu Dhabi’s public position clear: It backs Ethiopia’s federal government while calling for de-escalation and dialogue. It did not establish whether the UAE was providing military assistance or had secured commitments from the parties to end the fighting. The UAE also has commercial interests across the Horn of Africa. Dubai Ports World (DP World) operates Berbera port in Somaliland, and a shipping route launched in 2025 connects the port with Jebel Ali in the UAE, providing an additional corridor for cargo serving inland destinations, such as Ethiopia. Landlocked since Eritrea’s independence in 1993, Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti for access to international trade. These commercial links help explain Abu Dhabi’s interest in regional stability and its relationship with Addis Ababa. However, they do not establish that the UAE can influence the TPLF, persuade Eritrea to de-escalate or change Ethiopia’s military calculations. The extent to which Abu Dhabi can use its relationship with the federal government to encourage a political response to the conflict remains unclear. Saudi Arabia: Diplomatic experience, uncertain engagement Saudi Arabia has yet to publicly announce its position on the latest fighting in Tigray. The kingdom has not publicly commented on the renewed war, according to an October 1 analysis by Critical Threats, although it undertook diplomatic efforts earlier this year to reduce tensions between Ethiopia’s federal government and the TPLF. Saudi Arabia has previously sought to mediate between Ethiopia and Eritrea. In November 2025, Chatham House reported that sources said Riyadh had offered to mediate between the two countries amid rising tensions over maritime access and regional security. A June 2026 analysis by Germany’s SWP think tank said previous Saudi mediation efforts had failed, partly because negotiations did not address Ethiopia’s interest in the Eritrean port of Assab. The kingdom’s broader regional alignment also matters. An August 2026 analysis by the Soufan Center described Saudi Arabia and Egypt as backing Eritrea in opposition to Ethiopia’s ambitions for Red Sea access. This is an assessment of regional alignment, however, not evidence that Saudi Arabia is directly providing military support to Eritrea or the TPLF in the current fighting. Saudi Arabia has a strong interest in Red Sea security, a vital corridor for international shipping and its own oil exports. Whether Riyadh will take a more public diplomatic role as tensions escalate remains unclear. Egypt’s rivalry with Ethiopia adds to regional tensions Egypt’s role in the crisis is shaped by its longstanding dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) and its growing ties with Eritrea. Cairo has also stressed that responsibility for the governance and security of the Red Sea rests with countries bordering the waterway, a position shared by Asmara. The issue has added to regional tensions as Ethiopia seeks reliable access to the sea. In September, Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting armed groups fighting the federal government, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). His remarks, reported by Al Jazeera on September 28, did not provide evidence substantiating the accusation.

events.title: S’pore investors take stock risks abroad, but why not at home? SGX chairman Koh Boon Hwee weighs in
events.summary: SGX chairman Koh Boon Hwee explained that early-stage venture funding is relatively well supported in Singapore. Singapore investors take risks overseas, but SGX chairman Koh Boon Hwee says local shares still lack liquidity and sustained demand, so investors stay cautious at home. Koh says Singapore may need more capital injections, including the $6.5 billion EQDP, but warns these are not a natural, lasting flow like pension-backed markets in the US. He says Singapore must support more start-ups and growth firms, or they will keep listing overseas, which weakens local capital recycling and slows long-term economic growth. SINGAPORE – Singapore investors are willing to take risks on volatile growth stocks overseas, but are unlikely to make similar bets here, where the local market still lacks flow and liquidity, said Singapore Exchange (SGX) chairman Koh Boon Hwee. The problem, in his view, is that the Republic has yet to create a level of sustained demand for local shares to give investors enough confidence to take risks here, and until then, further capital injections will be needed to keep demand in the stock market up. Koh was speaking to The Straits Times on the sidelines of the Forbes Global CEO Conference on Oct 8. “Do they here have the appetite for risk? The answer is yes,” he said, pointing to younger investors who buy overseas stocks such as Tesla and even SpaceX, which is loss-making. But would they back similar businesses on SGX? “My honest answer is , right now it’s unlikely, because they understand the constraints here as well,” he said. This could help explain why many initial public offerings (IPOs) on the local bourse have recently struggled to gain traction after listing, despite efforts by the central bank, stock exchange and fund managers to revive the local equities market and attract new listings. Asked whether Singapore would need continued capital injections in the meantime, Koh said: “Personally, I would think so”, but noted that the decision was beyond him. While he commended the Government’s move to allocate $6.5 billion of investment capital into the local stock market through the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP), he noted that it is a “stochastic injection, and not a natural flow”. He distinguished such injections from the regular and sustained capital flows that pension systems generate in other countries. In the United States, for example, multiple pension funds make independent investment decisions and help circulate capital through the public markets, private equity and venture capital. An allocation under the EQDP, by contrast, leaves the question of what follows after the money has been committed. “You have to think about how much more for how much longer,” Koh said. While he stressed that the EQDP funds are being invested rather than spent, he noted that the wider concern is that the repeated allocations do not establish the recurring demand flows needed to sustain the market. “Our challenge right now is to create something that is circular and sustainable,” said Koh. “If you don’t have constant demand creation, it’s hard to sustain liquidity . And with no liquidity, there is no proper valuation.” Convincing investors to recycle capital here Koh explained that early-stage venture funding is relatively well supported in Singapore, but these investors eventually need a way to realise their investments and recycle the capital into other start-ups and ventures. A public listing can provide that route, but for it to work, the market needs investors willing to buy into a company’s next stage of growth. Without an attractive domestic market, founders must consider overseas listings to meet obligations to their backers, regardless of how committed they are to Singapore. Several prominent Singapore-funded companies have already taken that path through the years. Sea, the parent of e-commerce platform Shopee and gaming business Garena, for example, listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2017, while Grab debuted on Nasdaq in 2021 through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company. Singapore-headquartered data centre operator DayOne is now pursuing a similar route, having filed for a proposed Nasdaq IPO this month. The result is that SGX misses out on potential growth stocks that could attract a broader pool of investors, while early backers realise their investments through overseas markets, leaving a gap in the domestic capital cycle. “You can’t blame them for doing that,” Koh said, adding that Singapore may have provided the research funding, business environment, stability and security that helps young companies develop, but a lot more work needs to be done to offer a viable route for capital to be recycled here. “We need to create an environment that will not make it an automatic reflex that we list on Nasdaq or we list in Hong Kong.

events.title: Oil edges lower after rising on expanding Middle East conflict
events.summary: Oil has risen more than 70% in 2026 as the US war on Iran roils energy markets. Oil prices slipped after three days of gains, as traders weighed fears that the widening Middle East war could disrupt supply and lift energy costs further. Houthi drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia killed at least 16 people and wounded about 300, while Trump said he may back Saudi-led strikes and warned of violations of his “energy ceasefire”. Saudi Arabia is moving to reduce its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, with Aramco planning extra export capacity soon and a bigger bypass pipeline within two to three years, showing how fragile oil flows remain. Oil edged lower following three days of gains that were driven by concern the widening war in the Middle East could hamper a recovery in supply from the region. Brent traded below US$106 a barrel after rising more than 6% over the previous three sessions, while West Texas Intermediate was near US$93. Diesel fell a third day in New York after Russia agreed to release more supply following a request by US President Donald Trump. A barrage of drone and missile attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia’s main airport has intensified pressure on Washington to step up its efforts in the conflict in Yemen. Meanwhile, Trump said there had been violations of his “energy ceasefire” between Kyiv and Moscow. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine will continue attacks against Russia as his nation’s energy infrastructure is still being targeted. The attacks on Saudi Arabia came shortly after Riyadh-led forces in Yemen launched a campaign to retake Houthi-held territory, while strikes on tankers in the critical Strait of Hormuz have escalated. That has led to a growing number of supertankers turning away from the Persian Gulf in recent days. “It’s been a dizzying few days of headlines,” said Scott Shelton, an energy specialist at TP ICAP Group, pointing to issues including Trump’s claims of an “energy ceasefire” as well as the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. “We are off to a messy start this week.” Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s main airport over the weekend killed at least 16 people, including a US citizen, and wounded about 300. Trump has said he would consider joining Saudi-backed strikes against the Yemen-based group that is backed by Iran. Meanwhile, the kingdom is seeking to bolster its ability to ship oil without having to transit the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Aramco could add 1.2 million barrels a day of export capacity within seven to eight weeks by repurposing existing gas pipelines, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at a conference in Riyadh on Monday. The country also plans to expand a pipeline that bypasses Hormuz by 40% to 10 million barrels a day within two to three years. The push comes even after Middle East oil flows recovered sharply in recent weeks. Some Wall Street banks have said crude shipments from the region had returned to near pre-war levels. That recovery put downward pressure on prices, but has also left the market vulnerable to another major supply disruption, said Haris Khurshid, chief investment officer at Karobaar Capital LP. “Just because the system has found ways to keep oil moving doesn’t mean it can handle another major disruption. That’s the risk the market could be underestimating.” In Europe, Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff told Ukrainian officials on Oct 9 that allowing Russian diesel exports was part of efforts to bring Moscow back to negotiations to end the war, Reuters reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. events.title: 'Boring is not bad': CEO of Southeast Asia's largest bank pitches Singapore as a haven amid global turmoil
events.summary: Southeast Asia's biggest bank by assets is making a pitch to investors that Singapore and its businesses can help them navigate many of the uncertainties around the globe. Tan Su Shan, the CEO of DBS Group, says Singapore's reliability is helpful at such a moment. DBS can help customers diversify supply chains and pivot to new markets, she said. SINGAPORE — Southeast Asia's biggest bank by assets is making a pitch to investors that Singapore and its businesses can help them navigate many of the uncertainties around the globe. "I love it that the 'Little Red Dot' we all call home was open … predictable, and almost kind of boring," said CEO of DBS Group Tan Su Shan at the DBS Asia Future Forward conference in Singapore, referring to the city-state by one of its nicknames. "In this huge time of volatility, 'boring' is not bad, right?" The investing and business climate worldwide has been upended by everything from trade wars and El Niño-related weather issues to the Iran conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war. Singapore, with its AAA-rated debt, stable political environment and position at the heart of Asia, is seen by many as a bastion of stability. Tan said similar characteristics define DBS. DBS has "one of the safest credit ratings in the world," she told CNBC in an interview on the sidelines of the conference. Temasek, the state-owned global investment company that managed assets worth 518 billion Singapore dollars ($404 billion) as of March 31 and is seen as contributing to Singapore's fiscal stability, is DBS's biggest shareholder. DBS is also in a strong position to navigate the economic uncertainty around the world, Tan said. "Trade and supply chains are all fragmented," she said. "If you need to diversify your upstream supply chain, just because you're worried about geopolitics, because you're worried about blockages, because you're worried about the war and the Strait of Hormuz, DBS is a partner to help you ... We can help our customers pivot from one market to another quite quickly." Tan also addressed management of a workforce in the age of artificial intelligence, and how to find people who have the right skills to navigate the technology. "Humans intrinsically are nimble and agile ... I tell all my managers, hire for attitude – because you know you can't buy attitude, you can't train attitude." —CNBC's Ying Shan Lee contributed to this article.

events.title: Singapore PM Wong rejects weaker currency as shortcut to competitiveness
events.summary: Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong pushed back against the idea of weakening the Singapore dollar to boost competitiveness. He said the city-state must instead rely on its economic strengths even as a strong currency adds to costs for businesses. SINGAPORE — Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong pushed back against the idea of weakening the Singapore dollar to boost competitiveness, saying the city-state must instead rely on its economic strengths even as a strong currency adds to costs for businesses. Wong said Singapore could continue to expect a strong and stable currency if its economy performs well, emphasizing its role in containing imported inflation. "You're surely not suggesting that we depress our exchange rate in order to be more competitive," Wong said in a lighthearted exchange with DBS CEO Tan Su Shan at the bank's Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday. His remarks came after Tan highlighted Singapore's reputation as a safe haven, which has helped attract capital and support the local currency, while acknowledging that the city-state remains a relatively expensive place to do business. "The MAS will exercise monetary policy independently. The Singapore dollar will reflect our economic fundamentals, and if the economy does well, then we can continue to expect a strong, stable Sing dollar that is anchored on fundamentals and will also help keep imported inflation down," Wong said. Unlike most major central banks, which primarily use interest rates to manage monetary conditions, the Monetary Authority of Singapore conducts policy through the exchange rate. It manages the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies belonging to the country's major trading partners, allowing the exchange rate to fluctuate within an undisclosed policy band. The approach reflects Singapore's heavy dependence on international trade and imports, making currency movements particularly important for domestic prices. A stronger Singapore dollar helps cushion the cost of imported goods and services, particularly during periods of elevated global inflation. But it can also make Singapore-produced goods and services more expensive for overseas buyers, adding pressure on exporters. The Singapore dollar has strengthened almost 0.4% against the greenback since the start of the year. Wong acknowledged those trade-offs, saying businesses would have to account for currency strength alongside Singapore's other operating costs. "Companies that seek to export will have to factor that into the cost of doing business, together with the other costs that they experience in Singapore, as we all know, we are certainly not the cheapest location in Southeast Asia," he said. Still, Wong argued that competing on price alone was not a viable strategy for Singapore, which must instead differentiate itself through its capabilities, stability and predictability. "Companies are not looking for the cheapest locations," he said. "They are looking for capabilities. They are looking for stability. They are looking for predictability." Wong also said Singapore could not compete on cost alone, and was instead developing broader industrial ecosystems linking multinational corporations, domestic suppliers, research capabilities and skilled workers. Singapore's competitiveness ultimately depended on the value it offered businesses rather than its relative cost advantage, he added. "We have to again play to our strengths and compete on the basis of the value we bring to the table," he said.

CINCINNATI, Ohio – Kroger plans to cut roughly 3,000 corporate roles over the next three years, chief executive Greg Foran told staff in a memo, seen by Reuters on Oct 12, as the grocer integrates artificial intelligence into its workflow. Kroger should reduce duplicative work and adapt with technology, Foran wrote in the memo, adding that the job cuts would help the company cut prices and invest in in-store employees. Foran took over as Kroger’s CEO in February. Companies have been rethinking corporate structures and cutting jobs as they increasingly turn to AI to streamline workflows and divert more resources towards the technology, fuelling concerns over widespread disruption across sectors. In September, the company outlined the company’s AI strategy, including the use of models to manage workflows and leverage customer data to power tools such as its AI shopping assistant. The grocery retailer had also lowered its annual identical sales target and said it is seeking to cut prices to better compete with rivals such as Walmart and Aldi as consumers grow more frugal under pressure from high gas prices. Details on the job cuts, which would affect about 37% of its 8,200 corporate employees, would be shared in the coming months, Foran said in the memo. events.title: GM CEO: We're making leaps and bounds toward 'eyes-off, hands-off' driving
events.summary: General Motors CEO Mary Barra said the automaker is still on track to introduce "eyes-off, hands-off" driving technology by 2028, starting with the electric Cadillac Escalade IQ. After exiting its Cruise robotaxi business, GM is focusing on autonomous technology for personal vehicles. General Motors CEO Mary Barra said Monday that the automaker remains on track to introduce "eyes-off, hands-off" driving technology by 2028. GM announced last October that it plans to launch its next-generation driver-assistance system in the electric Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028 before expanding to other models. Unlike the company's existing Super Cruise system, which allows drivers to take their hands off the wheel but requires them to remain attentive, the new technology is designed to let drivers take their eyes off the road under certain conditions. Barra told CNBC's Jim Cramer on " Mad Money " that she recently tested the technology and was impressed by how much it had improved since an earlier ride in March. "They're making so much progress on our goal to have eyes off, hands off in the '28 time frame," the CEO said. "We're going to be well positioned from a personal autonomy perspective." She added, "When people want to drive, they can. When they don't, they won't need to as that grows." GM's push into personal autonomous driving follows its decision to exit its Cruise robotaxi business in December 2024 after spending more than $10 billion. Rather than compete in the increasingly crowded driverless ride-hailing market, the automaker redirected its resources toward developing autonomous systems for vehicles consumers own. "We're not in the taxi business. We're not in the bus business," Barra said. She acknowledged that exiting the robotaxi market was difficult but defended the move, noting that GM retained much of the Cruise team to work on personal autonomous driving. "It was a tough decision, but I think it was the right decision," she said. Barra also pushed back against the idea that widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles could eventually reduce the need for personal car ownership. She recalled earlier predictions that ride-hailing services such as Uber and Lyft would sharply reduce vehicle sales, something that never materialized because "people still value that it's in my driveway. events.title: Top execs say the $124 trillion Great Wealth Transfer, women entrepreneurs, and veterans are poised to remake the financial landscape
events.summary: The landscape for money is shifting, and top executives say that the Great Wealth Transfer, the new generation of entrepreneurs, and veterans are paving the way. At Fortune ’s 26th annual Most Powerful Women conference in Santa Barbara, Deloitte U.S. federal health sector leader Beth Meagher said that women are poised to play a huge role in shaping how wealth is invested and deployed. It’s estimated that around $124 trillion in wealth will be passed down by 2048, according to Cerulli Associates, with $54 trillion going to women, $52 trillion to children, and $18 trillion charity. On top of that, women entrepreneurs are on the come-up—Meagher said that they’re one of the fastest growing sources of wealth concentration, up over 125% over the past decade. And women who have served our country are also building momentum, reaching roughly 300% growth over the past couple of years, the Deloitte exec pointed out. “These trends are changing everything,” Meagher told Fortune executive editorial director Diane Brady onstage. “I think we spend a lot of time on frontier models, and we probably spend a lot of time on geopolitical [issues]. And this shift is something that I think we have a tremendous opportunity to lead from the front of.” Seema Hingorani, managing director and senior client advisor at Morgan Stanley , caught wind of this trend more than a decade ago. When she was working at the New York City Pension Fund in the early 2010s, she noticed something worrying. Every asset manager in the world was coming to meet with her, yet each had few to no women on their investment teams, Hingorani said. They wrote it off as a “pipeline issue”—but Hingorani didn’t buy it. So she started a nonprofit called Girls Who Invest to get more women into the industry, with 5,000 college women having gone through the program since 2011. Every year they receive around 4,000 applications, and support 700 women annually. Hingorani also pointed out that for the past seven years, Morgan Stanley has run an incubator helping to invest in more women starting tech businesses. And when they scale billion-dollar companies and take their successes to the bank, they’ll be looking for women to help guide their decisions. “[Women are] going to have all the wealth,” Hingorani said. “[For] those women—you guys—do you want to have a male financial advisor? If you had a choice, would you want to have a woman financial advisor? A lot of firms out there are hiring all my women, because they get it.” Beyond how they manage their wealth, women are also setting new expectations about spending it. Carmen James Randolph, founding president and CEO of the Women’s Foundation of the South, is seeing a major shift in her own backyard. Randolph said that the South is one of the fastest-growing regions in the country, and with 41.5% of America’s women of color as the area’s constituents, there’s a new frontier for wealth creation and investment. She’s already seeing that the old-school models of philanthropy are being rewritten to prioritize tangible impact. “I’ve worked in philanthropy now for about 28 years, and I understand that at its best, philanthropy can be a catalyst for what’s possible. Old models see philanthropy as charity, and new wealth recipients do not see philanthropy as charity,” Randolph explained onstage. “They want to understand and see firsthand the impact that their dollars can have.” The Deloitte and Morgan Stanley execs agree that the way women want to invest is different from previous generations, by prioritizing social impact in tandem with financial returns. Meagher said that women poised to inherit substantial wealth are focused on three key areas of investment: health, education, and justice. She’s picked up on a trend where wealth advisors are also specifically offering health services; and Randolph says that her foundation is making a big bet on improving maternal healthcare in southern states with difficult access to emergency and routine medical care. Hingorani also noted that every trustee has an interest in affordable housing—even if it means a smaller return than what they could earn at a venture fund. “Women are looking to pull their investments so that they can have an outsized impact,” Meagher said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: ‘If you take your foot off the pedal at all, you will start to stall’: Women in C-suite roles have stagnated, and the reasons go beyond the pipeline
events.summary: The rate of women being promoted into senior executive roles is slowing down, and experts warn a shaky labor climate and dearth of professional infrastructure are further exacerbating an already obstruction-filled pipeline for women to become CEOs. At Fortune ‘s Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara, California on Monday, Kelly Baker, executive vice president and chief human resource officer at financial services firm Thrivent, explained that there has been less of a focus on developing and recruiting women to join executive leadership. The slowdown is a byproduct of a frenetic environment that has deprioritized cultivating these leaders. “I don’t think we can ignore the fact that there is a climate where organizations aren’t quite as focused,” Baker told Fortune Leadership Editor Claire Zillman. “If you take your foot off the pedal at all, you will start to stall.” The Fortune 500 has 56 companies led by women, or about 11.2% of the list, up from 7.4% six years ago. However, women’s share of roles in both the C-suite and at the board level has stalled at about 30%, marking the first decline in women’s board representation in more than a decade. Toni Townes-Whitley, a former Fortune 500 CEO and Nasdaq corporate board member, suggested fewer discussions about workplace diversity has led to less of a spotlight on promoting and developing women leaders, and in an attitude shift toward women’s capabilities. “We can’t take away an environment where there is a question, almost a recalibration of women in the world, where unfortunately negative rhetoric from lots of different dimensions have women being challenged externally, internally, by the boards,” Townes-Whitley said at the summit. “That’s a concern, underlined, that’s just not talked about.” To be sure, problems in getting across the last mile before taking the helm of companies are persistent, and are also, in part, a result of women not viewing themselves as leaders. That’s despite having skillsets and experience that would qualify them for these roles. Only 36% of women in the workplace have considered becoming a CEO or said they wanted to be a CEO, according to Jenna Fisher, managing director of global leadership advisory firm Russell Reynolds Associates: “We can’t 3D print our candidates.” Hayden Brown, president and CEO of freelance marketplace platform Upwork, was one of those women who didn’t consider taking on the role of top brass, despite her mother running the women’s empowerment program at her workplace.   “I grew up in like the most pro-women household, and yet it took our board chair,, probably 10 years ago, to say to me, ‘You should be a CEO,’” Brown told Zillman. “And I was like, ‘Really?’” Brown has worked to change how women view themselves in relation to leadership roles in her own home, editing the books she reads with her children to be more gender inclusive, or to switch out adjectives like “smart” to “hard-working” to guide them toward the traits she wants them to embody. But making larger changes in the workplace will also require the awareness and backing of men, Baker said. Those in influential senior positions in the office, particularly men, will have to serve as both mentors, who support women through their careers, as well as sponsors, who advocate for high-potential women leaders in front of coworkers and other leaders. While creating systems to reinforce women’s leadership pipelines are perhaps not being discussed or strengthened as much today, there’s some good news, according to Fisher: AI has created pressure to have leaders who are adaptable and fluent in emerging technologies. Russell Reynolds Associates research indicates women are ahead of men in AI adoption and implementation, perhaps because of a willingness to adapt. “Even though DEI is not being talked about as much as it used to be,” Fisher said, “there is still so much demand for women in executive roles and board roles.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Houthi missile attack targets Saudi capital Riyadh for third day in a row
events.summary: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted a ballistic missile fired towards Riyadh, as Houthis say they targeted the King Khalid airport. Houthi missile attack on Riyadh airport: Saudi Arabia vows resilience The Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting in Yemen has said its forces intercepted another ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as the city reels from attacks that have killed at least 14 people in recent days. In a statement on X, Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the coalition, said the Houthis fired one ballistic missile at Riyadh and two towards Khamis Mushait, a city in the southwest. list 1 of 4 Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz list 2 of 4 Why are the Houthis striking Saudi airports? list 3 of 4 Giants Brigades lead southern Yemen fightback against the Houthis list 4 of 4 ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil? All three were “intercepted and destroyed”, he said. Residents of Riyadh reported several powerful explosions on Monday night, moments after a text message to their phones warned of an aerial threat. The Houthis, who control Yemen’s most populous areas, including the capital, Sanaa, said their target in Riyadh had been King Khalid International airport. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the group had also sent a drone towards a military airbase at Khamis Mushait, near the Yemeni border. He again warned international airlines and travellers “against operating flights to airports” in Saudi Arabia, except in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, saying the facilities were “unsafe”. The renewed attacks came as King Khalid International airport in Riyadh remains closed after a Houthi attack on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others. Another strike on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11. Saudi authorities said the airport would remain closed until this Saturday, and airlines have canceled flights. The Houthis have also struck Saudi oil facilities. The attacks come as the Houthis fight forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government for control of the country. The Saudi-led coalition has carried out an air campaign against the Houthis and backed the government’s ground forces. The fighting erupted amid regional tensions set off by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran. Speaking at an energy conference in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud said the attacks on airports over the last week have tested the kingdom’s resilience. “The events of recent weeks are serious,” the minister said. “Our response must be equally serious.” He added that Vision 2030, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plan to diversify the Saudi economy, “must continue. Investment must continue”. Saudi authorities have meanwhile opened an investigation into why the country’s air defences failed to stop the barrage, according to two regional officials who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity. An initial inquiry found that the Houthis first launched several drones to clear a path for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles, which then reached the airport, the officials said. The Houthis possess ballistic missiles with warheads that can change direction in flight, posing a challenge to the Patriot interceptors and other systems the Saudis rely on. One official told AP that investigators also wanted to know why the defences had not given earlier warning of an attack in which missiles and drones flew more than 1,000km, or 620 miles, to reach Riyadh. US President Donald Trump separately criticised the Houthis but gave no indication that Washington would intervene. “Well, the Houthis are misbehaving very badly. No good,” he told reporters when asked what he planned to do about the group. A Houthi official warned that US involvement would bring retaliation. “If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told the AFP news agency. Al-Bukhaiti also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”. The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme. The United Arab Emirates’s national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Monday that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week. It also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah. Bahrain’s national carrier Gulf Air said it, too, was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Saturday.

events.title: Scoop: Top Trump operative enlisted to rescue Kansas senator's campaign
events.summary: A top Trump political operative has been tapped to help boost Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall 's campaign in the weeks before the Nov. 3 election, the latest sign of how Republicans are scrambling to defend the red-state seat. Why it matters: The hiring of veteran strategist Chris Grant reflects the GOP's growing anxiety over Kansas' Senate race. Marshall is running neck and neck with Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state President Trump won by 16 points in 2024. Republicans fear losing Kansas could be a domino in costing them their Senate majority. Driving the news: GOP operatives have become increasingly frustrated with Marshall's reelection campaign, which they believe hasn't been aggressive enough at a time when soaring fuel prices have particularly hurt farmers in Kansas and elsewhere in the Midwest. Grant, who helped lead the main pro-Trump super PAC in 2024 and has remained involved in Trump's political operation, will be a senior adviser to Marshall and help guide strategy in the final three weeks. Grant also worked on Marshall's 2020 Senate campaign. What they're saying: "Chris is an absolute pro who has been a longtime friend to Team Marshall. Having him help land the plane these last three weeks is a no brainer," Brent Robertson, Marshall's chief of staff, told Axios. Zoom in: Two GOP outside groups — the Senate Leadership Fund and Club for Growth — are pouring millions into the Kansas race. SLF, the principal super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, is spending $14 million in Kansas after shifting resources from the Senate race in North Carolina, where Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper has a significant polling lead over former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley. Trump said in a social media post Monday that he would campaign for Marshall "very soon." A Democrat-aligned super PAC has announced plans to spend $5 million to help Hamilton. Between the lines: Marshall has faced damaging headlines recently, including a New York Times r eport that his medical practice sued more than 700 former patients over unpaid medical bills, and that 81 were later arrested for missing court appearances. The other side: Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, has won endorsements from two former Republican governors in Kansas, Mike Hayden and Bill Graves.

events.title: Publicly owned rail is popular. But is it making the trains run on time?
events.summary: The early afternoon of Wednesday 6 August was an unremarkable one on the rail network. Then suddenly, shortly before 14:00, a power failure brought trains across the north-west of England to a halt. Chaos ensued: passengers told the BBC they were stranded on platforms for hours, with some having to book hotels for the night. This incident, stemming from a short power cut that affected Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester, was, in itself, unusual. But it added to a difficult summer for train passengers. Repeated heatwaves required risk control measures like speed reductions to avoid tracks being damaged in the heat, leading to delays and cancellations. There was a serious derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, and another smaller-scale incident near Wickford in Essex soon after. Against a backdrop of relatively high cancellation rates and steep fares compared with previous decades, rail users could be forgiven for forming the impression that things are not working. Something is changing, though: Labour is steadily bringing nearly all passenger rail services into public hands. Nationalisation is a popular idea - a YouGov tracker poll suggests almost two thirds of the public support public ownership. August's 90-second power outage sparked chaos for rail commuters But in reality, plans are still in their early stages. Big structural changes have yet to be introduced. And experts caution that it's too early to say how successful these will be. So can rail nationalisation meet the public's expectations? Or are the ongoing delays and cancellations that we're currently seeing under a part-nationalised network a sign that it might struggle to deliver real improvement? South Western Railway (SWR) was nationalised in May 2025, the first of six services to be brought into public ownership under Labour so far. At Woking station, which is served by SWR, regular commuter Leo tells me he had been optimistic about public ownership, but hasn't noticed it making any difference so far: "I think the phrase 'emperor's new clothes' comes to mind… it's still unreliable." SWR saw a clear increase in cancellations during its first year in public hands. But how much of this was due to nationalisation? The Conservatives have cited SWR as an example of how public control does not necessarily mean improvements or fix key problems. But the government argues SWR's early period in public hands was affected by high summer temperatures, signal failures and trespass incidents. Lord Hendy, the rail minister, says work to turn the operator around has included introducing long-delayed new trains on suburban routes and recruiting more drivers, resulting in a drop in those cancellations that are due to staff shortages. TransPennine Express was nationalised in May 2023, under the Conservative government. Many passengers had been at their wits' end as the operator struggled to fulfil its timetable and suffered from poor industrial relations. A plan to improve reliability was put in place, which included cutting some services and even removing one type of train as a way of sorting out staffing problems. A new deal with the drivers' union also helped - something an insider at the former private sector operator claimed to me their company had not been permitted to do. So has it worked? Cancellations have fallen noticeably. But they were still above the Great Britain average in the year to August. It's really important to say the data can only tell us so much. There are so many different factors that might affect the performance of each service: for example, the state of the infrastructure it relies on, weather events or simply how well it was working before the government took over. Plus, of the operators nationalised since Labour came to power, only SWR and c2c have completed a whole year in public hands. Even for those nationalised years earlier, the picture is clouded by the impact of the pandemic, when passenger numbers fell off a cliff. But according to Alex Hynes, chief executive of DfT Operator Limited (DfTO), the government company that currently owns publicly-run operators, it has been possible to make some short-term changes. Notably, these include making one team jointly responsible for managing infrastructure and passenger train services in some areas including the south-west of England. "The railway is a system: track, train, people," he says. "So by putting one person in charge, they can fix all elements of the system to deliver a better service to customers." Hynes also gives examples of changes on the recently nationalised Thameslink; investment in better cleaning, improving toilets and replacing unpopular upright "ironing-board" seats. But when it comes to the pure performance data of operators nationalised in the past few years - delays, cancellations - can we really draw any conclusions yet to tell us whether the policy is working?

events.title: What we know about Lady Violet Bridgerton ahead of Netflix spin-off
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Netflix has announced a Bridgerton spin-off focusing on Lady Violet. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) This article contains spoilers from seasons one to four of Bridgerton. In previous seasons of the Netflix and Shondaland series Bridgerton, Lady Violet has expressed a great affection for her late husband Viscount Edmund Bridgerton. She experienced intense heartbreak and sorrow when he died. Now, fans of the television show will get to see their love story. In the same way Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story delved into the early life of Queen Charlotte, a yet untitled series will chronicle the early life of a young Lady Violet. It promises to tell the story of Violet's romance with Edmund (Rupert Evans). There have been two actors so far who have taken on the role of Lady Violet. Ruth Gemmell plays her in the main series and appeared in the Queen Charlotte spin-off, in which Connie Jenkins-Greig played a younger version in flashbacks as a then Violet Ledger. Lady Violet is depicted in Bridgerton as a kind, warm and wise matriarch with the interests of her family at heart. As we gear up for the spin-off, here's a trip down memory lane exploring some of what we already know about Lady Violet and her relationship with Lord Bridgerton. Violet Bridgerton (née Ledger) holds the title the Dowager Viscountess Bridgerton. Lady Violet is the family's matriarch and has eight children. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) A Dowager Viscountess is the widowed wife of a viscount who retains her aristocratic rank after her husband's death. Violet was pregnant with Lord Bridgerton's eighth child Hyacinth when he died from anaphylaxis. He'd suffered a severe allergic reaction after being stung by a bee. He was in his late 30s at the time. He'd been out hunting with eldest son Anthony and was picking hyacinths for his wife when it happened. In a conversation with Anthony in season two, episode eight of Bridgerton, titled The Viscount Who Loved Me, Violet tells her son she would go through the pain of losing her husband again because the beauty of love overpowers the risk of grief. "Losing Edmund was the most difficult time of my life," Violet said. "And the pain that I felt … beyond description. "But there is one thing that has given me at least some modicum of solace. "It's knowing that I would still choose the life I led with him, each and every time. "And I would undoubtedly feel the same pain I felt all over again if I had to because real, true love is worth it no matter what." Lady Violet is close friends with Lady Danbury (right). ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) Violet is keen to see each of her eight children marry, but she wants them, too, to experience true love, rather than marry for the sake of it. While no marriage is perfect, the union between Violet and Edmund is so idealised that each of her children aspire to live a similar fairytale. In season one, episode eight called After the Rain, Violet points out to her daughter Daphne that marriage is hard, and the reason why hers worked was because they chose to love each other through each obstacle. "It is a rarity, I have come to realise," Violet said. "That is not to say it was without its trials. "Your father and I faced many difficulties, indeed, but we overcame them. "We made a decision early on to do so. "We chose to love each other every single day. "It is a choice, dearest, one that is never too late to make." Lady Violet remains devoted to her late husband throughout the first few seasons of the television series. Lady Violet develops feelings for Lord Marcus Anderson, but not enough to marry him. ( Supplied: Netflix/Liam Daniel ) That is, until Lord Marcus Anderson (Daniel Francis) catches her eye. He is Lady Agatha Danbury's (Adjoa Andoh) younger brother, and they meet in season three of Bridgerton. In season four, they kick it up a notch into a steamy, passionate, but secret dalliance. Finally, Violet is exploring her own desires after mostly focusing her efforts on matchmaking her children. Lord Marcus wants to marry her, but the "not yet" response to his offer of engagement turns into a "not ever" in his eyes. With Queen Charlotte being as juicy as it was stunningly heartbreaking, this author cannot wait for the Lady Violet spin-off, dearest gentle reader. The spin-off will be written by showrunners and executive producers Shonda Rhimes and Nicholas Nardini. Bridgerton is based on the popular historical romance novels written by Julia Quinn. events.title: Elon Musk takes a dig at Waymo's pet collision history and says Tesla Robotaxi has a solution
events.summary: Elon Musk said Waymo's robotaxis are "pet destroyers." PATRICK PLEUL/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Waymo has previously caught flak for its robotaxis colliding with stray animals. Elon Musk took jabs at Waymo, calling the robotaxis "pet destroyers." Musk said Tesla gave itself challenges to solve the problem of robotaxis running over animals. Elon Musk took a dig at his robotaxi rival, Waymo , calling the vehicles "pet destroyers," and said Tesla Robotaxi has solved the issue of avoiding stray pets. During a livestreamed interview at an event hosted by Tesla Owners of Silicon Valley on Saturday, Musk called out Waymo for its reported collisions with animals. "What a lot of people don't know is that Waymos are like pet destroyers," Musk said, laughing. "Well, maybe Waymo's made some improvements on that front, but they do run over a lot of pets, and we don't want to run over pets." Waymo has gotten flak over animal collisions before, most notably after its run-in with a beloved bodega cat in a San Francisco neighborhood back in October 2025. The feline, named KitKat, died after it was run over by Waymo's rear right tire, video obtained by The New York Times showed. That is not Waymo's first collision with an animal. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Standing General Order requires autonomous vehicle companies like Waymo to report qualifying crashes. NHTSA data showed that between July 2025 and July 2026, Waymo reported at least 9 crashes involving animals, 6 of which Waymo described as domestic animals. A Waymo spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. Tesla's robotaxi service also reported a collision involving an animal during the same time period, but the incident involved a supervised robotaxi. Tesla also operated a smaller fleet, and most of its unsupervised operations were concentrated in one city: Austin. Musk said during the virtual interview that Tesla Robotaxi will be able to detect roaming pets at night. "We have these challenges of literally like: gray kittens on a gray tarmac with tar seams at night in low visibility. And it's like, 'Can we not run over the kittens,' type of thing," he said. Musk added that Tesla will deploy the update, though he did not specify when. Have a tip on Tesla or Waymo? Contact this reporter via email at lloydlee@businessinsider.com or Signal at lloydlee.71. events.title: Two deaths reported as Hurricane Simon, storm Rachel batter Mexico’s coast
events.summary: Simon caps a Pacific season of record-breaking intensity, as deadly storms wreak havoc from Hawaii to Mexico. At least two people have died in Mexico after Hurricane Simon and former tropical storm Rachel brought torrential rain and catastrophic flooding to Pacific coast communities. At a Monday news briefing, Guerrero Governor Evelyn Salgado confirmed that a 71-year-old man had died during Hurricane Simon after a retaining wall collapsed under the weight of intense precipitation. list 1 of 3 Hurricane Isaias: Four dead and thousands without power in US Southeast list 2 of 3 Isaias weakens after making landfall in US Gulf Coast as hurricane list 3 of 3 Hurricane Isaias leaves trail of destruction across the US Gulf Coast According to the Guerrero-based news agency IRZA, the man, identified by his family as Albino Moreno Jimenez, had been feeding his animals on the western outskirts of Chilpancingo when a wall came crashing down on him. A second death was announced later in the day in the state of Baja California along Mexico’s western coast. There, Governor Marina del Pilar said that a young girl had died from the effects of what was once Hurricane Rachel, which peaked in early October as a Category 3 storm. At least 10 more people remain missing in Baja California, according to the governor. Eight were reported missing in the city of Ensenada, on the Pacific coast, and two in the fishing town of San Felipe on the Gulf of California. The figures remain preliminary, with local newspaper La Jornada reporting a higher death toll of two in Baja California and 11 missing. Rachel made landfall in the Mexican state as a post-tropical cyclone, and its remnants have travelled north through southern California in the southwestern United States. Hurricane Simon, meanwhile, has churned off the coast of Mexico since the weekend. By late Monday morning, it had weakened from a powerful Category 4 storm to a Category 2. Its maximum sustained winds had slowed slightly to around 155km/h (100mph), according to the US National Hurricane Center. Its centre was about 115km west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, a cape in the state of Jalisco, drifting west at 3km/h. Forecasters predict Simon could make landfall on Thursday or Friday. Hurricane warnings remain in effect for western Mexico, which is vulnerable to landslides and deadly surf conditions as a result of the storm. Experts warn the death toll from both storms could rise, and officials have called on residents to exercise caution amid the devastation wrought by downed trees, high winds and floodwaters. The Spanish newspaper El Pais reported the death of a cliff diver, Juan Patines, who was killed in Mazatlan, the northwestern state of Sinaloa, after jumping into the sea on Saturday night. According to Mexican media, the heavy surf hampered his efforts to return to shore amid dangerous coastal conditions associated with Hurricane Simon. Local authorities later halted cliff-diving at the site due to hazardous sea conditions. Officials have yet to confirm whether his death was directly linked to Hurricane Simon. Rachel and Simon have battered Mexico’s western coast as part of an extraordinary stretch of hurricane activity across the Pacific. The northeastern and central Pacific Ocean has experienced a record storm season this year, fuelled in part by the El Nino weather phenomenon, which results in warming waters in parts of the region. Twenty-one named storms have been recorded in the Pacific so far. On Sunday, Simon tipped the region to a historic high for accumulated cyclone energy (ACE), a metric of the combined strength and longevity of tropical storms. This year has already surpassed the previous high set in 2018. The US island chain of Hawaii has been among the hardest-hit places. In August, Hurricane Lala unleashed ruinous flooding on Hawaii’s Big Island as a Category 1 storm, killing a 93-year-old woman and destroying some 100 homes, according to state officials. A few weeks later, Hurricane Lowell , a Category 4 hurricane at its peak, struck the Hawaiian islands of Kauai and Niihau, where powerful winds, storm surge and flooding overwhelmed towns and roads. Roughly 90 percent of Kauai’s power customers were plunged into darkness as a result of electricity outages. At least two deaths were linked to Lowell. In late September, Hurricane Nolo brought another round of flooding and landslides to the Hawaiian islands, though it did not make landfall.
