events.title: US archbishop says Catholics in army should not participate in firing squad
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Archbishop Timothy Broglio says the US plan to livestream the execution of the Fort Hood attacker is contrary to church’s teachings. United States Archbishop Timothy Broglio has urged Catholics who are members of the country’s armed forces not to take part in a planned public execution by firing squad, saying that it violates the teachings of the church. Broglio released a strongly worded statement on Monday raising a series of concerns about the US military’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army major who killed 13 people during a shooting attack at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. list 1 of 3 ‘Barbaric’: US lawmakers condemn plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution list 2 of 3 Pope says death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as US plans to livestream execution list 3 of 3 Christa Pike case underscores prevalence of botched executions in US “I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” Broglio said. He also asked whether the US wants to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries”. The plan to livestream the execution on December 3 was announced last week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who characterised the spectacle as deterrence. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told the right-wing media outlet Real America’s Voice. But the proposal has sparked backlash from lawmakers , rights groups and critics who warn that a publicly broadcast killing is not only unethical but could also be used as anti-US propaganda. Hasan, now aged 56, was shot by the police during the 2009 Fort Hood attack and is now wheelchair-bound. Critics fear livestreaming Hasan’s death could turn him into a symbol for armed groups that may be hostile to the US. Cardinal Blase J Cupich, the archbishop of Chicago, also condemned the plan to livestream the execution in a social media post on Monday, questioning the example it could set for children. “Capital punishment is unacceptable in any case,” he said. “The planned broadcast of the taking of a life by firing squad is nothing short of performative barbarism. Do we really want our children, who will inevitably view it, exposed to the pornography of a state-sponsored slaying?” Hegseth has said he wants the execution to take place at the same time and location as the 2009 shooting spree, and described using military members to carry out the death penalty. “It hadn’t been since World War II since we’ve done that,” Hegseth said of the firing squad. “Well, I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win.” The last US military execution by firing squad was of Eddie Slovik, who was accused of desertion in 1945. He was the only US soldier to have such a sentence carried out for abandoning his post. In Monday’s statement, Broglio also questioned the reasoning behind putting service members on camera to carry out Hasan’s death. He hinted that it could harm the US military’s image abroad. “The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio wrote. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheel chair to the whole world?” Without mentioning Hasan’s case specifically, Pope Leo also released a statement on Saturday condemning the death penalty. “The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” he said in a social media post. “The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.” President Donald Trump , who oversaw an unprecedented spike in federal executions during his first term in office, has approved Hasan’s execution. Still, on Saturday, he indicated that he has not decided whether to proceed with a livestream. “There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters. “I’ll make a decision.” Since the start of his second term as president, Trump has pushed for the increased use of the federal death penalty. In April, he also approved additional methods to carry out the death penalty, including the firing squad. In the past, Trump has also floated the death penalty as a punishment for crimes ranging from drug dealing to sedition, a term he has invoked against political rivals .

events.title: Heating oil customers face tough winter despite shake-up promise
events.summary: Heating oil customers facing soaring bills have been promised better regulation of the sector by the government. Ministers say they will tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed. With prices close to having doubled in the past year, some campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from the same cap as regular, variable gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales. But there is no sign of the government proposing such a change, nor when the stricter rules will take effect. Ministers said they would work with industry to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition". In the meantime, oil users have been offered discounts on heat pumps, a code of practice is in place, and industry practices setting minimum order volumes at 500 litres for some consumers will be reviewed. Domestic tanks typically hold between 1,000 and 2,000 litres. The government said this had left some people having to pay for more heating oil than they might need. Buy now or wait and hope? Families face gamble on heating oil Published 10 September Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil. The funding is distributed by local authorities, which set their own criteria for eligibility. A subsequent inquiry by the UK's competition watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority, found that 1,700 households were forced to "re-order at significantly higher prices or go without fuel" after the war broke out, costing them up to £350. But those whose orders were cancelled and prices raised were told they were entitled to compensation. The government has now announced it will accept the CMA's recommendation to strengthen regulation in the sector. Energy minister Polly Billington said: "Thousands of heating oil customers felt they had nowhere to turn when they paid the price of rising oil and gas costs earlier this year. "We won't accept that. Energy is an essential good and people should not have to think twice about whether they're protected in the market. That's why we will reform the sector." Nick, a heating oil customer from West Suffolk, told the BBC's Your Voice that "off-grid households remain a major policy blind spot" for the government. "Any protection from UK government for domestic heating oil users will be very welcome, providing this is for all domestic heating oil users," the 28-year-old said. He rents a three-bedroom home with his partner. He said they had seen prices more than double in a year, to quotes of 111p per litre. "Heating my home is now no longer another household bill, but almost an investment," he said. He called on tax cuts for customers, or the extension of the price cap to heating oil - a demand also made by charity National Energy Action. Tim Buckman, chief executive of price comparison site Boiler Juice, told the BBC he wants stronger protections for consumers but the main problem was that heating oil is twice as expensive as it was before the war. "Just putting regulation in place is not going to reduce the price for customers. What we would like to see is the VAT off heating oil or targeting that specifically." Some 1.5 million households depend on heating oil, but they do not have the same consumer protections as electricity and gas customers. However, energy regulator Ofgem, which sets the cap for standard variable tariffs, only covers England, Wales and Scotland. Most heating oil customers are in Northern Ireland, where 60% of households rely on it, but where regulation is separate. It is likely Ofgem will regulate heating oil in England, Scotland and Wales, and the UK government said it would "engage with the Northern Ireland Executive as they consider these recommendations in parallel". events.title: I earn £120,000 a year making social media videos go viral
events.summary: Eknoor Singh's successful social media video clips include one of popstar Dua Lipa Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year. The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral. "The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says. The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first. He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms. The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible. With clippers able to earn up to $3 (£2.30) per 1,000 views across platforms, it can be very lucrative if a particular clip does take off. Singh says he got hooked on clipping last year when he made $300 from posting a short video of popstar Dua Lipa on Instagram. "I was like, 'OK, this is a lot of money for simply posting a video.' I instantly knew how lucrative it could be." Now he says he is earning "at least £10,000 a month". He adds that he looks for clips that are funny, quick to watch and engaging, such as a short video he made in May of Sabrina Carpenter's reaction to having the tails of her dress stepped on at the Met Gala in New York. Singh did not reveal who the client was. Singh's clip of Sabrina Carpenter went viral For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping. He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests. Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says. Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says. Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world". Ethan Weems says the income helps him continue to work from home Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed. These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick. The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max. For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs. That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos. In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips. "The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions". Eknoor Singh says he can make clips anywhere with just his mobile and a good internet connection Evan Stanfield, the founder and boss of Clipping Culture, is himself just 21. He set up the business last year after dropping out of the University of Kansas. Stanfield says that the website connects brands to more than 340,000 clippers from all over the world. He has a simple theory for the popularity of short videos: "People's attention spans are getting shorter and shorter." He adds that making the clips is a young person's game because "they're most of the consumers of short-form videos". Back in London, Eknoor Singh says he is "kind of clipping non-stop", wherever he is. "I could be anywhere. I could go on holiday and make money." I paid £30,000 for an 'influencer' degree.

events.title: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: How a gold-buying spree helps the yuan go global
events.summary: China has increased its gold purchases every month for nearly two years. The stockpiling comes as Hong Kong plans to become a global gold trading hub, with support for yuan-denominated transactions. It's the latest sign of diversification away from the U.S. dollar. Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses. Buying gold every month for nearly two years is just part of China's plan to narrow a gap with the U.S. on holdings of the precious metal. What does that do to the yuan? China's decades-long push for yuan internationalization is getting a lift from the buildout of Hong Kong as a gold trading center — denominated in the Chinese currency. "As those trading volumes grow, there would be a growing volume of the physical gold trade that is denominated in RMB and not linked in USD," said Charles Chang, managing director and Greater China country lead for corporate ratings at S&P Global Ratings. The Chinese yuan, also known as the renminbi, accounts for a fraction of international transactions in a global financial system dominated by the U.S. dollar. Analysts I spoke with don't expect major changes to that dynamic anytime soon, but Beijing's gold purchases and Hong Kong trading platform are just the latest steps toward supporting greater use of the yuan globally. "The challenge with internationalizing the RMB it's somewhat more challenging to find places where you can use the RMB," Chang said. "In terms of gold particularly, if the RMB that the buyer receives can be converted to gold, then it gives more channels for the spending to be done." Hong Kong, home to one of the world's largest stock exchanges, last month confirmed its efforts to develop a yuan-denominated gold market . In a major move last year, the special administrative region of China linked its gold vault with one in Shanghai , allowing physical gold delivery to international institutions in Hong Kong denominated in yuan. Over the next three years, Hong Kong plans to expand the capacity of its Shanghai-linked gold vault from 150 tonnes to over 2,000 tonnes , S&P's Chang pointed out. That's nearly as large as all the gold reserves in China , he added. "If Hong Kong is able to complete this transaction, then it would become of the largest gold trading centers in the world." The U.S. still has the largest gold reserves in the world at over 8,100 tonnes, according to World Gold Council figures for the second quarter. China held about one-third of that at over 2,300 tonnes. "China's 23-month gold buying streak reinforces the credibility of the renminbi's internationalization drive," said Hao Zhou, head of research and chief economist at Guotai Junan International in Hong Kong. "By steadily increasing gold reserves, Beijing is strengthening the long-term backing of its financial system and reducing reliance on dollar-denominated reserve assets," he said. "While gold alone will not determine the RMB's global role, it enhances confidence in the currency and supports broader efforts to expand its use in trade, investment and official reserves." Gold accumulation by China and other countries' central banks will help reduce global reliance on U.S. Treasurys and U.S. dollar reserves, said Xia Yingying, head of the precious metals and new energy research group, at Hangzhou-based Nanhua Futures. That's according to a CNBC translation of the Chinese. "This will suppress the U.S. dollar's premium from being a core reserve currency, and raise the risk premium associated with the dollar regarding credit, fiscal policy and sanctions," Xia said. "In the medium to-long-term it will gradually weaken the U.S. dollar's monopolistic position in the global reserve system." China's growing gold purchases, however, also come as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday named gold-standard supporter Judy Shelton as a senior advisor focused on China . The Asian economy's rise as a manufacturing powerhouse benefited from the U.S. decision to abandon the gold standard more than 50 years ago. "With the delinking of the dollar and gold, and the consequent rise in the oil price, western manufacturing became less economic, and capital went to Asia in search of cheap labor and overall lower costs," wrote the central bank research group OMFIF in 2021. While China is the largest consumer and producer of gold, it is just one of many developing economies that has expanded its reserves since 2022, according to S&P. The World Gold Council showed Poland has increased its gold reserves by more tonnes than China. The trend goes beyond financial transactions. Like with rare earths, Beijing's gold ambitions start with control of some of the product. China has acquired major gold mines across Latin America, Africa and Asia, according to S&P Global Ratings. "China's plans for gold and its activities in gold are comprehensive and long lasting.

Two Turkish citizens have been detained in Germany over a fire at a Starlink station in central Poland that Warsaw has branded an act of sabotage carried out on Russia’s behalf. Polish officials announced the arrests on Monday, one month after the fire, which they say was aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine’s military. events.title: Airtable's new owner is laying off a 'large part' of its team
events.summary: Layoffs have hit Airtable. Illustration by Idrees Abbas/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images A "large part" of Airtable's workforce is being laid off, the company's new owner said. Bending Spoons' product leader said smaller teams and AI features are central to its new strategy. Cut employees will leave by the end of the week with "substantial separation packages," he said. Big layoffs are coming to Airtable. Airtable's new owner, Italian tech conglomerate Bending Spoons, said Monday it is laying off a "large part" of the software company as it reshapes the business around smaller teams and AI features. In an X post , Federico Simionato, Bending Spoons' product leader, said the cuts were not a reflection of employees' work but of the company's "deep belief that small teams ship more and better." "To everyone leaving: thank you. If you're hiring, these are excellent people and worth a call," Simionato said. Bending Spoons announced in August that it was acquiring Airtable , the spreadsheet and database app, for $1.28 billion. It was not immediately clear how many people would be affected by the layoffs. A Bending Spoons spokesperson said they were "not able to share additional details on the number of individuals impacted." Airtable product lead Alessandro Savarese said in a blog post on the company's website that the employees being cut will leave by the end of the week with "substantial separation packages." "At Bending Spoons, we've seen firsthand how smaller, faster-moving teams with streamlined responsibilities can have an outsized impact, and we have the same ambitions at Airtable," Savarese wrote. "We intend to make Airtable a better product while providing our customers with an exceptional level of reliability and support." Savarese said the company will focus on improving Airtable's core platform and investing in AI features. Laid-off Airtable employees may already have some job prospects: X product engineer Mridul Singhai responded to the job-cuts announcement in a post , saying X will "continue to hire & grow people who want to commit." President Donald Trump said Monday that he is "not happy" with Kimberly Guilfoyle , and is considering whether to fire her as U.S. ambassador to Greece . Trump's comments at the White House after a series of critical articles in The Wall Street Journal about Guilfolye's conduct before and after she became ambassador. The Journal on Sept. 25 published an article under the headline, "The Mystery Man Shadowing Kimberly Guilfoyle as She Pushes Deals Across Europe." The story detailed Guilfoyle's push to get U.S. allies in Eastern Europe to buy billions of dollars of American natural gas. The article said that Guilfoyle told people who were the targets of her effort that "they should deal with a Greek construction firm called Aktor Group, a newcomer to the gas business that had teamed up with a Greek state-backed energy company to bring in liquefied natural gas from the U.S." The article detailed how Guilfoyle had traveled frequently with a top lobbyist for Aktor named Christos Marafatsos, who has been "joining her for meetings at her ambassadorial residence and with government officials in countries around the region—a highly unusual move for a private citizen." On Oct. 7, the Journal published an article detailing how Guilfoyle allegedly asked a Trump donor named Eric Deters in July 2025 to pay $100,000 for what she said was an American Express bill before her upcoming Senate confirmation hearing for the ambassadorship. A lawyer for Guilfoyle told the newspaper that Deters owed her a balance for "traveling to and supporting" events where she was hired to speak. On Saturday, the Journal published another article that said during the January 2026 World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, she had "boasted ... about her close ties to two Greek tycoons and said they were bankrolling her high-rolling trips around the world." In a statement on Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers "denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from the Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid," The Associated Press reported. events.title: Why the Cornell gang rape case has raised concerns about fraternity culture
events.summary: Experts say many fraternities offer a sense of community, but some rely on hazing and coercive tactics to build loyalty. For more than 40 percent of US presidents, the fraternity hall was an early stop on the road to the White House. Fraternal organisations, more commonly known as fraternities or frats, have a long and storied history on college campuses in the United States. list 1 of 3 Cornell president says university ‘must do better’ after rape allegations list 2 of 3 Cornell rape allegations renew push to change New York sexual assault law list 3 of 3 Does the punishment fit the crime? Controversy erupts around ‘Cornell 7’ One industry group, the North American Interfraternity Conference (NIC), represents 58 fraternities spread across 600 schools. It claims nearly 200,000 undergraduate students as active members and an alumni population of 4.2 million. The draw for college-aged men is the promise of brotherhood, a bond that transcends keg parties and late-night revelry. Like sororities and other members-only student organisations, fraternities are often touted as pathways to personal, academic and professional success. But critics argue that some fraternities have leveraged their exclusivity to encourage and normalise violence, dangling social acceptance as a reward for compliance. “This isn’t [some sort of] a hobbyist club,” said anthropologist Aldo Cimino, a Kent State University professor who studies fraternity hazing. “It is the seriousness of the affiliation that has generated the intensity of these induction rituals.” In recent weeks, one case has renewed debate over fraternity culture and whether the campus organisations use their exclusivity to shield bad behaviour. In September, an anonymous woman known as Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell University and seven of its members, accusing them of gang raping her during a party on the night of October 19, 2024. Doe’s sorority, Delta Delta Delta, and Cornell itself are among the co-defendants. Her lawsuit raises questions about fraternity and sorority culture at US schools, collectively known as “Greek life” for the groups’ use of Greek lettering and symbols. Upon her admission to Cornell, Doe argues she encountered a “glorified – yet materially false and misleading – facade” for Greek life. “She arrived on a campus where the University actively promoted Greek membership as a ‘vital’ part of the campus community and endorsed these organizations as well-managed, worthy pathways to new friendships and improving one’s educational and professional opportunities,” the lawsuit said. The complaint accuses the fraternities of instead perpetuating a pattern of sexual assault and abuse. Now a multibillion-dollar industry, fraternities in the US trace their origins to men-only clubs established at some of the country’s oldest universities. The tradition began at the College of William and Mary in 1776, when Phi Beta Kappa was founded as a secret society for debate and scholarly exchange. Its adoption of the Greek alphabet, oath of secrecy, and arcane membership rites helped establish a blueprint for future fraternities and sororities. Often with houses of their own, fraternities eventually grew into informal extensions of the campus residential system. Historian Nicholas Syrett wrote about the origins of such groups in his book The Company He Keeps: A History of White College Fraternities. In an interview with Al Jazeera, he explained that fraternities have long embraced so-called masculine ideals. But those ideals have changed from generation to generation. In the past, fraternities sought to position themselves in “opposition to boyhood” by embracing “independence, strength of character, handsomeness and loyalty”, Syrett explained. But their modern iteration has shifted to include a greater emphasis on “athleticism, sexual success with women, and recklessness” as well as alpha-male posturing. Syrett argues that the fraternity system’s cult of toughness reflects a wider matrix of gendered expectations and social hierarchies. Early fraternity men, Syrett says, prized intellect and academic distinction, provided neither betrayed too much effort. But “this has largely taken a backseat in contemporary fraternities”, he explained. “When [men] are initiated, they are taught that loyalty to the brotherhood is of the utmost importance,” Syrett said of fraternities today. “This leads to the keeping of all kinds of secrets, including things that are against the rules and/or the law.” In the two and a half centuries since the first fraternities were formed, Greek life has expanded to include different races and identities outside of white men. Some Greek groups have even eschewed the traditional gender divide altogether to better embrace transgender and non-binary members.

events.title: Feds search Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in immigration probe
events.summary: Federal agents conducted a pre-dawn search Monday at the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) as part of an ongoing immigration probe, a DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Searching Omar's home marks a substantial escalation of the Trump administration's fight with the outspoken progressive, who has condemned the immigration crackdown in her state. It's also an unusual move against a candidate less than a month before an election, something the Justice Department has typically avoided . The latest: President Trump said authorities are looking at Omar "very carefully" when asked whether he knew about the search of her home in advance. "I've always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump said. "I think she's a terrible person. She comes from a country that is a non-country." What they're saying: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Omar said in a Monday afternoon post to X. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced." Driving the news: Fox News first reported that Homeland Security Investigations agents conducted the search, citing a Justice Department statement. A DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios that DHS agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice" as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. DHS referred Axios to the DOJ. The other side: Omar's office blasted the search. "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," Omar spokesperson Jacklyn Rogers said in a statement. "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong." House Democratic leaders separately issued a joint statement calling the search "deeply disturbing" and part of a "rogue abuse of power" by the administration. Zoom out: Last month, border czar Tom Homan confirmed an ongoing criminal probe into Omar, though he declined to offer details. Fox reported Monday that the search was tied to a fraud investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork. The Somali native came to the U.S. in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee. Between the lines: Trump has for years demanded that Omar leave the country or be deported , citing, among other things, unsubstantiated claims that she married her brother to help him circumvent immigration laws. Omar has dismissed the claims about the marriage in question as "baseless rumors." Trump has made Minnesota's Somali community one of the most frequent targets of his anti-immigration rhetoric, and Omar the face of those attacks. Just last week, he called on Minnesotans to " fight back " against the state's Somali population. Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from President Trump, as well as statements from Omar, her House office and House Democratic leaders, and with more context. Andrew Solender and Torey Van Oot contributed reporting.

events.title: Uber struggles to solve Broome's late-night transport issues
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Late-night transport issues remain in Broome despite arrival of Uber Travellers say they opt for e-scooters after failing to book an Uber. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Residents and tourists in Broome have long raised concerns about the lack of transport options late at night. The arrival of Uber was touted as a potential solution, but those in Broome say they have struggled to book a ride through the app. Police say the issues people have getting a ride home are no excuse for drink driving. Global rideshare giant Uber has struggled to fill the void of late-night transport in Western Australia's far north. Like many remote locations across Australia, transport options in Broome, 2,000km north of Perth, are progressively limited as the evening wears on. Buses cease at 7pm during the peak tourist season, and many taxi operators stop their service from a similar time. While some drivers continue throughout the night, residents say they face long wait times with expensive fares. Limited taxis operate during the night in Broome. ( ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler ) Uber was touted as a potential solution during its July launch, but those in town said the app has had little impact. Jenny Antonipillai recently travelled to Broome from Perth, and attempted to find a ride home from the pub. "We tried to get a taxi or an Uber, but there's not much available out here. It's very hard," she said. "We went on the Beam [e-scooter] and my boyfriend fell, so not a good idea." Jenny Antonipillai says she was not able to order an Uber home from the pub, despite the app launching in Broome two months ago. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Travellers Noah Clancy and Orlando Dixon said they had also had no luck with Uber and opted for e-scooters to get around. "There was nothing available at all in the area," Mr Clancy said. "We got taxis quite easily earlier in the day, but later at night it's a bit more trouble." Noah Clancy and Orlando Dixon opted for the e-scooters to get around in Broome. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Resident Lili Walker said she was used to long waits and expensive fares costing up to $60 for a 10-minute ride. The state government increased the flexibility of taxi authorisation in 2020, resulting in a number of drivers offering a private service throughout the evening. But their contacts are not always readily available. Matty Arai says many people struggle to organise a taxi through automated answering services. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Pub security guard Matty Arai said it was common to see patrons huddled out the front looking for a way home after close. "There are a couple of good guys around town that will be out all the time, but then trying to pick them up is also hard," he said. Partygoers said expensive fares, long wait times and limited options created a dangerous incentive for drink driving. Sergeant Tony Di Giuseppe says educating the community on safe e-scooter use is a priority. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) But Kimberley District traffic Sergeant Tony Di Giuseppe said inconvenience did not justify breaking the law. "I understand there are difficulties … transport, distance, everything else like that, but it's not acceptable," he said. Sergeant Di Giuseppe said police had been working to educate community members they were subject to the same road rules on an e-scooter as they were driving a vehicle. Broome and Karratha were the first off the rank for Uber's regional WA expansion in July. Broome Private Taxis owner Paul Rewell said he was not surprised the rideshare service has reportedly struggled to take-off. "If people like our group are struggling to find drivers, Uber won't be any different," he said. Paul Rewell says he is not surprised the app has struggled to attract drivers. ( ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson ) Mr Rewell has been operating taxis in the town for the past six years, and said his business had trialled working throughout the evening. Repeated incidents of vandalism during the night led to the decision to close after 6 or 7pm. He said he welcomed Uber's arrival should they have enough drivers. Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said she recognised the challenges of catching taxi services at night in remote towns. She said the government was committed to "providing accessible and affordable" public transport for regional communities, pointing to an expansion of Broome's bus timetable put in place for this year's tourist season. events.title: Susan Collins’s allies spent $25,000 attacking her rival in the Oregon version of Portland: ‘They can’t even find it on a map’
events.summary: Since 1997, Susan Collins has served as one of Maine’s senators, and she may be the epitome of Maine. She, like her opponent Troy Jackson, grew up in the state’s northern tip. Her family ran a lumber business for generations in Caribou, and she’s well regarded by Mainers as someone from “the County,” not a politician. During the Barack Obama era, her bloc of crucial swing voters included Arlen Specter from Pennsylvania and fellow Mainer Olympia Snowe, but she’s the last of those Republican moderates standing, giving Maine an outsize national footprint. So when a political attack ad ran in Portland last week, it would be safe to assume the Portland in question was in Maine. So why did Defending Main Street, a super PAC backing Collins, run an ad in the wrong Portland? Defending Main Street spent nearly $25,000 on digital placements for “So Many Taxes,” a 30-second ad against Jackson, to run the ad in hundreds of zip codes across Oregon and Washington State from Oct. 8 to Oct. 11, according to Google’s Ads Transparency Center . It came to light when an Oregon X user reported seeing five anti-Jackson ads in one day. “I choose to believe they mixed up Portlands,” the user wrote. The same ad aired on broadcast TV in the intended market, Portland, Maine, reaching about 675,000 impressions over the same four days, according to AdImpact data cited by MS NOW . Defending Main Street told Newsweek that its media vendor mistakenly placed the digital ads in the Oregon market, and Newsweek reported the targeting was fixed by Monday afternoon. Sarah Chamberlain, president and CEO of the affiliated Republican Main Street Partnership, told NBC News she was furious at the ad buyer, Cross Screen Media, which she said refunded the money. “I would never run an ad in Portland, Oregon, for Susan Collins,” she said. The mix-up didn’t stop Jackson’s campaign team from commenting on the snafu. “Susan Collins’s allies are so out of touch with Maine, they can’t even find it on a map,” campaign spokesperson Dan Gottlieb told Fortune . “Good luck convincing Mainers you know what’s best for them when you don’t know which Portland they live in.” Defending Main Street and the Collins campaign did not respond to Fortune’ s requests for comment. A $26.8 billion mix-up The super PAC got its money back, but the mistake mirrors a problem that costs corporate advertisers billions. The Association of National Advertisers estimates that $26.8 billion in global ad spending is lost each year to middlemen’s fees, fake traffic, unseen ads, and low-quality sites, up from $20 billion in 2023. That’s more than double the $11.6 billion AdImpact projects will be spent on political ads in the entire 2026 election cycle. Much of that waste comes from ads running in places advertisers never chose. In the ANA’s 2023 study, the average campaign ran on 44,000 websites , even though a few hundred sites would have reached most of the intended audience, and even as participants hadn’t approved about 38,000 of those sites . In the group’s latest benchmark, more than a third of automated ad spending still went to ads that failed basic quality standards. AdImpact has projected $384 million in ad spending on the Maine Senate race, nearly double the roughly $200 million spent when Collins last ran in 2020. And in this race alone, Republicans are outspending Democrats but getting less for each dollar. From July 26 to mid-September, Republicans spent $82.1 million on TV ads in the race to Democrats’ $55.5 million, according to AdImpact data . Super PACs pay full price for TV ads , while candidates’ campaigns get discounted rates. Location targeting, the tool that sent DMS’s ad to Oregon, can backfire. A 2019 analysis by data firm Location Sciences of 500 million location-targeted ads found that 29% were delivered outside the area the advertiser paid to reach. In 2017 the New York Times showed JPMorgan Chase one of its ads on a site called Hillary 4 Prison. The bank found its ads had appeared on about 400,000 websites in a single month, but only 3% of them produced any activity beyond someone seeing the ad. Chase cut its list to about 5,000 preapproved sites and saw little change in the cost or visibility of its ads, its chief marketing officer said. That same year, after activists flagged Uber’s ads on Breitbart, the company began cutting its online ad spending. Kevin Frisch, Uber’s former head of performance marketing, later said the company turned off $100 million of its $150 million annual online ad budget for riders and saw no change in app installs. He blamed ad networks that took credit for sign-ups that would have happened anyway. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Kroger to cut 3,000 corporate employees over the next 3 years. Read the memo.
events.summary: Kroger's corporate workforce is going to get leaner. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Kroger is making big cuts to its corporate workforce. CEO Greg Foran said about 3,000 roles will go away in the next three years. Foran said the corporate-level reductions will allow Kroger to invest in frontline workers. Kroger plans to cut about 3,000 roles from its corporate workforce  over the next three years  to simplify operations. In a memo to staff that the company shared with Business Insider, CEO Greg Foran said the corporate-level reductions will allow Kroger to invest in frontline workers. "Our business is becoming leaner, more focused and more competitive," he said. The former Walmart US CEO took the helm of Kroger earlier this year and has set to work cutting prices and tightening operations over the past several months. Foran also cited the impact of technology on the century-old company, saying that it merits a close look at where work can be done. Read the memo from CEO Greg Foran FROM: Desk of Greg Foran inbox TO: All company RE: Changes to Our Organization We shared important information on our all-company call today, and we're following up to make sure everyone is aware of the changes ahead. As a company, we have made great progress on many fronts with our customers. We started reducing prices and improving our customer experience in stores and online, and we made investments in simplifying our associates' lives through technology. Our business is becoming leaner, more focused and more competitive. We are working to be more agile; more precise in our execution; and deliver benefits to our customers, associates and our shareholders. This transformation will also result in fewer roles across the company, which means we will reduce our corporate workforce across many functions, by approximately 3,000 roles over the next three years. These reductions will allow us to continue to invest in our frontline associates. These are difficult decisions, and we do not make them lightly. This is the right thing for the company's long-term future. Here's why: Simplifying our operations is critical . Simplifying means making faster decisions and deploying more resources where they matter most, so that we deliver lower prices and a better experience for our customers. Our company has more layers, more handoffs and more overhead than we need, so we are addressing this issue. Technology is reshaping what's possible. The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done. We have the opportunity to make changes that will create broader roles and faster decision making. This lets us move vital resources closer to the customer to lower prices, invest in our associates and create a better shopping experience. When and how this will happen These reductions will take place across multiple years. We will share updates when we can. We expect decisions about impacted roles to start being communicated in the coming months. Our values at work During these difficult moments, we will continue to be guided by Our Values. We will communicate directly with impacted associates as we make decisions, and we will not ask anyone to wait longer than necessary for clarity about their roles. We are grateful for each one of you. With the Kroger Leadership Team, we are committed to leading this company through this moment with transparency, integrity and respect. events.title: Canada’s Carney calls for unity as Alberta prepares for secession vote
events.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Thanksgiving message comes a week ahead of Alberta’s vote on a separatism referendum. Prime Minister Mark Carney has used his Thanksgiving message to Canadians to call for national unity, a week before the oil-rich province of Alberta is set to vote on a proposal to secede from Canada. “We can’t build big things on fault lines,” Carney said in his video message on Monday, warning that Canada faces threats to its economy, security and way of life. list 1 of 3 US ban on $1bn of Canadian goods takes effect in Trump’s latest retaliation list 2 of 3 Canada to fast track oil pipeline meant to diversify economy away from US list 3 of 3 Secessionist party wins Quebec election in Canada “We have to be strong, and we are stronger together.” His comments come as Albertans head to the polls on October 19 to decide whether to begin the process of seeking independence. The initial referendum is non-binding, but it proposes to hold a binding vote in the future to decide whether Alberta should secede. The question facing voters is: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?” The vote follows a growing push by a vocal group of separatists, fuelled by longstanding grievances over federal energy and environmental policies. The secessionist movement has accused the Canadian government of unfairly targeting Alberta’s oil and gas industry, the cornerstone of the province’s economy. The movement is also being watched south of the border, as Canada’s relationship with the United States under President Donald Trump has become strained. An investigation by The Globe and Mail earlier this month revealed that US Republican operatives met with secession organisers in Alberta to talk about campaign strategies. Separatist leaders had reportedly offered access to the province’s water and oil royalties in exchange for US support for independence. Separatist leaders have disputed those claims. Carney’s comments also come after another secessionist movement, the Parti Quebecois, won the most seats in a provincial election in Quebec last week, allowing it to return to power after more than a decade. The Parti Quebecois, however, only won 59 seats out of a total of 129 in Quebec’s National Assembly, leaving it short of a majority government. Still, following that victory, US tech entrepreneur Elon Musk, considered the richest man on the planet, applauded the results. He has been known to use his wealth and influence to support political causes, particularly on the far right. “Good. Quebec should separate,” Musk wrote on social media. “They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.” Carney, who grew up in Alberta, said he was filming the message from a classroom at his former school, St Francis Xavier High School in Edmonton. “I’m back home a lot these days because we are building big things again in Alberta: thousands of new homes, high-speed rail, a new pipeline to the West Coast that will create lasting opportunity and prosperity for hundreds of thousands of people in this province and across the country,” he said. Despite the secessionist movement’s growing visibility, polls suggest most Albertans oppose independence.

events.title: Phillip Island business operators prepare for MotoGP's final lap
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Tourism and Leisure Industry Phillip Island has relied on the MotoGP to bring in tourists and revenue. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP race at the end of October before the race moves to Adelaide in 2027. The GP and World Superbikes inject about $80 million into the island's economy each year. Businesses, councillors and the island's tourism board are calling for government support. Every October, Phillip Island emerges from a sleepy winter season and roars to life with the sound of motorcycles travelling in convoy to the MotoGP. The weekend of racing turbocharges the island's summer tourism season, culminating in the World Superbikes event in February. But Cowes and the broader island community are preparing to host their final MotoGP later this month at the picturesque cliff-side track, before the race moves to its new home in Adelaide from 2027. The loss has hit businesses and residents hard, with many reeling emotionally and financially. During the 1990s, Bass Coast Shire Council Mayor Brett Tessari worked at a caravan park on the island. "The vibe of the motorbikes coming in and the people, it was awesome," he said. Brett Tessari says the region's tourism future will need to rely on new ideas. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "I remember being stuck on the [Phillip Island] bridge, trying to get over back to Wonthaggi and people were starting up barbecues and cooking sausages on the side of the road because we were at a standstill," Cr Tessari said. "Things like that are just etched in your memory. "To be the mayor, unfortunately, at the last one, it's pretty surreal and quite sad." For the past decade, Samantha Hampstead has run a tattoo business in Cowes with her husband Jason. They are both members of the social motorcycle club Trust No One, and are key organisers of the annual community motorcycle convoy that heralds the start of the motoring weekend. "We do it because of the love of the ride," she said. "It's a full-blown rush when you have all these riders together. "You look in the mirror and you can see this full parade of bikes behind you and it just goes on forever." Samantha Hampstead organises a community motorcycle run in Cowes. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Ms Hampstead said for many business operators the weekend was their busiest time of the year. "It's part of the island," she said. San Remo Fisherman's Co-Op chief executive Wolfgang Platzer said the GP brought thousands of visitors to the island who may not otherwise have visited the region. Wolfgang Platzer says the community needs develop fresh ideas to attract tourists. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "There would be a large portion of people that come here for the GP and see that the island and the area is very beautiful and then might think about, oh, we'll come back because we liked it and it was so beautiful," he said. Phillip Island is the state's most tourism-reliant region. According to Destination Phillip Island (DPI), more than $80 million in annual economic activity is linked to the World Superbikes and the MotoGP. The accommodation sector is the island's largest employer, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, accounting for almost 4 per cent of jobs. Cafes and restaurants are the third-largest employer. San Remo is the gateway to Phillip Island. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) DPI chief executive Kim Storey said while the event's loss had accelerated the need to broaden the island's outlook beyond motoring events, the role the track had played could not be understated. Economic uncertainty, a lack of infrastructure such as a car ferry and the potential toll of the H5N1 virus on the island's wildlife were all cited by DPI as upcoming barriers to success. "The MotoGP has provided that platform of security and the resource for businesses," Ms Storey said. DPI and Bass Coast Shire Council have called for government funding to help develop new events, such as The Hills are Alive music festival, the Island Whale Festival, the island hot springs, and a new festival of motorsports to capitalise on the island's motoring history. One Nation candidate for Bass Nikole Schellekens, Liberal candidate Rochelle Halstead and Labor candidate Chris Buckingham were asked what commitments they would make to the island's economy if elected at the November state election. All three candidates stressed the importance of tourism for Phillip Island and support for ongoing development of the island's resources.

events.title: LinkedIn is piloting a school to teach workers how to become their own bosses–no degree required
events.summary: The job market is getting harder to break into. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported employers added just 29,000 jobs last month , below economists’ expectations of 90,000 , and more than a quarter (27.1%) of unemployed Americans have been out of work for six months or longer. Now, LinkedIn—the platform built to help users network and find jobs—is launching a school to help workers become their own bosses.  LinkedIn started the Academy of Economic Opportunity in September, enrolling 30 LinkedIn employees in a free 14-week training program, according to a spokesperson. Students meet three times a week to learn things like handling PR crises, making hiring decisions, and pitching investors through simulations. Hari Srinivasan, the company’s chief product officer, told Fortune that one of the pilot cohort’s next sessions is on building an app from scratch. As AI changes the skills employers demand and casts uncertainty over traditional career paths, LinkedIn is betting more workers will seek opportunities beyond conventional jobs. Srinivasan wrote in an Oct. 9 LinkedIn post that the number of people putting “Founder” in their LinkedIn profiles rose nearly 23% over the past year.  “The program is focused on helping them learn how to build a business. Not because we believe everyone should become an entrepreneur, but because people are trying new ways to find economic independence in an uncertain world,” Srinivasan wrote. In a survey of 3,000 American adults, Intuit QuickBooks found that a third planned to start a business or side hustle this year, up from the 17% who said the same a year earlier. And a separate survey of 1,051 new business owners last year by payroll company Gusto found that about half (51%) cited building financial stability or a future asset as a motivation for starting their businesses, up from 42% in 2024. Srinivasan hopes to scale the Academy internationally and at an affordable price to workers outside of LinkedIn and wrote “figuring this out is integral” to the company’s mission. The company has not announced when enrollment will open to the public or what it will charge.  “There is not a current prerequisite for who can participate in this program,” he told Fortune. “We’re building an Academy that can serve people at any stage in their career and across industries and careers.” A business school without degrees LinkedIn isn’t alone in piloting a different approach to help people start businesses outside of traditional credentialing. Harvard Business School launched a $699 startup boot camp that lets entrepreneurs practice investor pitches, sales calls, and board meetings with AI versions of Harvard professors, without earning degrees there. Venture capital giant Andreessen Horowitz invested $42 million into an alternative to college, the Horowitz Andreessen Academy, which will offer 50 students courses in things like AI inference engineering and guest speaker sessions with leaders like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang in San Francisco next year—also without awarding degrees.  These programs differ in scope, but they share an emphasis on practical experience over traditional credentials. For LinkedIn, the approach is also a bet on how AI will change hiring. The company’s 2026 labor market report showed that U.S. job postings requiring AI literacy skills rose 70% year over year. Srinivasan wrote that AI is also making it easier for employers to evaluate candidates’ actual work—like portfolios, code, and products they’ve built—rather than relying on college degrees as “shorthand for talent.” “We’ve designed our program so students leave with real evidence of what they can do, not a degree,” he wrote.  But employers haven’t necessarily abandoned traditional credentials. A 2024 study by Harvard Business School and the Burning Glass Institute found that removing degree requirements increased the share of workers hired without bachelor’s degrees by about 3.5 percentage points in the 11,300 roles analyzed. But because so few roles dropped those requirements, the researchers estimated the change created opportunities for only about 97,000 workers annually, out of 77 million yearly hires.  “For all its fanfare, the increased opportunity promised by Skills-Based Hiring has borne out in not even 1 in 700 hires,” the authors wrote.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Conflict, drought increasing risk of famine in Sudan: Monitor
events.summary: El Nino-induced drought is affecting roughly half of the country as three-year long war continues. Conflict and drought are increasing the risk of famine across Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, warns a global food crisis monitor. “An El Nino-induced drought, affecting roughly half of the country, is compounding the impacts of conflict and displacement, reducing food availability, driving up prices and affecting livelihoods,” the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said on Monday in a statement. list 1 of 3 UN rights council condemns attacks on civilians in Sudan, calls for truce list 2 of 3 Sudan’s al-Burhan rejects talks, vows to retake all territory from RSF list 3 of 3 Drone strike kills 30 people in Sudan’s Blue Nile region “Healthcare is extremely limited, often entirely inaccessible, while clean water is becoming increasingly scarce, leaving a poorly nourished population highly vulnerable to disease and death,” it added. The IPC is an initiative aimed at enhancing food security and consists of 21 organisations and intergovernmental institutions, including the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the World Bank, the World Food Programme (WFP) and the World Health Organization (WHO). ‘Food insecurity, acute malnutrition and excess mortality’ Farmers’ livelihoods have deteriorated and dependence on food assistance is on the rise, said the IPC. “Food insecurity, acute malnutrition and excess mortality will likely intensify,” it warned. Poor vegetation growth affects nearly two-thirds of cropland in North Darfur and about half in South Darfur, West Kordofan and South Kordofan, where severe water shortages and limited opportunity for agricultural recovery threaten livelihoods. The IPC reported worsening acute malnutrition in additional areas, including Nyala, where the proportion of children accessing nutrition services who were admitted for severe acute malnutrition doubled from approximately 5% to 11% between January and August. Two displacement camps in South Darfur also recorded global acute malnutrition above famine thresholds. In North Darfur, delayed rains that impacted crop cultivation and “critically low” food stocks have worsened food insecurity, it added. Western Kordofan is suffering one of its worst droughts since 2004 amid poor rainfall. The lasting effect as conflict persists In May, nearly 19.5 million people, over 40% of the population, were facing high levels of acute food insecurity, according to an IPC assessment. Of those, 135,000 were in Phase 5, the most severe classification, characterised by extreme food shortages, starvation, very high levels of malnutrition and deaths from disease or acute malnutrition. Sudan’s war erupted in April 2023 when tensions between the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), escalated into open fighting in the capital, Khartoum, before spreading across the country. The conflict has killed at least 150,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, though aid groups say the actual toll is likely higher. About 13 million people have been displaced . The army holds sway in Sudan’s central and eastern regions, while the Darfur region in the west and parts of the south are under control of the rival RSF. The arid Darfur region, which is about the size of Spain, has faced some of the worst violence, with displacement camps invaded and ethnic cleansing killing thousands at a time.

events.title: Nasdaq falls ahead of earnings, economic data while oil rallies
events.summary: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange at the opening bell on Oct 5 in New York City. The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite closed lower on Oct 12 as oil prices jumped nearly US$2 (S$2.6) a barrel after attacks on a Saudi airport , and investors waited for banks to kick off the third-quarter earnings season and for economic data this week. The S&P 500 ended the session barely lower while the Dow advanced. Oil futures rallied after deadly strikes on Riyadh’s international airport over the weekend. The attacks overshadowed the prospect of increased supplies after US President Donald Trump hailed fresh Russian diesel exports and talked about a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on energy targets. In coming days, US investors will focus on corporate earnings, with major US banks including Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase reporting early on Oct 13. Analysts were expecting S&P 500 earnings to surge 30.6% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data. Also due out this week are September readings for US consumer and producer inflation as well as retail sales data. While the US Treasury market was closed on Oct 12 for Columbus Day, stock investors have been wary of bond yields’ recent advance to 24-year highs as elevated energy prices have stoked inflation concerns. “Looking out further in the week, we have some big economic reports,” said Tim Ghriskey, senior portfolio strategist at Ingalls & Snyder in New York. He said investors were also cautious due to a lack of direction from bonds. “We’re also waiting on earnings and that’s significant. The four large banks reporting on Tuesday can have a big impact,” he said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 195.60 points, or 0.38%, to 51,850.55, the S&P 500 lost 4.30 points, or 0.06%, to 7,807.24 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 120.27 points, or 0.44%, to 27,245.90. Trading volume was relatively light with 12.67 billion shares changing hands on US exchanges compared with the 20-day moving average of 17.62 billion. “There’s a lot to be wary of,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth in Fairfield, Connecticut, pointing to upcoming data and earnings along with rising oil prices. “You’re walking down a train line and you don’t know, because it’s dark, if a train is coming and so, you know, you’re just being real careful,” he said. With oil prices rising, energy outperformed among the S&P 500’s 11 major industry sectors with a 1.5% advance. The defensive consumer staples sector rose more than 1% along with the S&P 500 communication services index, which was boosted by a more than 3% gain in heavyweight Meta. Technology, down 0.9%, and consumer discretionary, off 0.7%, were the biggest sector laggards. Technology’s weakness was most pronounced among chip stocks with the Philadelphia semiconductor index finishing down 2.7% after hitting a three-week low. In consumer discretionary, Chipotle Mexican Grill shares fell 3.8% after Starbucks said it was not buying the burrito chain. Starbucks shares closed up 1.7%. Microsoft finished up 1.1% with its market capitalisation climbing above US$4 trillion for the first time in a year after it announced plans for major deployment of its own AI chips. Salesforce shares added 2% after BofA Global Research upgraded the stock to “buy” from “underperform.” And eBay rose 2% after Morgan Stanley added the stock to its top-pick list. Meanwhile, Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said the US central bank should move “relatively quickly” to a more restrictive monetary policy stance to fight inflation, which she feels has become more broad-based and is starting to influence firms’ price-setting plans. Traders were pricing in an almost 22% chance the US Federal Reserve will hike interest rates this month, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, up from 17.7% on Oct 9. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.09-to-1 ratio on the NYSE where there were 149 new highs and 272 new lows. On the Nasdaq, 1,888 stocks rose and 3,008 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.59-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 10 new 52-week highs and five new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 51 new highs and 318 new lows. REUTERS

events.title: Elon Musk gives $276 million to Republican groups, becomes biggest known 2026 midterm donor
events.summary: Elon Musk has poured more than $276 million into Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election. Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund and more than $76 million to America PAC, in newly disclosed spending, bringing his known federal political giving this cycle to roughly $366 million. His 2025-26 giving has already surpassed the roughly $290 million he spent during the 2024 election, despite saying last year he planned to spend “a lot less” on politics. Elon Musk spent more than $276 million in newly disclosed donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election as the party fights to hold its majorities in Washington this November. The largest share – $158 million – went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Republican Senate candidates, according to figures provided by Musk's representatives to The New York Times and confirmed Monday to CNBC by Lindsey Curnutte, a spokesperson for Musk's America PAC. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO also gave more than $76 million to America PAC , the group he founded during the 2024 election, which has built a large voter-turnout operation in competitive Senate and House races . The new contributions bring Musk's known federal political giving for the 2025-26 cycle to roughly $366 million, already surpassing the approximately $290 million he spent during the 2024 presidential election . The scale of the latest giving is historic: Musk's $158 million contribution to Senate Leadership Fund is among the largest known political donations by an individual in U.S. history. The new figures were disclosed days ahead of a Thursday Federal Election Commission filing deadline , when political committees are due to report their third-quarter finances. The Senate Leadership Fund has spent heavily this cycle to defend the Republican majority, including in Texas, where GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton is running against Democrat James Talarico . Talarico leads Paxton 48.4% to 45.0% in FiftyPlusOne's polling average as of Oct. 12. Musk separately gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC , which supports Paxton. He also contributed $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund , the leading super PAC supporting House Republicans, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association, the Times reported and Curnutte confirmed. The trillionaire's footprint in Texas has expanded rapidly in recent years, with Tesla, X and The Boring Company now headquartered in the state and SpaceX growing its manufacturing and launch operations there. The political spending is also a sharp reversal from Musk's public comments last year. "In terms of political spending, I'm going to do a lot less in the future," Musk said in May 2025. At the time, Musk was stepping back after a highly visible role in President Donald Trump's administration and a public falling-out with the president. The two have since repaired their relationship, appearing together at several recent events. Musk also retains deep ties to the federal government through SpaceX, a major NASA and Pentagon contractor . Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month also named him co-director of Project Meridian , a Pentagon panel studying the future of warfare. — Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

events.title: Anthropic is making a $100 million bet on deployed AI engineers, and it seeks 5 key attributes
events.summary: Anthropic's developer conference in May. Don Feria/AP Content Services for Anthropic Anthropic is putting $100 million into a new training program for other companies' workers. The push is an effort to create more "deployed engineers," who can ramp up AI usage at companies. Executives explained the program and described the ideal forward-deployed engineer. Forward-deployed engineers are all the rage in AI, and Anthropic is going to other companies to train up top talent. The AI company announced a $100 million investment into an FDE training initiative earlier this month. It's a quasi-fellowship that engineers from other firms have already begun applying for. They'll attend four-day on-site intensives and then complete 12-week "residencies" working with Anthropic's Claude tools at their own companies. The company says it hopes to train 10,000 people through the program by the end of 2027. As Anthropic approaches its gigantic initial public offering , it's using the new training model to get more of the corporate world used to AI — and ramp up Claude spending. Job postings for FDEs have boomed over the last couple of years, as more companies buy software from AI firms and need help deploying it. Two Anthropic executives leading the push told Business Insider that their customers see AI's advances, notice competitors grabbing market share, and feel pressure to change their own work. "Everybody understands the model capability is expanding extremely fast," said Shambhavi Shambhavi, Anthropic's head of go-to-market strategy and operations for partnerships. "So, what can be done with the technology is greatly appreciated by the customers." Enter the FDE — which Anthropic calls "Frontier Deployed Engineers," rather than the standard " forward-deployed engineer " title that Palantir helped popularize . Both roles essentially mean someone with deep technical expertise in AI and the mandate to create new modes of work at a company. Shambhavi and Steve Corfield, Anthropic's head of global business development and partnerships, broke down the FDE role as they see it and how Anthropic hopes to set a "gold standard" with its new skills push. Anthropic execs say FDEs are curious Shambhavi said that the best FDEs have four main attributes. They are familiar with agentic AI systems. They're good problem-solvers. They're excellent communicators. And they're experienced, skilled engineers. Corfield tacked on a point he thinks helps Anthropic thrive: "You've got to be super, super curious. If you walk around this organization, everybody talks about curiosity." Communication is particularly important, Shambhavi said. She said that as companies try to overhaul entire workflows and approach agentic AI holistically, someone who can navigate the interpersonal dynamics goes a long way. "Our own Frontier Deployed Engineers work with these kinds of problems day in and day out," Shambhavi said. "And so we kind of applied the mindset of, we need to take this skill and bring it to our customers and partners and to the top engineers in those organizations, so that they can derive the benefits from Claude." Anthropic wants to set the 'gold standard' for AI skills Engineers who can expand their teams' use of AI have become a hot commodity in Silicon Valley. Salesforce, a major Anthropic partner , announced a plan in May to recruit 1,000 early-career workers into "AI builder" roles. Anthropic's program, in Corfield's view, goes a step above other industry attempts to recruit and train FDEs. Combined with other company initiatives to teach people AI, he hopes Anthropic will set "the gold standard for AI skilling." The first cohorts have begun in New York and San Francisco, including engineers from Accenture, Bain, Novo Nordisk, and other organizations. Companies nominate engineers for the training, and Anthropic interviews candidates. If they're accepted, they work for the four-day residency on a "simulated environment," an agentic system that they have to learn how to build and deploy. Then they take a practical test, before returning to their companies while staying in touch with Anthropic mentors for 12 more weeks. Anthropic is still building its assessments throughout the program. Shambhavi said they'll focus on "what does a great FDE look like" — articulation, problem solving, coding skills. Corfield said corporate customers wanted a program like this to help them figure out how to deploy Claude more effectively, and the holdup isn't motivation. "This is a skills gap problem, and that creates a market problem," he said. "What we're trying to do is fill that gap," he added. Have a tip? events.title: Why do Iran’s oil ‘intermediaries’ owe the government billions?
events.summary: Iran says intermediaries handling its oil sales owe it billions of dollars, but how did the debts accumulate? As the United States maintains a naval blockade of Iran’s ports and imposes more sanctions on its oil exports, Tehran is confronting another problem: billions of dollars in revenue from previous oil sales that it says have gone missing. A spokesperson for Iran’s judiciary said in September that a network of oil intermediaries known as “trustees” owed the Iranian government between 10 billion euros ($11bn) and 11 billion euros ($12bn). That figure was equivalent to half of the total oil revenue projected in Iran’s government budget for the current fiscal year. list 1 of 3 Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz list 2 of 3 UK blames Iran for airbase plot, sanctions two Iranian nationals list 3 of 3 Iran-Saudi talks on Yemen’s Houthis: What’s in it for Tehran? US officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, have tied Iran’s struggles to access oil revenues as evidence that its economic pressure campaign is having an effect. In August, Bessent said that “Iran’s shadow banking system was buckling” under pressure from the US campaign against the country, which has been ramped up as Washington seeks a way to force Tehran to capitulate in the war between the two countries, launched by the US and Israel in late February. So who are the oil intermediaries, why does Iran depend on them, and what has happened to the billions of dollars they owe? Let’s take a closer look. The debt, and the crisis it has created for the Iranian government, both stem from an oil-sales arrangement Tehran adopted in 2012 in response to US sanctions targeting Iranian oil exports. American and European sanctions targeting Iranian oil sales and revenue collection began in 2012. The stated rationale behind both sets of measures was that revenue from oil sales helped finance Iran’s nuclear programme and that restricting Iranian oil exports could prevent the programme from advancing. In response, the Iranian government devised a way to circumvent international sanctions on its oil sales. Unable to sell oil through the Oil Ministry and receive the proceeds through the Central Bank, it began selling oil to domestic buyers or using it to settle outstanding obligations to institutions and organisations owed money by the state. This arrangement gave rise to a network of oil intermediaries often referred to in Iran as the “trustee network”. Rather than selling all its oil through official government channels, the state entrusted crude oil to institutions, individuals and companies to sell on its behalf. The proceeds were supposed to be transferred to the government’s treasury, with the sellers or recipient institutions subsequently recovering their agreed costs and outstanding claims. Some institutions sold the oil themselves, while others contracted private trading companies to handle the sales. The Oil Industry Pension Fund, established for retired Oil Ministry employees familiar with the oil-sales process, was among the first institutions to receive crude oil for sale. Other recipients included Khatam al-Anbiya Construction Base, a major hub for large-scale infrastructure projects. Even the municipal police received payments owed to them by the government in the form of crude oil. Even in those early experiments, discrepancies emerged between the revenue expected from oil sales and the amounts sellers actually deposited into the government’s treasury. These discrepancies eventually gave rise to some of Iran’s largest economic corruption cases. The accounting discrepancies and the government’s inability to recover money from private sellers entrusted with Iranian oil persisted until 2016, when the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) nuclear deal was signed and when sanctions on Iranian oil sales were lifted. The government was subsequently able to regain control over oil sales. Individuals who had sold Iranian oil but failed to return the proceeds were imprisoned. With the ability to sell oil again through legal and transparent channels, the government was able, for a time, to manage its oil revenues and spending with greater control. How did money from oil sales go unreturned? After US President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from the JCPOA in 2018 during his first presidential term, the Iranian government once again had to rely on private oil traders to sell its oil. But the problems associated with selling oil through intermediaries rather than official state channels, including delays in returning revenues, accounting discrepancies, debts owed by oil sellers to the government, and the occasional seizure of Iranian oil shipments at sea, once again constrained the government’s ability to manage its oil revenues.
