events.summary: Thousands of snow geese take flight at Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge near San Antonio, New Mexico. Ronen Tivony/NurPhoto via Getty Images Lonely Planet curated a list of the best places to travel to in 2027. Popular destinations like Prince Edward Island, Canada, and New Mexico made the list. It also includes lesser-known places like Bariloche, Argentina, and Šibenik, Croatia. As 2026 draws to a close , travelers are beginning to map out where they want to go next year. To help jump-start those plans, Lonely Planet in September released its annual "Best in Travel" guide for 2027, highlighting 25 destinations chosen by its global network of writers and contributors. The guide's destination picks span Argentina's mountains , Canada's red-rock beaches, a Caribbean island, and California's ancient redwood forests, among other places. Here are the 25 best travel destinations featured in Lonely Planet's annual list. The Tweed, Australia The Tweed is "best for Hinterland detours." James D. Morgan/Getty Images The Tweed region is in far northeastern New South Wales, between the Gold Coast and Byron Bay. Visitors can enjoy activities such as hiking and biking. The Veneto, Italy Morning mist on the Venetian Prealps, Veneto region, Italy. DeAgostini/Getty Images Veneto, the northeastern Italian region, is far more than just Venice . It stretches from the Prosecco Hill vineyards to the Dolomites and Lake Garda, offering visitors a bit of everything: historic cities, mountains, lakeside towns, and a top-class food and wine scene. New Mexico, US Carlsbad Caverns National Park - New Mexico. (Photo by: Edwin Remsberg/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) : Edwin Remsberg/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images New Mexico offers a range of activities and sights : desert landscapes, mountain towns, ancient sites, and a mix of Native American, Hispanic, and Anglo cultures. Prince Edward Island, Canada Beach along the North Shore of Prince Edward Island, Canada. (Photo by: John Lazenby/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) : John Lazenby/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Prince Edward Island is Canada’s smallest province. However, it packs in red sandstone cliffs, fishing villages, and a food scene centered on the sea. Fans of "Anne of Green Gables" can also visit the places that inspired author Lucy Maud Montgomery’s novel. Bariloche, Argentina A woman practices nordic ski at Otto hill near Bariloche, Rio Negro, Argentina, on June 24, 2020 amid the lockdown imposed by the government against the spread of the new coronavirus, COVID-19. - Though the city of Bariloche is already covered with snow, this year there will be no avalanche of visitors in this popular tourist destination due to the coronavirus pandemic. (Photo by FRANCISCO RAMOS MEJIA / AFP) (Photo by FRANCISCO RAMOS MEJIA/AFP via Getty Images) FRANCISCO RAMOS MEJIA/AFP via Getty Images Bariloche is a great destination to explore Patagonia’s lakes and mountains. Located within Nahuel Huapi National Park, the city is known for its alpine scenery, outdoor activities, and chocolate shops, giving Bariloche a distinctly European feel . Skanör-Falsterbo, Sweden Malmo, Sweden is the closest city to Skanör-Falsterbo. Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images Skanör-Falsterbo is on the Falsterbo Peninsula in southwestern Skåne, dotted with beaches, cottages and beach huts. The two towns have medieval roots and were once important centers for the herring trade, when merchants traveled from across northern Europe to take part in the annual Scania Market. Montserrat, Caribbean Plymouth is the capital of the Caribbean island Montserrat. Christopher Pillitz/Exclusive by Getty Images Known as the "Emerald Isle of the Caribbean" for its Irish heritage and lush, mountainous landscape, Montserrat offers black-sand beaches, hiking trails, and a quieter alternative to neighboring islands. The 1995 Soufrière Hills eruption and later ones buried much of the former capital, Plymouth. Visitors can tour the remains of Plymouth and learn about the volcano at the Montserrat Volcano Observatory. Granada, Nicaragua A juggler performs during the street art festival "Berrinche Ambiental" in the colonial city of Granada, Nicaragua on January 27, 2024. ( OSWALDO RIVAS/AFP via Getty Images Granada, the former capital of Nicaragua, is filled with bright buildings, horse-drawn carriages, and churches, with the yellow Granada Cathedral serving as one of its best-known landmarks and a backdrop to the city. Tsavo East & West National Parks, Kenya Mauro Flamini/REDA&CO/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Together, Tsavo East and Tsavo West form Kenya's largest protected area. Travelers can spot elephant herds, zebras, giraffes, and African wild dogs roaming across the two parks. León, Spain León is "best for Camino history and late-night energy." History buffs can also visit the ancient Roman mining site of Las Médulas , now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Bocas del Toro, Panama Bocas del Toro is "best for barefoot beach days." Sergi Reboredo/VW PICS/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Panama's Bocas del Toro is a series of islands along the Caribbean coast, making for a lively, beach-filled destination for those seeking sunshine and a relaxing vacation. Pack goggles and a snorkel: the water is crystal clear, and a coral reef lies below. Maryland, USA Maryland is "best for Underground Railroad history and Chesapeake flavors." events.title: 22 romance books to read while you wait for Emily Henry's next novel
events.summary: Emily Henry in September 2026. Cindy Ord/WireImage/Getty Images Emily Henry announced her next novel, "Modern Classic," will be published on April 6, 2027. Henry's novels are romantic and sexy, often leaving readers wanting more.  You can read similar romance novels to help pass the time while you wait for Henry's next book. Emily Henry fans are in luck. On September 22, Henry revealed her next romance novel will be released on April 6, 2027. She unveiled the title, "Modern Classic," by posting it on movie theater marquees across the US and UK. "Modern Classic" will be Henry's seventh romance novel to date. She smashed onto the romance scene in 2020 with " Beach Read " and has written five more books since then, each of which has made The New York Times' bestseller list.  Henry's summer romance books often approach love with a sense of honesty and fun that the genre needs to thrive. Her characters may be enemies who find themselves living next door to each other or best friends who are scared to risk it all for something more, as was the case in " People We Meet on Vacation ," which was turned into a Netflix film released in January 2026. Henry has yet to release a cover or description for "Modern Classic," but the marquee announcement and title have fans wondering whether the book will have anything to do with movies. It will be a while, though, before readers know for sure. Luckily, there are plenty of other romance books to pass the time with, including Henry's earlier works if you haven't read — or reread — them yet. "Beach Read" by Emily Henry Penguin Random House In Henry's 2020 novel "Beach Read," which is being adapted into a film , author January Andrews is in a writing rut. She can't seem to think of her next big idea for a romance novel, so she decides to retreat to the beach house she inherited from her father, hoping inspiration will strike. To her dismay, January discovers Augustus Everett, an acclaimed literary author who happens to be her college archnemesis, is living next door.  January plans to steer clear of Augustus for the duration of summer — until she finds out he's having writer's block, too. They decide the solution to their problem is for each of them to try their hand at each other's writing style. Augustus will have to show January the ropes of capital-L literature, and she'll have to make him fall in love with writing about love.  However, falling for Augustus was never part of the plan. As you dive into "Beach Read," it's easy to see how it turned Emily Henry into a household name. "People We Meet On Vacation" by Emily Henry "People We Meet on Vacation" by Emily Henry. Berkley No one expected Alex and Poppy to become best friends less than Alex and Poppy. After a fateful road trip in college, free-spirited Poppy and buttoned-up Alex become inseparable. To keep their friendship alive after graduation, the pair agreed to take a trip together every summer, exploring a new place side by side. The trip is Poppy's favorite week of the year, but when "People We Meet on Vacation" begins, they haven't been on a trip — or spoken — in two years, distance growing between them after one night changes everything. As Poppy feels more bogged down than ever by her life in New York, she knows reuniting with Alex would make everything better. So Poppy proposes one more trip, hoping a week together can get their friendship — and her life — back on track. Will Poppy or Alex be willing to face the feelings that sent them running from each other in the first place? "Book Lovers" by Emily Henry "Book Lovers" by Emily Henry. Penguin Random House "Book Lovers" is Henry's third summer romance book , and it's both an epic love story and an ode to books themselves.  Nora Stephens doesn't think anything is missing in her life. She loves her job as a literary agent, her apartment in New York, and living near her sister, Libby, and her nieces. When Libby asks Nora to escape to Sunshine Falls, North Carolina, for a month, Nora can't say no, especially since Libby is several months pregnant at the time. Libby has big dreams of small-town romance for Nora during their getaway, but instead of finding a local man to have a fling with, Nora keeps running into Charlie Lastra, a grumpy New York editor she's never gotten along with.  Despite their less-than-romantic history, Charlie and Nora keep crossing paths in Sunshine Falls, making the ever-growing list of things they have in common harder to ignore. And when Nora discovers her life as she knows it is about to change, Charlie might be the exact thing she needs. "Happy Place" by Emily Henry "Happy Place" by Emily Henry. Penguin Random House Henry is at her best in "Happy Place," a novel that ruminates on what it means to fight for love. Harriet has spent her entire adult life loving Wyn. Their relationship consumes her, and the fact that she met him through her best friends, Sabrina and Cleo, only makes her love him more. Between Wyn and her friends, Harriet found the family she had always wanted in college, and she plans to spend her entire life with them. When Wyn abruptly breaks up with her after she starts her medical school residency, Harriet is heartbroken and terrified she's going to lose everyone she loves. She manages to avoid telling Sabrina and Cleo what happened for five months, planning to burst their bubble on their annual group trip to Maine . Then Wyn shows up, telling her they'll have to pretend to be a couple for the duration of the trip, since it's the last vacation the group will ever spend in the house they've loved for years. Harriet doesn't want to cause her friends pain, so she's willing to torture herself for a week. All she has to do is stop herself from asking Wyn what went wrong for seven days, but as his displays of fake affection start to feel more and more real, Harriet might have to face her fear of rocking the boat if she wants a true chance at happiness. "Funny Story" by Emily Henry "Funny Story" by Emily Henry. Berkley In "Funny Story," Daphne Vincent thought she had everything figured out. She was going to marry her doting fiancé, Peter, quietly thrive at her dream children's librarian job, and settle down in his hometown of Waning Bay, Michigan. Then, Peter leaves her for his childhood best friend , Petra, leaving Daphne at a crossroads. As she tries to recalibrate her entire future, Daphne moves in with Petra's ex, Miles Nowak, a wild spirit with whom she doesn't think she has much in common. Then, a night of drinking leads the pair to realize they may be able to help each other get over their breakup embarrassment if they let their exes think there's more between them than just a shared living space . events.title: A PR pro says Kelly Clarkson made one big mistake in her feud with a Brooklyn toy shop
events.summary: Kelly Clarkson hosts "The Kelly Clarkson Show." Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal via Getty Images Kelly Clarkson publicly scolded a small business in Brooklyn after visiting the store. The store, Art of Play, responded with two public statements attempting to reframe the interaction. PR pro Evan Nierman says both parties attempted to position themselves as victims to gain sympathy. When a feud is brought into the court of public opinion, the winner isn't necessarily the one who's technically "right." It's the one who crafts the better narrative. That's the main thing that Kelly Clarkson is missing in her viral clash with a small business in Brooklyn , according to Evan Nierman, CEO of the global PR firm Red Banyan. "This is more about feelings than facts," Nierman said. The much-publicized kerfuffle started on Saturday, when Clarkson shared a post on X about her recent visit to Art of Play, a store that sells toys, puzzles, gifts, and other oddities. Clarkson said she was treated poorly at the store, comparing herself to Julia Roberts' " Pretty Woman " heroine — specifically, the memorable scene in which she is rejected and mocked in a fancy Beverly Hills boutique. Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me. Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale. But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in Pretty Woman. For sure, check it out 👎 — Kelly Clarkson (@kellyclarkson) October 10, 2026 Clarkson said she tried to buy something expensive at Art of Play but was treated as if she "couldn't afford it." However, the shop employee Clarkson dealt with remembers the interaction differently. Art of Play responded with a public statement , saying that Clarkson inquired about a one-of-a-kind mechanical bird puppet nicknamed "Molly," and she was told it wasn't for sale. When Clarkson doubled down , insisting that Molly came with a $15,000 price tag and calling the employee a "liar," Art of Play clarified its claim. In a follow-up statement on Instagram , the store said that Clarkson had been offered a nearly identical version of the bird, created by the same artist, for $15,000, as well as a comparable version by a different maker for $2,000. Who's right, and what really happened? We may never know, and it probably won't matter in the long run. But from a PR perspective, Nierman said this back-and-forth over trivial details is neither convincing nor productive. "Both Kelly Clarkson and the store are trying to play the victim card in this dispute," Nierman explained. "But the only people who really know what happened that fateful morning were the sales associate, Kelly Clarkson, and Molly, the bird, who will never sing." The 'victim card' can only get you so far Nierman pointed out that Clarkson doesn't have much to lose by airing her petty grievances on social media. She's a rich, famous singer with three Grammy Awards and nearly 9 million followers on X. "You'd be hard pressed to make the case that her life is going to be derailed in any significant way, even if she was mistreated by the store and its staff," Nierman said. But Clarkson doesn't have much to gain here, either. By playing the "victim card," she has ignored the etiquette of online power dynamics, siccing her loyal fans on a small business over a brief interaction. Even if everything she said was true and Clarkson really was mistreated by the store's staff, the fallout isn't flattering. "They both want to be right, whereas what they should be looking for is an off-ramp where they could both look good as opposed to being the victim in this circumstance," Nierman said. One idea? The fight started over a bird, so perhaps it should end with one. "The best possible outcome at this point would be to get her back to the store and find a way to get her a singing bird," Nierman continued. "That would tie this whole thing off very nicely, and everyone could move forward and deal with more important issues." You know what they say: It's not over 'til Molly the animatronic bird sings. events.title: Exclusive: Microsoft’s departing science president plans to join Mercedes F1 team as AI advisor
events.summary: Peter Lee, who recently announced his departure as president of Microsoft Science, plans to join the Mercedes Formula 1 team in a newly created AI advisor role, he told Fortune . Lee spent 16 years at Microsoft shaping its science and research efforts, exploring how AI can help doctors and scientists crack hard problems in the physical, biological, and medical sciences. At Mercedes, he said, he’ll focus on four main goals: using AI to tackle physics problems for the team’s car, breaking down organizational and data silos across departments, building financial and predictive data models, and advising the team on how the sport’s regulators might govern AI use. His exact title is still under discussion, but he’s expected to join on a one-year contract with an option for a second. “I have always wanted to be a racer. When I was young, I grew up racing carts,” Lee said. “I’m completely thrilled, and I’m in disbelief that they would think of me for something like this.” The Mercedes team didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Lee’s move is further proof of how AI is reshaping the job market, even at the highest levels of corporate America. The AI boom has set off an arms race for talent, and industries outside Silicon Valley are competing to secure expertise. In June, for example, Dr. James Smith, who once worked at Google’s AI lab DeepMind, joined the Williams Formula 1 team as its new chief information officer.  Lee’s change also comes amid a wave of departures from Microsoft this year, as CEO Satya Nadella reorients the company to win the enterprise and cloud sides of AI. Ryan Roslansky, an executive vice president who also served as LinkedIn CEO, recently announced he’s leaving, as is chief communications officer Frank X. Shaw. Earlier this year, longtime executives including gaming chief Phil Spencer and Rajesh Jha, executive vice president of experiences and devices, retired. At Microsoft, Lee’s responsibility was to “accelerate the pace of discovery in the physical, biological, and medical sciences through the use of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies,” according to the company. He worked on diagnostics, precision medicine, and clinician tools. One project, InnerEye, sought to automate the laborious outlining of tumors and healthy tissue for radiation-treatment planning. He also helped assess OpenAI’s GPT-4 before its public release and identify its potential in medicine. In 2024, Time magazine named Lee as one of the 100 most influential people in health and life sciences.  In 2025, Microsoft revealed an AI tool it said could diagnose disease four times more accurately than a group of doctors, at a fraction of the cost. The company also partnered with institutions such as the Mayo Clinic and Harvard Medical School to improve products like its Copilot AI assistant, though it has more recently focused Copilot on business use rather than general or medical use. Lee acknowledged that Formula 1 and health care are very different industries, but he said they share some traits. “In both health care delivery and in medical research, and in Formula 1, you are oftentimes in collaborative situations where a group of very well-trained people are working together with a deficit of information and having to make highly consequential rapid decisions,” he said. The question then becomes: “What is the best way to inject technology like AI into this in a way that helps as [opposed] to distract?” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Earnings beats are now the norm. What the stock market needs to keep rallying
events.summary: Analysts expect nearly 30% year-over-year earnings growth for the S&P 500, up from 26.7% on June 30th. Profits look robust below the Mag-7 surface, including 19% growth this year for S&P 400 MidCap operating earnings. Healthy beats are the new "status quo" while other forces could "gum up" a smooth earnings story. Will 30% profit growth and upbeat tech guidance be enough to keep the rally going? We'll soon find out. Third-quarter earnings season kicks into gear Tuesday with JPMorgan Chase and other big banks. Expectations are steep: consensus forecasts call for nearly 30% year-over-year growth, according to FactSet. That's up from around 27% three months ago. But 30% or more should be doable — S&P 500 profits have topped quarterly estimates by healthy margins since mid-2023. Tech will have to do its part at beating estimates and lifting guidance. For now, the sector shows no signs of slowing. Analysts expect 65% gains for tech profits, up from an estimated 57% growth three months ago. Upward revisions for Nvidia , Micron Technology and Dell Technologies are doing the heavy lifting, according to FactSet. Also positive, profit growth is broadening beyond the Mag 7. The other 493 stocks in the S&P 500 are forecast to deliver 27% year-over-year gains, topping the Mag-7 average, according to Russell Investments . S&P 400 MidCap operating earnings should rise 19% in 2026, notes Ed Yardeni, head of Yardeni Research. The first earnings test comes with the big banks. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs , Citigroup , and Wells Fargo , reporting Tuesday, should reveal how steeper interest rates are impacting loan growth, balance sheets, M&A activity and the IPO pipeline. JPMorgan — the largest U.S. bank — will be critical, along with comments from CEO Jamie Dimon who tends to move markets with his outlook. Financials are on a knife's edge; the sector is hovering around its 200-day moving average, a key technical indicator, after falling 5% since August 31. Analysts see rising interest rates starting to sting loan growth and fixed-income securities held on balance sheets. The weakness could make for a relief rally, but earnings and guidance could go either way, pushing the stocks up or down, notes Julian Emanuel, senior managing director at Evercore ISI. "There will be volatility as investors hang on every word from the Big Banks this week," he said in a note. Emanuel remains bullish on the market, however, and tech in particular. Several other strategists concur. Goldman Sachs shifted to an "overweight" stance on equities Monday, saying "growth remains supportive." The bank's strategists see a favorable macro climate with low recession risk. And they expect inflation to ease in 2027 — all of which points to "more of a 'Goldilocks' backdrop," according to a note by Christian Mueller-Glissmann, head of asset allocation at Goldman Sachs Research. For positioning, he recommends a "barbell of AI beneficiaries and selective rate-sensitive, high-dividend and low-volatility stocks that could benefit from eventual rate relief." The setup also looks favorable because multiples have fallen, notes Lisa Shalett, chief investment officer for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management. Stocks are trading at 19 times forward earnings, down from 21 times over the summer, despite the fact that earnings growth has picked up. While rising bond yields have compressed multiples, "that's typical of a midcycle expansion when rate hikes have yet to truly bite," she points out. Shalett also takes solace in the market's growth drivers. "While many sectors will likely eventually be impacted by higher-for-longer rates, the key growth vectors for this boom — AI capex and wealth-linked consumption — have thus far proved rate-insensitive," she said in a note Monday. UBS sees gains for equities too. "Investors should remain positioned for market upside, and we forecast the S&P 500 to reach 8,400 by June next year," said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and Global Head of Equities for UBS Chief Investment Office in a recent note. More critical than bank earnings may be tech — a sector accounting for 40% of the S&P 500 and about a third of its estimated $800 billion in profits this quarter. Analysts will be looking for signals that AI chip and infrastructure demand are powering through a tough macro climate and higher energy prices, and the stocks will move on 2027 guidance. The first clues may come when Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company reports Thursday. Third-quarter profit estimates for TSM are up to $4.45 a share, from $3.42 in January, according to FactSet consensus forecasts. TSM has beaten forecasts in 19 of the last 20 quarters, including a 10.8% beat in the second quarter. Its outlook on chip demand will be a key indicator for Nvidia and other chipmakers. The Nasdaq 100 is sitting near record highs, however, thanks to a swath of AI companies issuing upbeat reports and new products — easing some of the consternation about the cycle topping out.

events.title: I broke into tech sales after working in construction. Here's how I landed a more flexible job with higher earning potential.
events.summary: Bryan Ruiz. Courtesy of Bryan Ruiz Bryan Ruiz transitioned from construction to tech sales for a higher earning potential. Ruiz used online courses such as CourseCareers to gain the skills needed for a career in tech sales. His perseverance led to a flexible and profitable career path at a SaaS company. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Bryan Ruiz, a 27-year-old tech sales representative based in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. It has been edited for length and clarity. I grew up in Puerto Rico, and about seven years ago, I moved to the US to look for construction work . After working in construction for a couple of years, I found it to be really back-breaking work. It didn't matter how hard I worked or how many skills I developed; there was always a cap on what I could earn because I was paid by the hour. I tried to get noticed and eventually get a raise, but it didn't work. I started thinking about pursuing a career where I'm really rewarded for the amount of work I put in. Within a year, I went from earning $18 an hour doing physical labor to a new career that put me on track to earn six figures. I decided to look into sales I was drawn to sales because it offered more upside than hourly work, and I liked the idea that strong performance could directly affect my earnings. I didn't know anything about sales. I watched a ton of YouTube videos trying to understand the space and what sales was about. I listened to podcasts on the job site, watched videos after work, and read books whenever I could. One podcast that helped me later on was " 30 Minutes to President's Club ." I also took a course through CourseCareers . The track I did was specifically for tech sales. I don't think you necessarily need a course to break into sales, but it helped me because it gave me a structured path to follow. It cost around $500, and I split it into a few payments. I finished the course in about a week because I desperately wanted to start my new career. I started applying to almost anything and everything I could find Landing interviews was a struggle at first, but eventually I got three interviews — and you only need one yes. I tried to schedule them during my breaks or see if I could get time off work to do them. My first interview completely destroyed my confidence. The hiring manager challenged me about not having any sales experience, and I reacted poorly. I started doubting whether this was for me. At the end of it, the hiring manager told me I should go sell cellphones, and then maybe we could talk. In my third interview, the manager really liked that I had reached out to him — that's exactly what you need to do on the job. He said he would give me a trial. I quit my construction job and, in January 2024, I started my first sales job. The money was a step back at first, but I wanted to focus entirely on proving I belonged. During my time there, I moved into an account executive role, and after about two years at that company, I moved to my current role at a SaaS company. Construction has a lot more in common with sales than I expected You deal with a lot of different people in construction: electricians, plumbers, and people from different walks of life. You learn social awareness skills that you might not realize you have. I was also already used to working long, hard hours. In every interview, when I mentioned my background in construction, the sales managers would say they knew I was used to working hard and that was not their concern. The hardest part about sales is accepting that most people won't be happy to hear from you You're interrupting someone's day. Even if what you're selling could genuinely help them, most people don't want to talk to you. It's something you have to accept and understand that you'll encounter this every day for the rest of your career. You just have to learn not to take it personally. I try to remind myself — and my team now — that this is work, not life. You spend eight or 10 hours doing your job, but that's not your whole identity. You leave work at work. Financially, I took a step back to take a big step forward In construction, I was earning around $50,000 a year. In my first year in sales, I made around $30,000. This year, I'm on track to pass six figures. In the tech sales roles I see, many base salaries are in the $60,000- $70,000 range, plus commission. It depends on the sales field you're in. Selling condos will have a very different structure from selling tech, but you should be earning a base salary of around $50,000 once you gain some experience. The best part of my new career is that I get to set my own schedule I work from home , so I can literally brush my teeth and sit down at the computer. I don't have to wake up early and drive to a job site anymore. Most days, I work a normal 9-to-5 schedule, but I also have flexibility. During the winter, I'll sometimes work from 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. to take advantage of the daylight and handle school pickup. My advice to anyone who wants to get into sales is to make the leap It doesn't really matter what job you're doing — some of the sales VPs at my company used to work in customer service. If you want to get into a career where you can earn more money by working harder, start watching some YouTube videos to learn the basics of sales. Prove that you can do the job, because sales managers are looking. It's not like other industries, where they only look at your résumé. If you can get in front of the people hiring and show that you can do the job, they'll be more willing to give you a shot. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Dario Strangelove, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the AI Bomb
events.summary: Recently, my wife and I have been rewatching prestige TV classics. First, The Americans and, just now, Mad Men . Both period pieces today read as statements not only about the 1980s and the 1960s, respectively, but about where we still are. One thing stood out in the season two finale of AMC’s booze-soaked Madison Avenue epic: a feeling of living on the eve of destruction that has lasted 75 years and counting. In the finale, “Meditations in an Emergency,” Don Draper watches Kennedy announce Soviet missiles in Cuba. Characters work out where they’d want to be if war occurs. Joan raises civil defense, and Don waves it off. Arguably, nothing about the crisis changes the plot. One critic calls it a clever backdrop. Another says it pushes characters to face what’s already in them. Don has just returned from one of his disappearing acts, and the anxiety of potential annihilation makes people do strange things. The AI safety debate is different in substance but raises the same fears we haven’t shaken since our grandparents’ generation. What happens in a society that is told, over and over, that the end is near? Every generation’s basement I remember it even as a little kid in the ’80s. The Berlin Wall fell when I was 6, and the threat of a nuclear face-off was everywhere in the culture. It didn’t have to be as obvious as Barry McGuire’s “Eve of Destruction.” I heard it in Bob Dylan’s “Subterranean Homesick Blues,” where Johnny is in the basement and the narrator is on the pavement, thinking about the government. I heard the basement as a fallout shelter, though the ever-elliptical Dylan seemed to be paying tribute to the “underground” culture of 1950s Beat poetry. Cue at least one Jack Kerouac quote in your high school yearbook. (The Americans soundtrack was much more Peter Gabriel–coded, as seen in its use of “Games Without Frontiers,” with a character named “Willy,” potentially after West German Chancellor Willy Brandt. The song’s title was the English translation of Jeux Sans Frontières , a European TV game show where teams from different countries dressed up in silly costumes to compete at goofy tasks. Kate Bush sang the French phrase in the backing vocals.) The Beats themselves drew on the French existentialists, a movement reckoning with a godless universe in the age of the bomb. One of the defining blockbusters of the 2020s, of course, is Christopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer , dramatizing the moment this entire culture was created. Naturally, one of the most influential AI-doomsday narratives from the science-fiction canon, 1984’s The Terminator , was the product of action auteur James Cameron, who often references the influence of being 8 years old and watching the Cuban Missile Crisis unfold and reading through his father’s bomb-shelter pamphlets. (Cameron told Rolling Stone in August 2025 that he still fears a Terminator -style apocalypse where you put AI together with weapons systems, even up to the level of nuclear weapons systems, nuclear defense counterstrike, all that stuff.) How much are Cameron’s ideas informing the latest version of American apocalypse? Who’s holding the bomb Stanley Kubrick’s 1964 comedy, Dr. Strangelove, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb , imagined a rogue general ordering an unauthorized attack while the War Room scrambled to stop catastrophe. Its joke was that the machinery meant to prevent the end could cause it. This year’s Tom Cruise megabomb, Digger , seems to be a self-conscious attempt to bottle Dr. Strangelove’ s over-the-top energy, although its subject being climate appears to be misplaced—the real parallel is artificial intelligence. Kevin Roose’s new book, The AGI Chronicles , reveals Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as a man obsessed with atomic questions of risk and danger. He used to hand every new Anthropic employee a copy of his favorite book, The Making of the Atomic Bomb . It also reports that Amodei’s personal hero is one Leo Szilard , the scientist who conceived the nuclear chain reaction (to his own horror) and later drafted the 1939 Einstein letter to FDR that helped lead to the Manhattan Project. Is Amodei’s Szilard-worship so sincere that he’s self-consciously replaying the same steps? On Sept. 12, Amodei published a 3,800-word essay called “We Must Pace the Frontier.” “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote. He said the risks include losing control of AI systems and misuse for cyberattacks and bioterrorism. He proposed outside monitoring, coordination among labs, and international cooperation. In late September, Reuters reported on a prospectus for Anthropic’s planned IPO that warns its technology could pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity,” an odd choice for a financial disclosure because the market would not exist without humans to run it. Cal Newport, the New Yorker columnist and Georgetown computer science professor, recently described this mindset to Ed Elson on Prof G Markets as a “weapon of mass anxiety.” The AI doom talk coming out of Silicon Valley, he argued, is largely the product of an ideological community that has been saying the same thing for 15 years. In his telling, OpenAI, Anthropic, and their loudest critics are in a “family fight” about whether the world is ready for an AI “god” and that many of their concepts, such as recursive self-improvement, are straight out of futurist theory, not computer science. Real wolves To be fair to every generation’s doomsayers, they didn’t make it all up. Janan Ganesh, a Financial Times columnist I admire and read often, made the point in an Oct. 10 column titled “The danger of pessimism fatigue.” The panics of yesteryear, he wrote, “were founded on large, concrete events: Pershing missile deployments, 9/11, a coronavirus.” He walks through the same scares I grew up with: nuclear annihilation in the 1980s, then al-Qaeda, then the pandemic. And he opens with the number that hangs over this whole debate: a 10% chance, according to some in the field, that AI causes human extinction. By Ganesh’s own accounting, though, the alarm outran the threat nearly every time. “Turns out the Cold War was ending, not turning hot,” he wrote, and on al-Qaeda: “The threat was not invented but nor was it ever remotely existential.” There’s also a serious case that the AI wolf is wearing the wrong costume. Arvind Narayanan, a Princeton computer science professor who directs the university’s Center for Information Technology Policy, wrote an influential essay with his colleague Sayash Kapoor called “AI as Normal Technology.” They argue that AI looks a lot like earlier revolutionary technologies, which means we already have a road map for managing it. On Ezra Klein’s podcast last week, in an episode titled “Intelligence Isn’t Power,” Narayanan and Klein debated whether AI is comparable to “electricity, the internet, the bicycle” or “something more like an alien mind.” The “swarms” of agents, Narayanan argued,

events.title: Oil company wins tenders in Channel Country with supply to stay in Australia
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bridgeport Energy already has oil wells in the Cooper-Eromanga basin. ( Supplied: Bridgeport Energy ) An Australian oil company has won tenders to explore for more oil and gas in the Channel Country. Bridgeport Energy has been allocated 270,000 hectares of land with new supply to stay within the domestic market. Traditional owners and graziers want assurances that "significant" flood plains will not be damaged. The head of an Australian oil company says any fossil fuels taken from new land in Queensland's Channel Country will stay in Australia, but it could take years before oil or gas flows. Bridgeport Energy has been declared the preferred tenderer across an extra 270,000 hectares of land between Innamincka and Thargomindah along the South Australian-Queensland border. Bridgeport already has about 90,000 hectares of "oil-producing acreage" in the Cooper-Eromanga basin and processes oil at Queensland's only inland oil refinery in Eromanga. The land allocated for exploration is on the Queensland-South Australia border. ( Supplied: Google Maps ) The state government has been ramping up land allocations to mining companies since 2025. Bridgeport Energy chief executive Christian Lange said he wanted to work "very, very closely" with landholders including graziers and traditional owners before any exploration began. "We need to be cognisant that our disturbance on that land is zero effectively by the time we pack up and leave," he said. Agriculture-conservation alliance wants assurances Western Rivers Alliance is a cooperative between graziers, traditional owners and conservationists advocating to stop new oil and gas activities on Channel Country flood plains. The latest sites are not within the protected Channel Country flood plains where fracking was banned two years ago , but parts are within 5 to 10 kilometres of the boundary. Coordinator Riley Rocco said the alliance was "neutral" on mining outside the flood plains. "But the activity could come quite close to the flood plain and obviously we are keen to make sure that any oil and gas or any industrial activity stays managed well outside of the flood plain in order to not have an adverse impact on those significant river and flood plain areas." In May 2013, a major oil spill in the Channel Country at a Santos-owned well involved the loss of 250,000 litres of crude oil, which flowed for 2 kilometres before the leak was stopped. The Queensland Department of Environment did not prosecute Santos at the time but admitted damage could have been severe if the leak had occurred during floodtime. Mr Lange said impacts on groundwater, fauna, flora, roads and other "land disturbances" would be considered before new exploration begins. He said the small-scale company would use seismic waves to determine whether there were enough "commercial flows" of oil or gas underground. "I would anticipate that it's probably the best part of two years to obtain your authority to prospect, and then preparing to do seismic surveys, whether it's 2D, 3D or a combination of all those things," he said. Gas exploration was banned in some parts of the Channel Country in 2024. ( Supplied: Pew Charitable Trusts ) The latest round of tenders also included 62,500 hectares for the ASX-listed Vintage Energy in the Channel Country, while a four-business consortium won 30,600 hectares of land in the Taroom Trough. In a statement, Queensland Resources Minister Dale Last said increasing the supply of fuels was the "only solution to bring down the cost of energy". The state government has awarded 12 sites for oil or gas exploration since 2025.

events.title: I'm a working parent who's built over 150 AI agents to help run my life. I get digital overload, but I'm getting more time back.
events.summary: Tristen O'Brien has built over 150 AI agents, including an AI family assistant. Sarah Lutomski/Sarah Lu Photography Tristen O'Brien is a working dad who built over 150 AI agents to manage his life and get back time. O'Brien's family has mixed opinions on AI, but they all use the AI family bot he built. He built an AI video game to help manage his agents and reduce digital overload. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tristen O'Brien, a 44-year-old AI educator and content creator who works in cybersecurity based in Indiana. His words have been edited for length and clarity. For a long time, I've felt like I can only focus on three things at a time without everything falling apart: family, work, and school. If I tried to add something else, one of those three things would fail. I've been in the tech industry for over 20 years, and I'm working toward my doctorate in AI . I'm also a YouTuber. I spent years learning the programming language Python because I wanted to create a world where I could automate parts of my life, giving me more time for hobbies and other things. Then ChatGPT came out , and I realized I had wasted about five years doing that. Since learning how to build AI agents , I've built over 150 of them to help me run my life. I'm now down to using around 70. I've always wanted to automate parts of my life There's a book about automating the boring parts of your life with the programming language Python. Years ago, I found this book and decided to learn it. Then, when ChatGPT came out, I quickly got into it. I'm not a developer; I do this by vibe coding. I first used ChatGPT to make funny songs and things like that. My interest kept growing, and I kept doing more with it. I've switched to Claude as my main model now, but I still use ChatGPT , Perplexity, and Gemini. Two years ago, I went to an AI conference where I learned about AI agents. I remember being so excited about what I had learned that I told myself that as soon as I got home, I was finally going to automate my life with AI. I use a specific prompting technique to build my agents The very first agent that I built after the conference was a Chipotle burrito agent that could order my burrito for me. I love Chipotle , and it was silly, but that agent helped me see the power of AI. When I build agents, I'm never just like, " OK, Claude , this is what I want you to do, do the whole thing." Claude has a command called "/goal" that keeps the agent going until it gets the goal right. I think it's helpful, but I've learned to be very clear, or it will mess up. I do what I call my BIP process: Braindump, interview, prompt. I brain-dump everything, explaining what I want it to do, then I have Claude ask me questions about anything unclear or that it thinks I didn't ask. Then it gives me this crazy long prompt. So I might've started with a 15-word prompt , but now I have a 500-word prompt on everything that I want the agent to do. I've built over 100 agents and stopped using some of them In total, I've built five research and education agents, four research and news agents, one agent that builds new products, 18 financial agents, 27 home and family agents , 26 inbox and communication agents, 42 agents for my YouTube channel, and another 27 agents for publicity and outreach. Not all of those agents run at once. For example, I only have 12 active home and family agents: Four run every day for reminders about birthdays, softball, the dog, and school paperwork. Four run weekly for groceries, meal planning, a Sunday family brief, and a weekly check-in coach. One runs monthly for house maintenance reminders, and three run only when something comes up, like travel, packing, or gift ideas. I also had an agent who looked at a Google Sheet with all of my friends' and family's birthdays. If it were two weeks before their birthday, the agent would go to a webpage for a service that would send them a birthday card with what looks like my handwriting, then postmark it from my address. But I stopped using that one because it didn't feel personal enough. AI is more powerful once you learn how to use plug-ins I have a wife and two kids. I think my daughter likes AI a lot, too, because we talk about it a lot, and my wife sometimes gets into it. But my son is an artist , so he's not as big a fan, and I agree that there's definitely a line with creative work and industries. However, one of my favorite agents I've built is our family AI bot, which we all use. I used the texting service Twilio with a Claude plug-in to create an AI agent that is a custom chatbot and assistant for our family. It pings us, and we're able to vote on things like what we want for dinner that week, or see our calendars side by side. This agent helps us organize our lives and stay on the same page. AI gets really powerful when you start using connectors. My Claude agents wouldn't be as powerful if it couldn't connect to my Gmail, my calendar, or Twilio. So, from a technical standpoint, I'd suggest learning how to sign in on those kinds of plug-ins first. I spend around $600 a month on my AI subscriptions, which also support my YouTube channel and other work. If I were just using this for my personal life, I'd probably scale back to the $200 Claude Max subscription. I created an agent hierarchy game I get digital overload sometimes, and there is a point where too much is digital. It was hard to keep up with all my agents, so, in addition to getting rid of some of them, I had to create a digital hierarchy. I'm the chief human officer. I have my AI chief of staff , who works with a handful of director-level AI agents, and those directors each have AI worker agents under them. My chief of staff will relay updates from other agents, so now I'm mainly communicating with one agent who's relaying updates to the rest, which helps with the overload. I also created an animated game world where I can see all my agents running around a village. The different levels of agents have different outfits, so I can tell which one's which. I can run around the game world with my chief of staff and go talk to one of my agents any time to check in on what it's doing. Tristen O'Brien's video game village for his AI agents Courtesy of Tristen O'Brien I can also press a button to call a meeting, and we all go to this meeting hall in the game. It's more of a visual way to see all of my agents, and talk to them individually if I want to. The AI agent meeting room inside O'Brien's AI agent village video game. Courtesy of Tristen O'Brien I worry about privacy, but I'm getting more time back There are a lot of things I don't share with AI, like my Social Security number, but you have to have a level of trust, as you do with Gmail or any other service that is using your data or has access to it. events.title: Fortune’s AIQ Summit: The conversation has moved from experimentation to execution
events.summary: As companies race to adopt generative AI, agents, and new data tools, leaders face a more demanding question than whether to use the technology: How can they turn it into measurable value without creating new costs, risks, and organizational confusion? At the Fortune AIQ Summit at the New York Stock Exchange, executives from the technology, finance, industrial operations, travel, and human resources sectors explored what separates meaningful AI transformation from scattered pilots. The discussion made clear that the strongest companies are not simply distributing AI tools. They are redesigning workflows, developing talent, strengthening governance, and building the data and operating discipline needed to scale responsibly. Together, we explored these key trends: Moving from experimentation to enterprise transformation Building an AI-ready workforce Managing governance, trust, and risk Applying AI in physical and regulated environments Measuring ROI, controlling costs, and creating growth From AI adoption to AI transformation THE MOST IMPORTANT AI QUESTION IS NOT WHETHER A COMPANY HAS DEPLOYED TOOLS, BUT WHETHER IT HAS CHANGED HOW WORK GETS DONE. Speakers warned that widespread access to AI does not necessarily create productivity, business value, or organizational maturity. Diana David, director of futures at ServiceNow , said leading companies distinguish themselves through their commitment to people and operational discipline, not technology alone. In ServiceNow’s Enterprise AI Maturity Index, 57% of “pacesetters” invest in ongoing AI upskilling, compared with 4% of other organizations. The widest gap involves attracting, hiring, and retaining AI talent: 68% of pacesetters do so, compared with 10% of other companies. “Talent investment. That was the biggest gap,” David said. David cautioned against treating broad employee access to AI as proof of success: “95% of everybody has X, Y, Z,” she said. “But it is not translating into productivity, and it’s often not with training, and that doesn’t equal maturity.” The work, she argued, begins with leadership, a clear vision, transparent systems, the right data foundation, and iterative redesign of specific workflows. Paul Fipps, president of global customer operations at ServiceNow, made a related point: The greatest gains will not come from automating old processes faster, but from rebuilding them around new capabilities. “If I just automate or drive autonomous agents to drive the current processes I have, that’s a choice that might get some productivity bump,” Fipps said. “But the ones that are actually rethinking and reimagining the business processes … are really making the difference.” Fipps said companies should deploy AI horizontally, across employee-facing functions such as HR, legal, and technology, rather than isolating it in one department. He cited Standard Chartered , where AI has helped deflect 77% of employee requests. “If you get 25% to 30% deflection in those use cases, it’s game-changing,” he said. “If you get 75% to 80%, it is life-changing.” Amy Webb, founder and CEO of Future Today Strategy Group, was more blunt about the gap between ambition and readiness. “Let’s be fair, Fortune 500 companies are pretty late to the party on this,” she said. “Artificial intelligence didn’t just show up a couple of years ago.” Webb warned that companies are pouring significant capital into pilots without sufficient strategy, leadership, or planning—creating isolated projects that fail to produce durable value. Building the AI-ready workforce AI TRANSFORMATION IS A WORKFORCE TRANSFORMATION. The summit underscored that organizations need more than new software: They need employees and leaders willing to rethink established processes, learn new skills, and make room for new ways of working. Stacy Dillow, executive vice president and chief people officer at HPE , said companies must resist simply inserting AI into existing systems. “We’ve got to force ourselves to think differently, because if we’re not trying to change how we work, we’re just trying to retrofit and put AI in a process that isn’t going to give us a different answer,” she said. For senior executives, she added, AI adoption and transformation have become central management responsibilities. Danielle Gonzalez, chief people officer at Palo Alto Networks , described how AI is already changing the employee experience. A custom AI agent has reduced IT tickets by 83% and supports workflows across HR, finance, and legal. Instead of turning to a human HR partner or business contact, employees can increasingly ask an agent for answers tied to their role and location. Gonzalez said companies should hire and develop people who can adapt rapidly—not only learning new skills but questioning assumptions that no longer hold. “We’re looking for curiosity,” she said. “We’re looking for agency, and we’re looking for those people who can not only learn something at a fast rate … but also unlearn what they thought to be true, so that they can make space to move forward.” Drew Holler, chief human resources officer at Lennar, stressed that the responsibility is shared. “We’re going to give you all the tools, but it’s your responsibility to upskill yourself as well,” he said. “We’re going to give you trainings, but you, as an individual, have to upskill.” The workforce implications extend beyond reskilling. Francis Shanahan, chief technology officer at Peloton , warned that AI-enabled creation can create its own challenge. Employees are “inundated now because they can literally build anything,” he said, and “burnout” is becoming more of an issue. Michelle Kwon, chief operating officer at Runway, urged leaders not to mistake volume for productivity. “Just because you are using AI, that is not a proxy for your productivity or for doing a good job at work,” she said. AI should improve how people work, she argued, without generating additional work for colleagues or overwhelming them with output that has not been properly assessed and synthesized. Governance, trust, and control THE CASE FOR AI MUST BE MATCHED BY A CASE FOR OVERSIGHT. In regulated industries and high-stakes applications, leaders emphasized that successful deployment depends on selecting the right technology, understanding the risk, and keeping human judgment where it matters most. Hari Gopalkrishnan, chief technology and information officer at Bank of America , cautioned companies not to reach for AI reflexively. “One of the biggest mistakes we see ourselves and others doing is rushing to AI as a solution, when deterministic models do a plenty good job,” he said. Bank of America begins with client needs and a detailed inventory of the relevant process; sometimes a conventional mobile feature or real-time decision rule is the better tool. Musk is considered a close ally of President Donald Trump , the leader of the Republican Party, and was a special government adviser to the White House last year. Musk’s political action committee, America PAC, has confirmed the spending totals. In a statement to The New York Times, a spokesperson framed the record amount as necessary to defend Congress from a Democratic takeover during the midterm races. “These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo told the Times. The barrage of spending by Musk comes as Republican candidates are fighting to overcome Trump’s low popularity and rising concerns about the cost of living among US voters. Democrats are hoping to capitalise on voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s tenure to seize control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The influence of wealthy donors and PACs has long been the subject of criticism. Opponents argue that such spending distorts US politics in favour of powerful interests . Musk became the world’s first trillionaire in June, when his aerospace company SpaceX made its initial public offering (IPO) on the Nasdaq stock exchange. The tech entrepreneur had previously said that he planned to step back from his involvement in US politics, stating in May that he had “done enough” and did not have plans for large spending efforts. Still, Musk has leveraged his tech holdings and wealth to support right-wing groups around the world. Last year, for instance, politicians in Germany accused Musk of trying to meddle in the national election. Musk has been a vocal backer of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which has been accused of adopting a discriminatory stance on immigration and other issues. Voters in the US will head to the polls on November 3 to cast their ballots in the midterms, which will decide key state and local races, as well as congressional majorities. The Republican Party is considered to have a sizeable financial advantage over the Democrats ahead of the race, with heavy spending from groups such as MAGA Inc, a pro-Trump super PAC named for the president’s “Make America Great Again” movement. As of August, MAGA Inc reportedly had $416m in its coffers. The tracking site AdImpact found that it had spent $22m over the past month alone on the tight race unfolding for the open Senate seat in Texas. Trump has also increased his campaign activities, hosting a string of rallies in the final weeks before the election to help Republicans push their message . But Democrats appear confident that the Republicans’ spending advantage will not be enough to counter the effects of growing dissatisfaction with Trump. “Republicans are hoping to buy these elections, injecting tens of millions into races to try and outrun their unpopular candidates, unpopular president and unpopular economy,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Democrats’ Senate Majority PAC.

events.title: How to make economy feel like an upgrade, according to a travel expert who's spent 3,500 hours in premium cabins
events.summary: Flight expert Zach Griff shares how to bring the luxuries of first and business class to the economy cabin. Courtesy of Zach Griff Flying economy can feel crowded, cramped, and generally unpleasant. But it doesn't have to be. Here's how to give yourself an upgrade when you're stuck in economy. Economy seats may be smaller than those in upgraded classes, but that doesn't mean you have to be cramped between passengers. Economy tickets may not include a meal, but that doesn't mean you can't have a fine-dining experience. The economy cabin will never be as comfortable as first class , but that doesn't mean you can't make the most of it. Enter Zach Griff, travel expert and author of the travel newsletter From the Tray Table . Griff estimates he's spent 3,500 hours flying more than 1.8 million miles in business and first-class cabins . He flies 150,000 miles a year on average, including roughly 50,000 in economy. With so much experience in premium cabins , Griff has a few tips that make his economy flights feel like an upgrade. Start by booking a flight during an unpopular travel time. Joey Hadden/Business Insider One of the big perks of premium cabins is having more personal space. If you can avoid flying in a crowded economy cabin, you may be more likely to end up with an empty seat next to you, which can feel like an upgrade, Griff told Business Insider. According to Griff, the earliest and latest departures of the day tend to have the most empty seats. Aim for a Saturday or midweek booking, he added. Try to find a flight with two-seater rows. Chris Cooper/Bloomberg via Getty Images Griff said sitting in a row without a middle seat can make economy feel like an upgrade, too. There are rows like this on some wide-body planes, which have two aisles and are typically used for long-distance travel. So while you're searching for flights for your next international trip, take a look at the seat map before you book. Keep checking for open seats until boarding and move to the row with the most space. Joey Hadden/Business Insider When Griff flies economy, he starts checking the seat map for his trip two days before departure to see how full it is. "If it's looking like maybe another row has more space, I'd always move to that row to see if that may end up open," he said. "Monitor the seat map until the minute before boarding starts and move around to optimize your chances of finding an empty seat." You may even end up with your own row. Treat yourself to a nice meal. Courtesy of Zach Griff In many cases, business and first-class tickets come with the added perk of an in-flight meal. If you're in economy, Griff recommends bringing your own dish or getting some takeout on your way to the gate. "Treat yourself to something a little bit nicer because you're sitting in economy," he added. Make sure you're not missing out on any perks from airline status or credit cards. Lino Mirgeler/picture alliance via Getty Images Even if you're flying economy, having a credit card or elite status with the airline may make you eligible for free checked bags, earlier boarding, or possibly better seats, Griff said. Finally, pack your own amenities to stay comfortable. Courtesy of Zach Griff To make flying economy more comfortable, dress in athleisure and pack a sleep mask and noise-canceling headphones, Griff said. If you have a small massage gun, toss that in your carry-on, too, he added. With your mask on, earbuds in, a full belly, and an empty seat next to you, you may feel like you're on the other side of the cabin curtain. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Renewed mineral sands mine bid 'a turd in glitter', resident says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Victorian government 'manipulating' planning laws to win critical minerals race, expert says Kane Busch and his family have been farming vegetables in the Lindenow Valley for 100 years. ( ABC Rural: Fiona Broom ) The Victorian government is assessing a mineral sands mine project it has already rejected. The global critical minerals race is behind the renewed attempt to green light the project, experts argue. The company behind the proposal says claims the project has not been altered since its previous rejection are "misleading and false". The Victorian government is "manipulating" its own planning system to fast track approval for a mining project it already rejected, a leading planning expert claims. The Fingerboards Mineral Sands Project proposed for eastern Victoria was knocked back by the government in 2021, because it would "pose a significant risk to the environment and valuable horticulture industry". But the government is now considering what it calls a "new and modified" bid to get the project off the ground, a description that RMIT emeritus professor of planning and environment Michael Buxton said was a "blatant deception". "The project is not a different project and it's not substantially altered," he said. Michael Buxton worked at the Victorian planning department for more than a decade. ( ABC News: Sean Warren ) Nearby residents who have spent years fighting the mine have a different description of the latest proposal. The company behind the project, Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM), rejected these claims and said its new bid for approval included significant changes. GCM said the site was a rich source of a range of minerals, which had been deemed critical by the Australian government. Miners have been exploring the Lindenow Valley, 270 kilometres east of Melbourne, for mineral sands since the 1970s. Irrigated areas of the Lindenow flats. ( ABC Rural: Emma Field ) Between 2015 and 2023, global demand doubled for mineral sands, which contain concentrated amounts of heavy minerals such as rare-earth elements. Organisations from mining giants such as Rio Tinto to junior mining companies have had a stake in the region, but no project has ever been considered commercially or environmentally viable. After almost a decade of review, in November 2021 the Victorian government rejected a mining project proposed by Kalbar Resources, later Kalbar Operations. In 2023, Kalbar was renamed to Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM) and submitted a "rescoped" proposal. Gippsland Critical Minerals has dug a test pit on its Fingerboards mineral sands site. ( ABC Rural: Fiona Broom ) Dr Buxton, who has been involved in planning for 50 years, including at the Environment Protection Authority and state planning department, said the government failed to follow proper process by accepting the Fingerboards project for a second review. "The minister could have just refused to consider this application — and in my view, should have," he said. Australia's strategic focus on critical minerals for economic and national security reasons was behind the renewed push for the East Gippsland mineral sands mine, he said. "This has provided companies with the opportunity to argue that it's a critical resource." Under the state government's critical minerals road map launched in December 2024, which outlines efforts to build a globally competitive critical minerals sector, eight mines are at various stages of approval. University of Sydney professor of global governance Susan Park said she was "not surprised at all" that rejected minerals projects were getting a second look. Dr Park said trade and security agreements between Australia and allies such as the United States were driving state and federal support for mining projects. The proposed Fingerboards mine site, 25 kilometres west of Bairnsdale. ( Supplied: Gippsland Critical Minerals ) In February, the Australian government gave the Fingerboards proposal Major Project Status, which gives "strategically significant projects" extra support to navigate regulatory approvals. GCM bills the project as a major source of "ex-China production" of the rare-earth oxides dysprosium and terbium, elements on Australia's critical minerals list. China controls almost all of the world's production and rare-earth refining. Terbium and dysprosium oxides, used in renewable energy and military technologies, are almost completely supplied by China. The Lindenow Valley is a highly fertile region known for its leafy salad vegetables, brassicas and sweet corn. Up to 2,000 workers harvest about 200,000 tonnes of food every year.

events.title: Satya Nadella went from H-1B worker to Microsoft CEO. The Trump administration just shut that path for his employees
events.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has written that his story wouldn’t be possible anywhere but the U.S. On Thursday, the Trump administration moved to block his company from helping its own foreign-born employees follow the path he took. Vice President JD Vance announced on Oct. 8 that the administration is suspending Microsoft from the Labor Department’s Permanent Labor Certification Program, known as PERM—usually the first step when an employer sponsors a foreign worker for a green card. Adobe and six IT services firms—Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services , Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini —were also suspended . Hours later, President Donald Trump presented Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, one of the country’s highest honors for innovation. What the suspension actually does The Labor Department said it won’t accept new PERM applications from the eight companies, nor process those already in the pipeline . The move doesn’t touch H-1B visas, the temporary work permits overseen by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. PERM comes later: To use it, an employer must advertise a job and show that no qualified, available U.S. worker can fill it before sponsoring a foreign employee for permanent residency . Most applicants are already working in the U.S. on H-1Bs. Microsoft is the program’s biggest user. The Labor Department ruled on 3,161 of its applications in the fiscal year that ended in September 2025, more than for any other employer, according to a GeekWire analysis . Asked how long the suspension would last, Vance said it would “last as long as it needs to,” adding that the administration has “a number of tools to suspend it indefinitely.” Doug Rand, a former senior USCIS advisor in the Biden administration, called the move “incoherent,” telling the Associated Press that a green card frees a worker from depending on an employer for immigration status. Vance singles out Microsoft “So if the H-1B visa is how the people get into the country, the PERM program is how they stay in the United States to begin with,” Vance said at a White House news conference . “Now there has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft. “Microsoft laid off last year 6,000 American workers,” he said. “At the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.” He added: “In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants.” Vance also took aim at the H-1B program as a whole. “The H-1B visa program is meant to allow companies to bring in really the best of the best from outside the United States of America for positions that are completely impossible to fill with American workers,” he said. “Unfortunately, the program has become rife with fraud over the last several years, probably the last several decades.” The White House has not provided evidence of fraud by Microsoft, the Seattle Times reported . Federal data complicates Vance’s framing. Microsoft received 6,258 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, ranking third behind Amazon (19,178) and Meta (6,294), neither of which was suspended, CNBC reported based on USCIS data. About two-thirds of Microsoft’s approvals went to people already working at the company. Vance acknowledged the awkward timing. “Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them,” he said, but added that the administration would “deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.” Microsoft pushes back In a statement , Microsoft said: “We believe in the strength and talent of the American workforce. That is why the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans. We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information. “Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people,” the company said. “The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country.” The company also rejected the suggestion that its visa holders are underpaid. “Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” it said. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.” The statement did not directly address the PERM suspension. Nadella’s own path from H-1B to CEO Nadella was born in Hyderabad, India, and came to the U.S. in 1988 to study computer science, earning a master’s degree from the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee in 1990. He worked at Sun Microsystems before joining Microsoft in 1992, and later earned an MBA from the University of Chicago. He has been CEO since 2014. His route to citizenship wasn’t a straight line. In his 2017 memoir, Hit Refresh , Nadella recounts marrying his wife, Anu, in India in December 1992, while he was a permanent resident. Her visa application was rejected because she was married to a green card holder, and the wait could have stretched for years. So in June 1994, Nadella went to the U.S. embassy in New Delhi and gave up his green card, reverting to an H-1B so his wife could join him right away, GeekWire recounted . He later regained permanent residency and became a U.S. citizen. The PERM program itself didn’t exist then; it took effect in 2005 , replacing an older labor-certification process. But the route—H-1B, employer sponsorship, green card, citizenship—is the one many of Microsoft’s foreign-born employees are now on. Nadella has not commented publicly on the suspension. He did thank Trump on X for the medal, writing that he was “humbled to stand alongside so many giants of American innovation.” A medal, hours later At the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit at the U.S. Institute of Peace, Trump called Nadella “a key figure in the transformation of Microsoft, revolutionizing the company and empowering businesses, students, and consumers from all over the world with some of the most capable software ever built or ever even conceived.” Nadella shared the technology medal with Michael Dell of Dell Technologies . Trump also awarded the National Medal of Science to Elon Musk, Sergey Brin, Jensen Huang, and Lisa Su. Of the six honorees, only Dell was born in the U.S. Musk was born in South Africa, Brin in the Soviet Union, Huang and Su in Taiwan, and Nadella in India.
