events.title: Losing your job after age 50 could derail your career
events.summary: Thomas Heep (left), Steven Fielding (center), and Jon McCarty (right) struggled to find work after losing their jobs later in life. Thomas Heep (left), Steven Fielding (center), and Jon McCarty (right) Some Americans who lose their jobs after age 50 spend years struggling to find comparable work. In September, the average unemployment duration for workers ages 55 to 64 was over eight months. Some older job seekers suspect age discrimination is hurting their chances of finding work. Cathy Valentine lost her job as a transformation lead in 2023. After three years struggling to find a comparable full-time job, the 61-year-old is now a prep cook at a cafe. She said she earns about an eighth of her previous salary. "It just feels like I tried to do everything right and I still am stuck," said Valentine, who lives in Florida. Some older workers who lose their jobs can afford to retire, while others find a comparable role fairly quickly. But those who don't risk getting stuck in a job search that drags on for months or even years — and is getting longer. On some metrics, older Americans are doing just fine in the job market . As of September, older workers had lower unemployment rates than younger workers, and when they were jobless, the median length of that unemployment was shorter. But those figures obscure a worse trend for older job seekers . While half of 55 to 64-year-olds were jobless for a relatively low three months, the group's average unemployment duration was more than eight months in September. That means some older workers have been unemployed for so long that they're pulling the average way up. The gap between the average and median has widened in recent months, suggesting the longest job searches may be growing even longer. In September, about 173,000 unemployed Americans ages 55 to 64 had been out of work for at least six months, and some are facing far longer stretches of unemployment. A Bureau of Labor Statistics analysis found that only 57% of workers ages 55 to 64 who lost their long-held jobs any time between 2023 and 2025 had found new jobs as of January 2026. By contrast, 73% of workers ages 25 to 54 who lost long-held jobs in that period had found new work. Some older workers may have taken their job loss as a sign they should retire. But for others, it marked the beginning of an uphill battle to find another job. The struggle to get hired after 50 As their searches drag on for months or years, older job seekers like Valentine often blame age discrimination for at least part of their struggles. Thomas Heep, a Denver resident in his 60s, has been searching for full-time work since losing his operations manager role in April 2025. He's struggled to pay his bills and filed for bankruptcy earlier this year. Heep suspects some employers may favor younger job seekers over someone his age because they worry he won't remain in the workforce much longer. "Even if a company loves my résumé, skill set, and work history, they're going to look at my age and go: How long is he going to stay? He's close to retirement age. It's too risky." he said. Thomas Heep has struggled to find full-time work since losing his job last year. Thomas Heep Other older workers suspect their salary expectations may be working against them. A former Big Tech employee in her early 60s who lost her job last year said she worries her years of experience may put her at a disadvantage compared with younger candidates willing to accept lower pay. "There's so many people getting laid off at this point who are younger, willing to take these ridiculously low salaries with no benefits," she said. While some research suggests age discrimination plays a role in hiring, proving it in any individual case can be extremely difficult. And for older job seekers who suspect their age is holding them back, there's often no clear path to addressing the problem. Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . When finding another job feels out of reach For some older workers, a prolonged job search eventually leaves them with two options: settle for lower-paying work or give up looking altogether. Jon McCarty spent 18 months trying to find another software engineering job after losing his role in 2022. Earlier in his career, it typically took him about a month to find a new job. But he said that as he got older, his stretches without work grew longer. McCarty, who's in his early 60s and lives in Virginia, eventually took a part-time cashier job at Home Depot. He's come to believe he'll likely never return to his former career. Jon McCarty spent more than a year searching for another software engineering job. Jon McCarty Steven Fielding, 58, has been laid off more than five times during his career in tech communications. He's been looking for work since April and said the employment gaps over the course of his career have taken a toll on his finances, leaving him with little in savings. Fielding, who lives in Washington state, said he's trying to adapt to the changing job market, including by developing his AI skills . He suspects his age may be contributing to his difficult search, in part because he believes some employers prefer younger workers who are willing to accept lower salaries. Still, he's hoping his decades of experience can help him land another opportunity. "It's like my house is down to the foundation and I'm going to have to rebuild again," he said. "It's pretty daunting to think about." Do you have a story to share? Reach out to the reporter via email at jzinkula@businessinsider.com , or via Signal at jzinkula.29. events.title: IonQ to acquire cybersecurity firm Elisity in an all-stock deal for up to $1.3 billion
events.summary: Quantum computing platform IonQ said it will acquire cybersecurity company Elisity in an all-stock deal for up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in performance-based earnouts. The combined entity will give IonQ expanded tools to detect and defend against AI-driven cyberattacks. IonQ's shares were down about 9% Monday. Quantum computing platform IonQ said on Monday it will acquire cybersecurity company Elisity in an all-stock deal worth up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in performance-based earnouts. The move is designed to defend against and uncover attackers targeting generative artificial intelligence large-language models and AI agents, and to protect against emerging quantum threats, the companies said in a press release . CEO Niccolo de Masi told CNBC's Morgan Brennan on Monday that the addition of Elisity's platform will help bolster his company's quantum security strategy. "This means that we can protect not only critical infrastructure — we believe better than anyone in the world — but of course the Fortune 500," de Masi said. The all-stock deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to regulatory approval, and would expand the quantum-computing company's cybersecurity portfolio. IonQ shares fell more than 9% in afternoon trading. Other quantum computing stocks, including Rigetti Computing and D-Wave Quantum , also traded lower. Elisity will retain its current leadership, including CEO James Winebrenner. AI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlight Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans control Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them Hollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AI IonQ's stock has surged in recent months amid a buying spree. Most recently, the company bought semiconductor maker SkyWater Technology for $1.8 billion in July. In the past year and a half, IonQ has acquired several quantum companies, most notably U.K.-based quantum computing startup Oxford Ionics . The deal follows two June executive orders from President Donald Trump aimed at building a quantum computer for scientific research by 2028 and protecting government systems from cyber threats. IonQ said in the release that the orders underscored the urgency of preparing for quantum computing threats. De Masi told CNBC on Monday that the need for quantum-level security integration into government and business as outlined in the executive order will become all-important as "Q-Day" — the era where quantum computers can break today's standard encryption software — draws closer. "Lab leaks" from frontier AI companies such as OpenAI 's high-profile Hugging Face hack are just the beginning compared to cyber capabilities a year from now, de Masi said. "Our technologies help you today. They also set you up, of course, as well as you can today, for an era where the bad guys will eventually get quantum computers. They will eventually be able to marry them, I fear, with LLMs, and so the world that we're in today is already dangerous," De Masi told CNBC, adding that LLM's "could do even more dastardly things." "Frankly, people are not ready," he said.

events.title: NATO says will do ‘anything and everything’ if alliance is attacked
events.summary: NATO commander issues warning as European officials suggest potential Russian attacks. NATO’s top commander has warned that his forces would destroy “anything and everything” if someone was “foolish enough” to attack the alliance, as European concerns have mounted over a potential Russian attack on its territory amid the war in Ukraine. “We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us,” US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich told the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, without mentioning Russia by name. list 1 of 3 ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil? list 2 of 3 Ukraine’s Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ list 3 of 3 From a ‘dangerous competitor’ to an unknown: Who could replace Zelenskyy? Grynkewich stressed that NATO is a defensive alliance and that he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable. The most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to “resolve misunderstandings”, he added. European governments have accused Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks against them, while Russia warned last month it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Baltic Kaliningrad exclave where it has a major military outpost. NATO’s 10-year strategy, created in 2022, described Russia as the alliance’s most significant security threat. “We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile,” Grynkewich said. Attacking anything that ‘supports, sustains and controls that force’ Grynkewich added that NATO’s response would not be limited to forces involved in an initial attack. “Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us,” he said. “This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls that force.” Russian President Vladimir Putin said this month that Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully. Such declarations have not reassured European leaders, who cite similar statements by Russia before its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Moscow has also repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage and other hybrid operations. Grynkewich said he had decided to talk publicly about NATO’s plans because recent acts of sabotage and arson had made people around the alliance nervous. “What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it,” he said. Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington’s commitment to the alliance , citing President Donald Trump’s reception at a NATO summit in Ankara in July. “I was in the room and I felt the love,” he said.

events.title: One chart shows white-collar biz is thriving even as jobs dry up
events.summary: Employment in white-collar sectors has dipped, while output is surging. Maskot/Getty Images Employment has dropped in white-collar sectors, while output has continued to surge. AI and economic uncertainty are two likely reasons for the sluggish white-collar job market. Still, how productive AI makes companies remains a question. The white-collar sector is doing more with less. While the number of total jobs has slid in industries like finance, tech, and professional services, output has been on a tear. Gad Levanon, the chief economist at the Burning Glass Institute, examined how employment in white-collar-heavy sectors compares with real gross domestic product . He wrote in a Substack article that employment in finance, insurance, information, and professional and business services is collectively down roughly 2% since the end of 2022, while real output for these sectors has soared by 16%. The ongoing slow decline in employment for this group goes against historical patterns and highlights how workers and job seekers are facing a largely frozen, low-hire, low-fire job market . "A growing share of the work businesses used to get done by consultants, contractors, call centers and their own back-office staff is now delivered by software, cloud and IT firms, which produce far more per worker and add almost no staff," Levanon told Business Insider. "That is why the sector's output keeps rising while its hiring has stopped." The divergence also risks breaking the traditional link between economic growth and rising fortunes for everyday Americans. "Even a strong, continual growth in GDP may not translate into jobs for people, may not translate into a higher quality of life for people as well," said Cory Stahle, an economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab. People looking in these kinds of sectors may be having a challenging time. "It's important to remember for these job seekers that a career is not necessarily built over the course of two or three years," Stahle said. "It's usually built over the course of two or three decades. So what the pattern is now could easily shift a couple of years from now. So it's important to be reactive but not overreact to what we're seeing in the data, either." Have you been job searching in these white-collar sectors? Have you had to make a career pivot? Reach out to this reporter to share what that's been like at mhoff@businessinsider.com . Levanon said on Substack that there's demand in these white-collar fields, but firms can meet it with fewer workers. Part of that could be due to employers shifting their priorities toward leveraging AI . Levanon said "the back-office and junior tasks" that AI performs best at are concentrated in the white-collar sectors he looked at. Dante DeAntonio, senior director at Moody's Analytics, previously told Business Insider that the lack of hiring in white-collar fields is largely due to uncertainty around economic policy and AI. Other job market experts have noted that in Big Tech, employers pulled back after the pandemic-era hiring surge. The job market's woes can be especially difficult for people who lack years of experience. "Firms, I think, are certainly diving in with both feet, trying to find ways to gain efficiency from AI," DeAntonio said. "And certainly the first domino to fall is likely to be a pullback in hiring amongst younger workers, new college grads, positions where firms think they might be able to get some uptick from AI, and some sort of replacement value from AI." Whether companies are actually more productive because they're incorporating AI tools remains a question. Eric Kutcher, a senior partner and chair of McKinsey North America, recently said that there are individual productivity increases , rather than institutional-level gains. "You have people that are getting more productive as individuals, but they're just changing some of the work that they're doing," he said. Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed general labor productivity has increased, but not at a wildly accelerated clip. "We have seen that things have slowed down in the last few years, but output per worker and productivity was climbing even before we saw ChatGPT and AI starting to come onto the scene," Stahle said. "To me, that says that AI is part of the story here, but not the complete story. This is part of a longer-term trend." Have you been job searching in these white-collar sectors? events.title: Airlines raised fares as fuel costs surged, but Delta’s CEO says those higher ticket prices could be here to stay as long as demand holds up
events.summary: Airfare has shot up this year partly because of the war in Iran. But even if oil prices ease, higher ticket prices may be here to stay because travelers keep buying, said Delta CEO Ed Bastian. The CEO of one of America’s biggest airlines said in an interview with CNBC Friday that he was surprised the airline’s profits held up despite a 60% jump in fuel prices, as demand for tickets stayed resilient. In July, after the airline’s second-quarter results, Bastian told CNBC that Delta was passing along 60% of its higher fuel costs to consumers, and expected that to reach close to 100% in the third quarter.  “To not dent those profits, to me is incredible,” said CEO Ed Bastian in an interview with CNBC. He added that the 60% increase in its jet fuel costs in the third quarter was a $1.6 billion increase. “In past cycles, past shocks, if we saw a 60% increase in fuel prices, we’d be flat on our back.” The company last week reported $17.6 billion in adjusted revenue for the third quarter, a 16% year-over-year rise but just short of analysts’ $17.67 billion estimate. While the company spent an adjusted 62% more than the same time last year in jet fuel, its revenue per seat mile—the measure of how much money an airline earns for each seat it flies one mile—went up 15%, reflecting higher fares and strong demand. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Bastian credited consumers for helping the company maintain its profits, despite these price increases. “Fuel has been the impetus for the industry to move quickly to adjust the pricing environment. But given the fact that the market has accepted these price points,” and given that the company still views airfare as reasonably affordable, Delta’s position is very sustainable, he said. “I think we’re going to be fine as you look forward. Hopefully, we will see fuel recede into the next year at some point, and that’s when I think you’ll see the real earnings power of this franchise be amplified,” he said on the earnings call. The continued strength in the airline sector comes as the average price for domestic trips hit $445.26 in the second quarter, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics . Airline ticket prices increased about 23% year over year, according to the U.S. Travel Association . Skyrocketing oil prices Higher oil prices are partly to blame for the increase in airfare. Oil surged this year due to the war in Iran, which has crippled transit through the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the war. The price of Brent crude oil on Monday stood at $108, up more than 70% from a year ago .  Airlines are particularly susceptible to increases in oil prices. After labor, fuel costs are airline companies’ biggest expense , making up about 21% of their operating costs as of earlier this year, according to Airlines for America, a trade association and lobbying group.  Because jet fuel prices generally move with oil prices, they rise in tandem, and as such, jet fuel prices are already up more than 100% compared to a year ago, according to the International Air Transport Association. U.S. Gulf Coast jet fuel cost $4.34 a gallon on Thursday, almost double the $2.19 of a year earlier, according to CNBC . Unlike their European counterparts, U.S.-based airlines also don’t hedge against rising oil prices, meaning increases often get passed on to the customer. Delta, for its part, bought an oil refinery more than 10 years ago through a subsidiary, which helps offset fuel costs. Delta is the first major U.S. airlines to report third-quarter earnings, but other CEOs have also noted airlines’ sales resilience in the face of rising fuel costs. Southwest Airlines CEO Bob Jordan told CNBC in July, “Despite high fuel and high prices, we’re seeing really strong demand.” In prepared remarks during American Airlines’ second-quarter earnings call, CEO Robert Isom said , “Consumer spending remains resilient, underpinned by a healthy labor market and a sustained preference for travel relative to other discretionary categories.”  Higher fares haven’t fully protected Delta from rising fuel costs. The airline last week cut its full-year profit outlook to between $5.10 and $5.60 per share, down from its previous forecast of $6.50 to $7.50. It also missed Wall Street’s earnings estimate for the first time in two years . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Jeremy Strong argued with Aaron Sorkin in-character as Mark Zuckerberg over this one line in 'The Social Reckoning'
events.summary: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Reckoning." Sony Jeremy Strong loves going Method, talking and acting like his character even when cameras aren't rolling. So "Social Reckoning" director Aaron Sorkin wasn't surprised Strong acted like Mark Zuckerberg on set. He was surprised, though, that Strong became such a big Zuck defender. Jeremy Strong is known for his intense Method acting on set. But even "The Social Reckoning" director Aaron Sorkin was surprised by how all-in Strong went in embodying Mark Zuckerberg . Sorkin, who had worked with the acclaimed actor on two of his previous directing efforts, "Molly's Game" and "The Trial of the Chicago 7," wasn't shocked when Strong showed up on " The Social Reckoning " set speaking and acting like the Facebook founder. But Sorkin never imagined Strong would end up becoming a staunch Zuckerberg defender in the process. "I knew he's a very immersive actor," Sorkin told Business Insider . "I never heard him use his own voice. He only spoke as Mark, he only behaved as Mark. But I didn't expect that he was going to be a constant defender of Mark. Not just on the set, but the emails I would get at night at the hotel." Sorkin said this continued even in post-production, when Strong, still in-character as Zuckerberg, argued with his director over a line in the movie. "The Social Reckoning" tells the story of former Facebook employee turned whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), who leaked hundreds of thousands of documents to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen-White) that revealed Facebook's algorithm was designed to spread inflammatory content and encouraged extremism, at the expense of users' safety and mental health. Jeremy Strong and Aaron Sorkin. Sean Zanni/Getty Images Strong-as-Zuckerberg wrote Sorkin about a scene in which his character has been debating Bill Burr's character Charlie, a fictionalized former Facebook investor, about free speech and fact-checking advertisements. "He ends the debate by saying, 'It's a business, Charlie. You know why we don't fact-check ads? Because we don't have to. Are you new?'" Sorkin recalled. "Jeremy felt that it was just about money. That Mark was saying this is a business, it's about money, and that's why we do it," Sorkin continued. "But that was not the argument that Mark had been making for the entire movie, which is that it's a free speech thing. That Facebook is the town square. So my feeling was Mark isn't saying it's about the money, Mark actually, in that moment, is making the same argument Frances is making at the end, which is, talk to the people who make the laws. I'm not your guy, talk to Congress . Well, that line is in the movie, so I won the argument."  Despite the challenges, Sorkin said he wouldn't change anything about how Strong goes about his job. And it doesn't sound like Strong has plans to. "If some people feel that I'm taking it too seriously, or it changes the molecules in the room in a way that makes something uncomfortable, I guess that's something that I don't feel that I need to apologize for," Strong said in a recent interview with The New Yorker about his acting style. "The Social Reckoning" is in theaters now. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Businesses blindly sending billions in profits to the tip with their food waste
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Food waste costing Australian businesses and the economy billions Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Karl Riseborough was shocked when he realised how much food was wasted at his brewery each week. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Australia wastes about 7.6 million tonnes of food each year, costing the economy more than $36 billion. Less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspect their food waste, and operational methods mean it can go unnoticed. The federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030, but some experts are concerned about progress. When Karl Riseborough realised how much food went to waste each week at his Sydney pub and brewery, he was shocked. Grain left over from the beer-making process was thrown out, as well as food waste from the kitchen. What surprised him most was the volume of waste on top of the spent grain. "The food scraps coming back, the plate waste, the kitchen prep waste … you don't really notice when it was all going straight into the bin," Mr Riseborough said. Food waste expert Belinda Chellingworth said many traders had no idea how much waste they were generating, or how much it was affecting their bottom line. The capacity of landfill is reaching a critical level in some areas. ( ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale/File photo ) Every year about 7.6 million tonnes of food is wasted in Australia at a cost of more than $36 billion to the economy . Of that wasted food, 70 per cent is edible and there are critical knock-on effects for landfill management, food security and the climate. With the support of Ms Chellingworth, who happily calls herself a "garbologist", Mr Riseborough has stopped throwing away 50 kilograms of spent grain from each batch of beer he brews. Karl Riseborough is saving thousands a year after some simple changes. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) "Now I have regular users who come and collect it once I've brewed and use it for the benefit of their gardens or their animals," Mr Riseborough said. "We had two 240-litre bins that were getting collected each week. We're now down to one bin collected each fortnight." He said that saved him about $5,000 a year. Australia's hospitality sector wastes 1.2 million tonnes of food each year, according to the Sustainable Restaurant Association. The economic impact of food waste in the food service sector is about $6.4 billion , averaging about $66,000 annually per business. Belinda Chellingworth says many businesses do not realise how much food they waste. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Ms Chellingworth said less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspected their food waste. "Typically, many businesses, if they've got food left over at the end of their operations or the end of the day, then it will be landfilled," she said. "For many businesses, and particularly large businesses, the cost of food waste across their operations isn't fully realised because they incur it multiple times, but it's not obvious." Food waste will be a point of discussion at the COP31 conference. ( ABC South West WA: Jacqueline Lynch ) For example, over-ordering food is a cost to the kitchen. If it is not sold, that is a revenue cost, and then whatever goes into the bin also involves a cost for collection. "So they're paying for it multiple times, but they're different departments, different cost centres, and it's often not added together, so they don't understand the full cost across the whole business," Ms Chellingworth said. Landfills are nearing capacity in parts of Australia. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) She said landfill capacity was reaching critical levels in many areas. Some tips in Perth are set to run out of space in two years and sites in New South Wales are set to reach capacity in four years . Victoria's capacity is expected to be reached in the next 10 years. To combat the economic and environmental impacts of food waste, the federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030 . But UNSW food and health professor Johannes le Coutre does not believe the plan is on track. Johannes le Coutre says tackling food waste will help to ease food insecurity. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) "I'm not sure if that's attainable or achievable with the current landscape," he said. "In Australia we have a unique situation in that we are dealing with a big distance and that even in the food industry a lot of value-added manufacturing occurs overseas.

events.title: Cuba forges ahead with renewable energy plans amid US oil blockade
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Cuban energy minister denies link to fuel shipments intercepted by US, says oil imports by private firms insufficient. The Cuban government is pushing ahead with its plans to transition to renewable energy, amid a de facto oil blockade from the United States that has strangled the island’s economy. In an interview with the Reuters news agency on Monday, Cuban Minister of Energy and Mines Vicente de la O Levy explained that the blockade has forced Cuba to explore domestic alternatives to foreign fuel imports. list 1 of 4 Cuba works to restore power after another major nationwide blackout list 2 of 4 US open to Cuba talks on government change, Marco Rubio says list 3 of 4 Cuba condemns US ‘collective punishment’ as Trump predicts deal list 4 of 4 Cuba accuses US at UN of deliberately inflicting humanitarian suffering “We are seeking our own alternative solutions, using our own resources, our sun, wind, tides, fuel, Cuban crude oil and the gas produced in our wells,” de la O Levy said. He said 144 solar farms with a combined capacity of about 1,418 megawatts have been installed on the island in recent years. China has been the largest supplier of solar panels to the island, and shipments have increased since the blockade began in early January. At the time, US President Donald Trump halted all oil shipments from Venezuela, a close ally of the Cuban government. Later that month, Trump also announced he would impose heavy tariffs on any country that exported oil to Cuba, justifying the threat by calling the island’s government a “national security” threat. Since then, only a single oil tanker from Russia has reached Havana. The US has increased its shipments of oil to Cuba’s private sector, but it has largely barred fuel exports for nationalised industries on the communist-led island. The government-run electrical grid, widely considered to be antiquated, relies heavily on fossil fuels. Only 40 percent of Cuba’s electricity comes from ‌‌‌‌domestic ‌‌‌‌oil production, according to the International Energy Agency. As of 2023, only nine percent of the country’s energy consumption was covered by renewable sources. De la O Levy admitted in his interview with Reuters that the country was facing difficulties. The blockade has caused shortages of medicine, water and fuel, pushing Cuba to the brink of a humanitarian crisis. “We are surviving and moving forward, little by little, even if not at the pace we would like,” he said. “We face long hours of blackouts and lack fuel for cooking and transportation. We lack fuel, but we are gradually making headway through our own solutions and our people.” Cuba’s production of domestic crude oil remains stable, he added, but is almost entirely allocated to power plants. The United Nations and human rights watchdogs have criticised the oil blockade as a violation of international law. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla also condemned the oil blockade in his speech at the UN General Assembly last month. “It is an unusual and unprecedented action,” Rodriguez said of the blockade. “A superpower unilaterally deprives all states of their right to export the commodities that they wish to the country that they wish.” The US has maintained an economic embargo on Cuba for more than 60 years, since the Cold War era. But since taking office for a second term as president, Trump has sought to squeeze Cuba’s economy further, as part of a “maximum pressure” campaign. His administration has indicated that it wants to topple Cuba’s government . On October 7, US authorities announced they had seized 90 biodiesel fuel shipments valued at over $2.8m destined for Cuba. “These shipments were part of an attempt to unlawfully export fuel to Cuba in violation of federal export laws,” US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said in a statement. But in his interview with Reuters, de la O Levy denied the Cuban government had any link to the shipments. “No Cuban state-owned company has managed to secure a fuel contract, whether for small or large quantities,” he said. He added that any US oil shipments to private firms fall far short of the country’s requirements. “I would venture to say that the amount entering the country doesn’t even cover 3 percent of its fuel needs,” de la O Levy said.

events.title: This entrepreneur says Amazon nearly destroyed his business. He still shops on it every week. 'It's crazy.'
events.summary: Business Insider Jack Nekhala's Bed Scrunchie sales faced a major hit after Amazon deactivated his seller account. Nekhala says the loss left the founders in debt, yet he still shops on Amazon several times a week. The habit bothers him more than he can explain. Jack Nekhala has every reason to stop shopping on Amazon . His company, Bed Scrunchie, generated about $4.5 million in 2024 and was on track for more, Nekhala said. However, Amazon deactivated its seller account just before the holidays that year, cutting off its biggest sales channel. "Once the collapse happened through Amazon, it basically collapsed the entire business," Nekhala told Business Insider for our So Expensive video series. That makes his next admission harder to say. "I still shop on Amazon ," Nekhala said. "I have a daughter. She needs bikes. She needs a scooter, she needs all sorts, she needs different things. And that's the place we go to." He said he shops on Amazon two to three times a week and sometimes has several orders in a single day. The habit bothers him more than he can explain, he said. "Continuing to shop there feels like being forced to sit down to dinner with the institution that upended your life." Founders of the Bed Scrunchie: Jack Nekhala (left) and Michael Nusinkis (right). Courtesy of Jack The account shutdown, he said, left him and his business partner carrying debt and trying to rebuild the financial security they had spent nearly 20 years creating for their young families. "My life has not been the same," he said. For Nekhala, his Amazon shopping habit reflects how deeply the online marketplace has become embedded in everyday life. In a recent survey of shoppers across the US and Europe, 75% of consumers said they buy from Amazon at least once a month. "I do not shop there because I have forgiven what happened. I shop there because Amazon has made itself so convenient and embedded in everyday life that even people who feel harmed by it continue to depend on it," Nekhala said. "It's crazy," he added of his own shopping habits . "It's really incredible what they've accomplished." Amazon became the default Jack Nekhala launched his Bed Scrunchie product in 2019. Business Insider The appeal of Amazon isn't just price. It's the convenience, Nekhala said. Amazon already has his payment information, shipping addresses, and purchase history. Adding one more item to an order is often easier than creating an account somewhere else, he said. "They remove all the friction," Michael Nusinkis, Nekhala's business partner, said. "I think you just have this muscle memory. I need to buy something — Amazon," Nusinkis added. The founders saw that same behavior from their own customers. Before Amazon deactivated their seller account, the pair aired a national television infomercial directing viewers to a website where they could buy the Bed Scrunchie directly for $39.99. On Amazon, the product sold for $44.95. And they said Amazon sales of the item consistently spiked whenever the infomercial aired. "All advertising roads lead back to Amazon," Nekhala said. Nekhala said customers would likely discover the product on television or the company's website, then go to Amazon to compare options, read reviews, and buy it—even at a higher price. Surveys suggest up to three-quarters of Amazon shoppers start their product searches there. Even after losing their account, the business couldn't leave Amazon The bed scrunchie is designed to prevent sheets and mattress toppers from sliding off a mattress. Business Insider After months of disputes with Amazon , including allegations that the company had infringed its own patent and violated Amazon's review policies, Nekhala and Nusinkis lost their seller account. The founders dispute both allegations. They now sell Bed Scrunchie to a third-party distributor, which keeps it available on Amazon for $49.99. Nekhala estimates that Amazon still accounts for 70% to 80% of the company's sales. That means shoppers may see the Bed Scrunchie name on Amazon without realizing they are buying from a reseller—not the small business that created it, he said. "Amazon shut out the people who invented and built the product, yet the product remains on its platform at a higher price," Nekhala added. "That contradiction is what makes continuing to shop there so painful." Nekhala said the company would rather sell the product for less on its own website. But he believes Amazon's pricing policies make that difficult: Listing it more cheaply elsewhere, he said, could mean the product loses visibility or prominent placement on Amazon. As a result, he said, sellers keep prices in line across retailers, even when it means customers pay more. That's one of the practices at the center of a lawsuit California's attorney general filed against Amazon, alleging it pressures brands and third-party sellers to raise prices at competing retailers so Amazon isn't undercut. In a statement to Business Insider, Amazon says its goal is to protect customers from overpaying and maintain trust in its marketplace by comparing prices with other reputable retailers. If a product is listed for less elsewhere, Amazon says it may choose not to prominently feature that offer, though it remains available for purchase. Amazon also argues California's case relies on a handful of emails taken out of context and says the challenged practices are common retail negotiations designed to deliver "low prices, vast selection, and unmatched convenience" for customers. events.title: Loophole allowing new coal and gas to avoid stricter climate laws
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coal and gas avoiding stricter laws by expanding existing mines, Climate Council warns Hunter Valley Operations was recently approved for an extension that will include mining new seams and additional emissions. ( ABC News ) Coal and gas mines have to follow less strict emissions laws when they are expanded compared to outright new mines. The Climate Council says that amounts to a "loophole" being used by the industry to add new emissions without having to follow "best-practice" limits. The Safeguard Mechanism, which sets emissions laws for heavy industry, is under review. Coal and gas mines are using what the Climate Council warns is a "loophole" to expand operations and add new emissions while avoiding stricter laws imposed on new coal and gas projects. The Climate Council says unless emissions from mine expansions are treated the same as emissions from new mines, it will cause an additional 4.5 million tonnes of CO2 a year by 2035. Coal and gas mines are among the roughly 200 facilities covered by the Safeguard Mechanism — climate laws that require Australia's biggest polluters to cut or offset emissions by about 5 per cent a year or else face heavy penalties. Under the laws, which are currently being reviewed, new coal and gas facilities are required to follow more strict, "best-practice" limits that take into account the most efficient technologies available for mines. But existing facilities are not required to meet that higher standard when expanding or extending the life of an existing mine. Modelling by Reputex has estimated that across 22 planned coal and gas expansions and extensions over the next decade, which will be treated as existing facilities, they will be able to emit 11 times more than if they were treated as new facilities. The Climate Council says expansions are being used widely across the industry, taking advantage of that favourable treatment and leading to more emissions. "Companies have an incentive to characterise everything as an expansion rather than a new facility," chief executive Amanda McKenzie said. "We're arguing that is one of the loopholes that needs to be shut." Amanda McKenzie says less stringent climate laws for mining expansions compared to new facilities amount to a "loophole" that should be closed. ( Supplied ) The Safeguard Mechanism is under review and due to be revisited next year, when the government will decide whether to set a steeper trajectory towards net zero emissions by 2050. The Climate Council says when that time comes, "best-practice" CO2 limits should be applied to all new coal and gas emissions, regardless of whether they come from a new mine or an expanded one. It says fossil fuel facilities are not doing enough to transition to net zero, and those covered by the Safeguard Mechanism actually increased emissions in the most recent year. Most new coal and gas emissions from expansions The council says since the Safeguard Mechanism laws were amended in 2022, more than three quarters of all new coal development have been expansions or extensions to projects. It pointed to last month's approval for an open-cut coalmine in the Hunter Valley , which owners Yancoal and Glencore applied to extend by more than a decade. Its life extension into the 2040s, which includes the mining of deeper coal seams, represents an additional $2.7 billion capital investment and will add an extra 809 megatonnes of CO2 emissions — or a bit less than two years' worth of Australia's annual emissions. The NSW Independent Planning Commission approves plans that will allow Hunter Valley Operations to continue coal mining at a site near Singleton until 2045. Because the Yancoal-Glencore owned coalmine was already covered by the Safeguard Mechanism, the extension will be treated under rules for existing projects, which the Climate Council estimates will result in emissions 60 per cent higher than if it was treated as a new project. The NSW Independent Planning Commission, which approved the life extension, said while it would contribute to climate change and add to Australia's emissions, that was outweighed by its benefits, including supporting up to 1,400 local jobs and ongoing tax revenue from the mine. "Despite these new investments being significant enough to require a new environmental approval, the vast majority of their pollution will not be considered 'new' by the Safeguard Mechanism," the council said.

events.title: A massive trade just happened in surging shares of Snap
events.summary: Don't call it a comeback yet, but shares of beleaguered social media stock Snap Inc. are up almost 20% this month and options traders are betting it's about to go on a big run. Snap shares have traded under $10 since July 2025 following a near-complete collapse from over $80 at the stock's high in 2021 to a low of $3.81 in April. But now, as excitement swirls over social media giant Meta Platforms' AI agent, traders are pouring into Snap call options on Monday, propelling trading volume to more than four times the month-long average, Cboe LiveVol data show. Almost 140,000 options on Snap traded Monday, including about 64,000 call trades that were likely initiated by buyers, compared to under 7,000 puts. Traders sold more than 12,000 puts, and just over 34,000 calls. The net trade sentiment, as well as net directional bias according to options deltas, was positive, according to Barchart. Nine out of the top 10 trades by volume were calls, and of the $5.5 million in premium exchanged, $5 million was tied to calls, SpotGamma data show. The most popular contract to buy was the 8-strike call expiring Dec. 18, which traded 26,000 times. That contract costs about 37 cents and needs Snap to rally 30% before expiry to pay off. If that happens, it would be the highest the stock's traded since February. The owner of photo-sharing and messaging app Snapchat also offers augmented-reality `Specs' glasses. Shareholder Blue Duck Capital issued an open letter to Snap's board of directors last week urging the company to raise dedicated capital to support the product, saying it could lead to a $12-$14 share price.

events.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
events.summary: Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros. Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected. The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack. More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them. Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss. The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely. Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process. Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified. The firm added in s statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date. "Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to." The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France. Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed. In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon. The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible". Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported. As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires. French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C. Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions. French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France". European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality." In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible". He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable". Have you been affected by this cyber attack? Share your experience . events.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar blasts federal criminal raid on home: 'I will not be silenced'
events.summary: The Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, was raided as part of a federal criminal investigation. Omar, who was born in Somalia and brought to the U.S. as a child, has been repeatedly criticized by President Donald Trump. The raid took place less than a month before November's midterms, where Omar is seeking reelection. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced." Federal authorities raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation of the Minnesota Democrat. Omar, who has not been charged with a crime, said she was being targeted for political purposes because of her opposition to President Donald Trump . A person familiar with the situation, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the nonpublic investigation, told CNBC that the probe of the 44-year-old congresswoman is complex and has been going on for years. MS NOW reported that a law enforcement source with direct knowledge of the raid — which comes weeks before November's midterm election — said the investigation into Omar is based on allegations of fraud. Fox News , which first reported the raid, cited a source familiar with the probe as saying it is focused on her immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her father when she emigrated to the U.S. with him from Somalia as a child. Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the Department of Homeland Security , conducted the raid. HSI investigators were seen outside Omar's home in the Northeast quadrant of Washington throughout the morning. Omar, who is seeking reelection, has been a target of criticism by Trump for years. She heckled the president during his State of the Union address to Congress on Feb. 24, which came on the heels of aggressive immigration enforcement actions in Minneapolis by federal authorities. Omar, who is deputy chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, blasted the raid and the investigation in a post on X on Monday. "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she wrote. Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 at 17. She was elected to Congress in November 2018 to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis. She and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., became the first two Muslim women elected to Congress. Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' The Department of Justice, in a statement to CNBC when asked about the raid, said, "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice." "This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," the DOJ said. Omar's spokeswoman, Jacklyn Rogers, in a statement said, "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies." "For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," Rogers said. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies." In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that DHS was investigating issues around Omar and her family's immigration to the United States. "There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with," said Mullin. He said the investigation could end with deportations. The DOJ, for years, has had a policy regarding the announcement and initiation of federal investigations and prosecutions close to elections. The policy discourages beginning an investigation, taking investigative steps, bringing criminal charges, or making public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or to give a candidate an advantage or disadvantage. The person familiar with the raid on Omar's home told CNBC on Monday that the DOJ does not consider that action to violate the policy because the raid was not meant to be public. Republican John Nagel is running against Omar in a race the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates "solid Democrat." The general election is just over three weeks away on Nov. 3.

events.title: I'm a former flight attendant who still travels all the time. Here are 6 dos and don'ts for surviving long-haul economy.
events.summary: As a former flight attendant, I've learned ways to make long-haul economy flights more bearable. Alona Vasylieva I was a flight attendant for nearly 10 years and still fly frequently as a passenger. I bring different outfits for the plane and the airport, and a plastic bag for clutter. I skip the neck pillow and never drink airplane coffee. Before I stepped away from my flight attendant job after nearly 10 years in the sky, I picked up a lot of tricks for making long-haul travel more bearable. Now, as a passenger who regularly flies economy, I stick to the same system every time. From packing multiple outfits to deplaning last, here are my 6 dos and don'ts for long flights . I get to the airport extra early — and I switch outfits twice. I get lounge access via credit card benefits. Alona Vasylieva Some people want to spend as little time as possible at airports , but I prefer to arrive super early to take advantage of my credit card's lounge benefits for a mental preflight. Having that quiet, unhurried time allows me to get into the right headspace before stepping into a metal tube for hours on end. And right before boarding begins, I head to the restroom and change out of my street clothes for a soft, breathable tracksuit so my body can relax right away. Then, right before landing, I pop into the lavatory to change back into my original outfit. That quick final wardrobe change acts as a complete mental reset — it switches my brain into "arrival mode," so I step off the aircraft feeling fresh , organized, and sharp. I bring a small plastic bag to keep from feeling cluttered. I always bring a way to keep my already small space clear of litter. Alona Vasylieva I don't want to linger in the aisle during boarding, so I split my packing into two categories: my main carry-on suitcase stays overhead until after landing, while a compact pouch under the seat holds my earplugs, snacks, cables, a change of clothes, and moisturizer. But my favorite habit for long-haul comfort is tucking a small plastic trash bag into my seat pocket. Flying with my family always turns into a quiet contest of how fast snack wrappers, empty bottles, and used wipes can take over our row. Bringing a small trash bag keeps everything in one place, so we aren't stuck spending a long flight sitting in a pile of clutter . I book seats near the emergency exit and use the call button sparingly. I always try to book an aisle seat near the exit row. Al Drago/Getty Images Old habits run deep, so I always book an aisle seat — mostly because my flight attendant brain still feels a deep need to be within quick reach of an emergency exit. It's an instinct I can't shake from years of safety drills. My flight attendant days also guide how I interact with the crew. I remember answering endless call lights for simple requests during busy meal services or safety checks, so I make it a point, as a passenger, to save the overhead button for urgent needs or when I can't safely wait. Instead, I wait until the crew isn't mid-service and it's safe to move around the cabin to stretch my legs or walk to the galley for more water. And when nature calls, I time my trip using operational cues: I find the lavatories are often cleanest and have the shortest queues right before the galley carts head out for meal service or halfway through trash collection. I skip the neck pillow and sleep aids in favor of a simple eye mask. I prefer the airline's provided linens when flying. Aviation-images.com/Universal Images Group via Getty Images As soon as I sit down on the plane, I adjust my watch and phone to my destination's local time. If it's 2 a.m. there, I try to rest right away, even if it's bright outside or meal service carts are rolling down the aisle. I used to take sleep aids like melatonin, but stopped because it often left me groggy after landing. Now I rely on a light-blocking eye mask, magnesium, which I find helps me unwind, and mental timing. I also skip the neck pillow. A hoodie hood and a standard airline pillow work for me. What I've found works best for sleeping upright in economy is using the headrest, reclining slightly, supporting my lower back with a rolled sweater, and keeping my seatbelt fastened so flight attendants don't have to wake me during turbulence. And I don't recommend trying TikTok sleep hacks without first checking the airline's rules: those viral Amazon foot hammocks, for example, are banned by some carriers because they attach to the tray tables and could hinder evacuations. I stick to bottled water and lighter meals on overnight flights. One of the meals served on defunct Ukraine International Airlines, the carrier I worked for before leaving during COVID to be a journalist. Courtesy of Alona Vasylieva I avoid tap water, coffee, and tea on flights. Aircraft water is regulated and often safe, but a January 2026 study by the Center for Food as Medicine & Longevity, a nonprofit, found that water quality and tank maintenance can vary by airline. So, personally, I prefer to bring my own sealed water bottle. I also add electrolytes to my bottled water because I find they help me feel better in the dry cabin air, which can otherwise leave me with post-flight headaches and exhaustion. And I completely skip the late-night hot meal service on overnight flights. For me, digesting a heavy dinner at 30,000 feet while sitting leaves me bloated and makes it harder to sleep. Instead, I always pack a small tote bag full of healthy, high-protein snacks from home — like nuts, seeds, and berries — to keep me nourished without feeling heavy. I'm always among the last people to deplane. Unless I'm rushing to make a connection or an activity at my destination, I am the last person to deplane. Patrick Smith/Getty Images The exact moment the plane touches down and the seatbelt sign turns off, people often leap out of their seats and stand, squeezed shoulder to shoulder in the aisle. I do the exact opposite: I sit back, let the initial crowd filter out, and take my time. I use those extra quiet minutes to check every seat pocket, the floor, and the overhead bin above me. In my crew days, I handled plenty of forgotten items, and the process of getting them back is nowhere near as quick as people think. Once you step off the plane, you usually can't simply walk back on to grab a lost phone or passport. In many cases, the crew has to log every item on an official form, hand it over to ground staff, and wait for it to be processed through airport lost and found. Spending a few extra seconds taking inventory can save hours of bureaucratic panic later. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tasmania's financial windfall from mine leads to creation of future fund
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Windfall from King Island tungsten mine shares to support new Tasmanian future fund The Dolphin Tungsten Mine recommenced operations at Grassy on King Island and in 2023 started commercial production of tungsten concentrate. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) In 2023, the Tasmanian government acquired 12 per cent of the shares of a struggling tungsten mine after its owner could not repay a $10 million loan. The price of tungsten has since significantly increased. A recovery fund will be set up to insulate Tasmanians in major industries from workforce impacts. The Tasmanian government will create a $20 million future fund to help regional communities "navigate economic disruption" and "attract new investment". It follows the government stepping in financially to save King Island Dairy, and industrials Bell Bay Aluminium and Nyrstar from collapse, as well as dealing with the loss of more than 200 jobs after Australia's last manganese smelter Liberty Bell Bay shut down. The money for the new Recovery Fund for Regional Resilience will come from the government's $10 million investment in King Island's tungsten mine. The mine is on King Island's south-east coast. ( Facebook: Group 6 Metals ) The Dolphin mine, which boasts the largest tungsten deposit in the country, is owned by Australian company Group 6 Metals. The mine shut for more than two decades due to low tungsten prices, but reopened in 2023 with the help of the $10 million loan. Under new ownership, the initial $10 million loan was converted into shares, of which Tasmania's government holds 12 per cent. The mine has since experienced a significant financial turnaround, rewarding investors like the government. Tungsten is classified as a critical mineral used in heavy machinery and defence manufacturing. The state government also lent the mine a further $7.5 million last year. The Dolphin mine is Australia's largest mined tungsten deposit. ( Supplied: Group 6 Metals ) Mine proceeds to help reduce state debt Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the government's investment in the mine would allow it to reinvest in regional communities. Government issues loan to mine after becoming a shareholder A struggling tungsten mine couldn't pay back a $10 million loan as it sat on the brink of administration. So a state government became a shareholder — and issued a new loan. "Our regional communities are at the heart of Tasmania's economic success and they deserve the confidence that comes from knowing support will be there when it is needed most," Mr Rockliff said. ​"The strong investment made by the Tasmanian government to support the future of the King Island tungsten mine has allowed us to reinvest a significant portion of the windfall back into the very regions that helped generate that success. ​"This fund is about transforming a one-off financial return into an enduring asset for regional Tasmania." The government said the fund will be able to support communities experiencing significant economic disruption, including responding to major industry change, employer closures, workforce impacts and other economic shocks. "Too often, governments are forced to react after a major employer closes or an industry undergoes significant change," he said. ​"Instead, we are getting ahead of those challenges by establishing a fund that will help communities navigate economic disruption, attract new investment and create new opportunities for the future. ​"The Recovery Fund for Regional Resilience will help support economic diversification, workforce transition, investment attraction and community-led recovery initiatives when communities face significant economic disruption." The government said proceeds from the mine investment would also go towards reducing the state's debt, which is estimated to peak at just under $10 billion by the end of the decade. Speaking on King Island on Tuesday morning, Premier Jeremy Rockliff shed more light on the significant windfall from the state government's investment in the mine. The original $10 million loan, which later became equity, is now worth in excess of $75 million in shares it will now look to sell, he said. "Well, at this stage we've got the $20 million fund for regional resilience fund, $5 million for the school, and we expect to put about $50 million back to paying off the debt," Mr Rockliff said. "Our expectation … was to see the revival of the mine and for us to recoup the funds that we invested, of course, but it's exceeded expectations," he said.

events.title: What colleges and universities need from donors to thrive
events.summary: Graduates pass the John Harvard Statue during Harvard University's commencement on May 29, 2025. Harvard was the school's first big donor. Craig F. Walker/The Boston Globe via Getty Images In 1638, John Harvard , an English-born Puritan minister and teacher in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, bequeathed 400 books and half his £779 estate, today equivalent to roughly US$2 million, to the college that would be renamed in his honor after his death. In addition to launching America’s oldest university, Harvard’s donation began a tradition of philanthropy for U.S. colleges and universities that has continued ever since. Today, philanthropy is an important source of higher education funding that covers an average of 10% of college and university budgets . Based on our decades of experience as scholars , academic administrators and school fundraisers , we believe that donors – and not just big ones – are especially important to colleges and universities in tough times. In the crosshairs Since January 2025, the Trump administration has targeted colleges and universities with research funding cuts , student financial aid caps and new restrictions on how long international students can stay in the United States . University endowments have been in the crosshairs since the first Trump administration’s 2017 tax reform package . The big 2025 tax-and-spending package Trump signed raised the taxes on some schools’ endowments . A rule the Trump administration proposed in September 2026 would threaten private schools’ tax-exempt status if any of their programs use race-based criteria. There are demographic problems too. Fewer students are choosing to go to college, and the number of high school graduates who could attend is falling due to a declining birthrate . Although colleges and universities are providing more financial aid than ever , students and their families are still struggling to pay for college . Some schools are being forced to close their doors. Sixteen colleges shut down in 2025 alone , including Indiana’s only predominantly Black college, Martin University, and ecologically focused Sterling College in Vermont. And at least 40 colleges have been acquired by other schools since 2020, including Marymount Manhattan College and Mills College , which are now part of Northeastern University’s global network. A sticky note spotted at Hampshire College’s Harold F. Johnson Library on May 16, 2026, months before the school was slated to be closed for good, assured students that alumni would support them. Finn Gomez/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Higher education giving Donors contributed $79 billion to colleges and universities in 2025, up 4% in constant dollars from the year before. The richest Americans dominate giving to higher education: 89% of the funds raised came from only 2% of donors in 2025. Also in 2025, Phil and Penny Knight, the Nike co-founder and his wife, made what was then the largest single gift to a university in history when they gave the Oregon Health & Science University $2 billion for cancer research . On Sept. 30, 2026, investor Ken Griffin broke that record by giving Carnegie Mellon University more than $3 billion to build a new campus in Miami and meet some other priorities. It’s hardly the only megagift a university has received in 2026: Michael and Susan Dell, whose fortune comes from his computer hardware company, gave the University of Texas at Austin $750 million for its medical center. The Knights gave $1 billion to the University of Oregon for a new engineering college. Software billionaire David Duffield pledged $371 million to Cornell University . And many other schools have drawn gifts in excess of $100 million . The vast majority of these huge gifts are reserved for specific purposes . The share of totally unrestricted gifts to colleges and universities , those given with no strings attached, has been dwindling for decades . In 2024 it slipped below 7% . Unrestricted giving did pick up somewhat in 2025 . Perhaps that was a sign that some donors were responding to federal funding cuts with their gifts. Michael Dell, CEO of Dell Computer, and his wife Susan have given more than $1 billion to the University of Texas at Austin, with much of that funding reserved for specific purposes. Robert Daemmrich Photography Inc/Corbis via Getty Images How donors can help In an article in Change: The Magazine of Higher Learning in September 2026, we listed ideas for college and university fundraising efforts. These tie to three recommendations for donors – and not only those making multimillion-dollar gifts. 1. Pooling donations Donations to colleges and universities don’t have to end in lots of zeros to make a big difference. In 2015, the grassroots Saving Sweet Briar campaign kept the small women’s college operating even after its trustees had voted to close it. The largest gift the rural Virginia school received was $2 million, and the smallest was $1.50 from a graduate’s grandchild. This is the exception rather than the rule. Financial pressures were too much for Hampshire College, a New England private college that is slated to close after the fall semester of 2026, to withstand – even with a fundraising campaign and $5 million gift from alum and documentary filmmaker Ken Burns. Giving Days are high-profile fundraising campaigns through which many alumni and other supporters raise millions. For example, Oregon State University Dam Proud Day 2026 drew 12,400 gifts and raised over $4.1 million. Purdue University’s annual “day of giving” has generated nearly $500 million over the past decade. In 2024, it garnered $76 million from 32,000 donors. Sweet Briar College alumni take a selfie in 2015 at a pop-up fundraiser to save the womens’ college in Virginia. Evelyn Hockstein/For The Washington Post via Getty Images 2. Donating with few or no strings attached Donations with few restrictions or none at all help colleges and universities meet their greatest needs. Even if they’re mostly intended for a new building or to fund a particular program, large gifts can also include unrestricted portions to help cover costs as needs arise and priorities change. Brandeis University , Indiana University , Princeton University and other schools encourage unrestricted annual gifts. These flexible funds are helping to cover research funding shortfalls at Cornell University, undergraduate scholarships at Georgetown University and general operations at the College of the Atlantic. Novelist and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, the former wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, has given more than $26 billion in unrestricted donations to nonprofits, including to colleges and universities. Historically Black colleges and universities as well as other schools with diverse student bodies , such as Robeson Community College in rural North Carolina, Oklahoma’s Carl Albert State College and Wisconsin’s Fond du Lac Tribal and Community College, have received Scott’s big gifts. events.title: 7 red flags to look out for when getting a manicure, according to salon owners
events.summary: There are a few things clients should look out for before sitting down for a manicure. ViewStock/Shutterstock Business Insider asked salon owners about the red flags to watch out for when getting a manicure. Unidentifiable products and overly aggressive techniques can make for a poor experience. Look for dirty or loose tools and poor ventilation when entering a salon. Whether you want a Japanese gel manicure or French tips for your next big event, choosing the right nail salon is crucial to achieving the look you desire and preserving your long-term nail health. That's why Business Insider asked salon owners about the red flags clients should look out for when getting a manicure at a new salon. Here's what they said. Check to make sure your nail tech isn’t using dirty tools. Lipatova Maryna/Shutterstock Patricia Reign, a licensed manicurist and the owner of Traveling Aura Mobile Spa in Florida, told BI that one of the most important things to check for before getting a manicure is that the tools are properly sanitized. "Tools like nail clippers, cuticle nippers, and pushers should be taken from a clean, sealed packet — which often indicates the salon uses an autoclave, a professional-grade sterilization device," Reign said. "However, be cautious. Some salons may use these packets without sterilizing the tools." She added that if the nail technician pulls tools directly from a drawer, they may have been placed there after being used on another client. Misused sanitization boxes can also be an issue. webphotographeer/Getty Images Amy Ling Lin, CEO and founder of the nail-care brand and NYC salon chain Sundays , told BI that misusing sanitization equipment, notably LED-light sanitization boxes, is just as bad for clients as using dirty implements. "For salons that use an LED light sanitization box, ensure no paper towels are under the tool plates. Paper towels can block the light, preventing proper sterilization of the tools," Lin said. Beware of unusual odors and poor ventilation in the salon. Edvard Nalbantjan/Shutterstock Reign told BI that unusual odors in a salon are a major red flag health-wise. "Any strange or strong odors in the salon could signal poor ventilation or the use of low-quality products, which might contain harmful chemicals," Reign said. "A salon should be well-ventilated and free from overpowering chemical smells." A messy workstation is a no-go. Patricio Nahuelhual/Getty Images Jessie Pang, owner of New York-based business Jessie P Nails , told BI that a messy workstation containing spilled nail products or personal items is one of the biggest red flags to watch out for. She said to take note of any nail clippings, food crumbs, or stains left at the station. "Cleanliness should be the priority at the station," Pang said. Unidentifiable products are often a bad sign. Anton Starikov/Shutterstock High-quality salons will typically use well-known, professional products, according to Reign. "If the products being used are not clearly labeled or identifiable, this could be a sign that the salon isn't using professional-grade products," Reign told BI. Don't hesitate to ask questions about any of the products a nail technician uses. Not including nail preparation and cuticle care in the service can lead to poor results. Marc Calleja Lopez/Getty Images According to Kasia Pukeca, owner of Gloss Nail Co. in Florida, some salons don't offer full manicures as part of services like gel polish or dipping powder. However, she said things like nail preparation and cuticle care are a must. "There is no way to achieve an ideal product application if the nail plate and cuticles are improperly prepared," Pukeca said. Overly aggressive techniques during a service can cause issues for the client. Yuliia Pavaliuk/Getty Images Monica Victoria, owner of Nail Garden Austin , encourages all salon goers to pay attention to any pain or discomfort they experience during their manicures. "Aggressive filing, cutting, or scraping of cuticles or nails can lead to small cuts or tears in the skin, resulting in open wounds, infections, or long-term damage to your nails and the surrounding skin," Victoria said. The best way to avoid long-lasting, unnecessary issues from aggressive techniques is to tell your technician to stop as soon as possible. "Promptly addressing these issues allows the technician to adjust their technique or properly clean and disinfect the area to prevent further harm," Victoria told BI.
