One of the core promises of AI is that the more it knows about a person, the better it will be able to assist them with tasks and make appropriate suggestions, which, if you’ll believe the tech companies, requires apps and devices to listen, watch, or record users’ activity all the time and gather all possible context. There’s obviously privacy and data security concerns with anything that’s collecting data about you continuously. But startups are building such apps undeterred anyway, arming themselves with the belief that the market for personalized assistance is big enough to swallow such concerns. Former Plaud exec Peter Mo is building Ambi to do something similar. The app aims to provide real-time intelligence and insights to people by listening to them all the time. The company said on Monday that it has raised $26 million across multiple funding rounds led by Luminous Ventures, which has backed companies like Meituan and Unitree Robotics, and original design manufacturer (ODM) Huaqin. Ambi is also releasing apps for iPhones, Macs, and Apple Watch. These apps act like meeting notetakers, but users can choose to have them listening so they can capture context all day. Meeting notetaking companies have been working to automate tasks that follow once calls are done, based on the summaries and action items they gather during the conversation, and using multitudes of connectors to software systems. Ambi wants to take this a step further by having its agent start the work during the meeting itself. The company’s promise is that its AI agent can proactively give you suggestions or surface relevant knowledge while you are in a meeting, based on your calendar, meetings, knowledge base, and web data. Users can also start a task on one device and continue it on another. “The way we interact with intelligence is limited. Often the intelligence is trapped on the screen, and if you use hardware like Plaud, you need to wait for recording to transfer to the phone, upload to the cloud, and get intelligence after processing. That’s why we are building Ambi to use AI anytime and anywhere,” Mo, the company’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch. The company has ambitions to capture more information. Its upcoming desktop app will be able to look at the work that users do and store important parts in its memory to give more personalized suggestions. Apps like Littlebird or Minimi already do something similar. The startup is also planning to launch its own hardware device, which will have a screen, a speaker, a camera, and microphones to capture context and display information. Ambi’s launch comes amidst growing concerns around AI devices that don’t have enough indicators to suggest they are capturing data on people around the user. It is not clear if Ambi’s apps or its upcoming device will have enough indicators to alert third parties that their conversations are being recorded if the user doesn’t disclose their use of Ambi’s tech. Some meeting notetakers have even been sued because their tech recorded people’s conversations and data without their consent. Plus, the recent release of Apple’s Audio Intelligence feature, which transcribes speech continuously, has raised privacy concerns . Mo said that users can turn off ambient data capture on Ambi’s apps and devices at any time, and the feature is off by default. The startup said it doesn’t store any recordings of users and encrypts the data, but it didn’t specify what kind of encryption it uses. Despite these measures, the onus of declaring ambient capture is still on the users. He classified this as an industry-wide problem. “We have to inform our users that they have to tell others about ambient capture. We, as an industry, haven’t solved this problem [of disclosure]. We have tried to put the information about disclosure in every place possible, but if users try to hide the capture, we can’t just solve the problem,” he said. Ambi currently has over 50 staff across offices in San Francisco, Beijing, Shanghai, and Shenzhen. The company is hiring for its go-to-market function and AI engineers for working on speech-recognition models. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Saudi plans to expand oil export routes to cut Hormuz reliance
events.summary: Saudi Arabia plans to expand its oil pipeline network to cut its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz. Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said today that a gas pipeline is being converted to carry crude as well and could move around 1 million barrels a day within eight weeks, rising to 3 million with further investment. “We may end up with 10 million barrels of pipeline within two to three years, that can divert oil to a different destination,” he said, adding that the government, not Aramco, is footing the bill. The urgency is growing as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine strain global oil supplies : Goldman Sachs raised its year-end oil price forecast over the weekend citing thinning inventories. But Iran is “ not likely to stand by ” as new export routes emerge, experts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies warned. — Matthew Martin

events.title: Turmoil within Dolly Parton’s estate underscores the precariousness of family businesses after founders die
events.summary: Dolly Parton waves to her fans at Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., in March 2024. Amy Harris/Invision via AP Dolly Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver announced the legendary singer’s death on Aug. 25, 2026, in a prerecorded video. Seaver, the son of one of Parton’s 11 siblings , had been her head of security for many years. But Seaver is currently embroiled in a messy dispute with She’s Alive LLC, the company Parton established to manage her business assets after her death . This unusually acrimonious fight highlights some of the business succession problems that can arise when the founder of a company dies but wants its other leaders to keep it going. Parton, a legendary American singer, actress, entrepreneur and philanthropist, left behind an estimated US$450 million estate . She’s Alive LLC terminated Seaver’s involvement with the business, and a court has issued a restraining order against him. Seaver is accused of engaging in “ an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats” against Parton’s estate . He denies the allegations. As professors who research and teach topics related to inheritance law, we are fascinated by the Parton case. It illustrates some of the pitfalls of planning for the transition of a privately held business after the founder’s death – a concern for celebrity and noncelebrity estates alike. Following Dolly Parton’s death, there has been turmoil in her management involving her nephew Bryan Seaver. Managing celebrity estates after death Celebrity estates, like Parton’s, are distinct because they often contain valuable intellectual property. This includes copyrights, which protect creative works , such as songs and recordings, including Parton’s catalog of hits. Another valuable asset in these estates are publicity rights , which protect the use of the celebrity’s name or likeness, such as the use of Parton’s face on a T-shirt sold for profit. These rights can be enormously valuable long after the celebrity has died. Without careful planning beforehand and appropriate management after death, the estate may never get the full value of these property interests. Prince, for example, died in 2016 without a will or any formal estate plan. The twice-divorced Minneapolis pop star had no surviving children. His estate passed to his siblings, who were his sole heirs . It took more than six years to administer his complicated $156 million estate , which concluded with the heirs establishing corporate entities to manage his intellectual property rights. One of those entities, Prince Legacy LLC, recently became embroiled in litigation when some of Prince’s heirs sought to fire the managers who had been hired to manage their share of the intellectual property rights. Marilyn Monroe, who died in 1962, also without any children, left behind a professionally drafted will under which her longtime acting coach, Lee Strasberg (and his then-wife) inherited most of her publicity rights. But Strasberg remarried, and his widow – a woman whom Monroe never met – hired various professional managers, including a company known as CMG Worldwide , which specializes in the management, marketing and promotion of publicity rights associated with dead celebrities. Because of the successful management of her estate’s publicity rights, Monroe became known as one of the highest-paid dead celebrities – with large sums enriching a woman she’d never met. Marilyn Monroe’s will is seen on display at Julien’s Auctions in Beverly Hills, Calif., in 2012. Joe Klamar/AFP via Getty Images Should a founder’s relatives remain in charge? Many much-less famous family businesses face similar questions about how to keep their profits and revenue flowing and who should manage the company after the founder of a family business dies. A continuation of business operations may have many benefits for a deceased founder’s family. The founder may have relayed their succession plans to them. Relatives often have institutional knowledge and loyalties that can enhance the value of the business and make it last longer. Studies have not conclusively shown, however, whether continuing a business within the family is clearly better or worse for its bottom line than having outsiders manage it. As one study found, family managers often have a “ sense of kinship obligation ” and enjoy “personal and social fulfillment” from working together in the business. That, in turn, creates incentives to manage the firm carefully with an eye toward long-term survival. By contrast, another study of small and medium-size businesses after the sudden death of a CEO-owner found that, in the short run, nonfamily successors are better equipped to run the company . Relatives, by contrast, may be hampered by grief and the emotional impact of the death. But the study also found that in the long run, family members may be more successful in managing the business because they “are likely to view the firm’s survival as a way to stay connected with the deceased family member and keep their memory alive. In turn, this is expected to inspire great stewardship towards the firm.” Other studies, however, have found that maintaining family control over the management of a company after its founder’s death can hurt its performance. Restricting the pool of potential managers to relatives excludes better-qualified candidates who can bring expertise and experience that members of the family lack. Research has shown that hiring pros tends to be best for the business . Death can be bad for business When the owner of a privately held business dies, their assets, including real property, intellectual property and investments, will pass to others according to the estate plan, if the owner created one. But in many cases, the true value of a business is more than just the sum of all its assets. Some of the value may reside in the owner’s talent, knowledge and business acumen. In some cases, the owner maintained personal relationships with employees or customers that may have played a key operational role. In others, the owner may have relied upon unique personal qualities to achieve success in business. Parton herself, for example, was likely the most significant driver of value for her business because of her creativity and star power. According to a 2022 study by economists who studied what happened to startups following the death of nearly 1,500 business founders, growth and profitability fell after the founder’s death. Smaller companies are at risk of having to close altogether. The study found that the negative effects on business continuity “appear to be driven by entrepreneur specialness rather than leadership transition,” which suggests that the founder’s unique contributions to the business can be difficult to replicate after death even with excellent transition planning. events.title: Business faces a more interventionist Washington post-midterms
events.summary: Both parties will be pressured to intervene more in markets after the midterms as economic frustration animates the new Congress, according to an FGS Global sketch of 2027 Washington scenarios, shared first with Axios. Why it matters: In a Trump-dominated Washington, Congress ceded much of its power and relevance. That'll change three weeks from Tuesday if Democrats win the House, as expected, and perhaps the Senate in the midterms. The new analysis by FGS , a worldwide strategic leadership advisory with huge clients, is a sequel to a popular FGS report that Jim VandeHei and I used as the basis for a series of popular "Behind the Curtain" columns before the 2024 elections. FGS bills "Alternative Futures: Beyond November" as a framework for processing the epic battles ahead: how power will get used, how both parties will evolve, and how business leaders can navigate the uncertainty. "The 2026 midterms will begin — not end — a 27-month period of unusually high strategic uncertainty," the report says. Zoom in: Michael Feldman — FGS partner and co-chairman, North America — tells me that for Republicans, "intervention may mean tariffs, industrial policy, domestic manufacturing incentives, and other measures aimed at strengthening U.S. production capacity, economic security, and competitiveness." "For Democrats, intervention may mean affordability policies, labor protections, antitrust enforcement, plus regulation designed to reduce costs, curb concentrated corporate power and address inequality." "Everyone is focused on who controls Congress," Feldman added. "We think the more important question for business is what happens next. The midterms are the beginning, not the end, of a period of significant political and policy uncertainty." Left: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) campaigns in Linden, N.J., last year. Right: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) campaigns in Davenport, Iowa, last week. Photos: Getty Images Zoom out: Three structural shifts will drive the post-midterm operating environment for businesses of all sizes, FGS warns. " Voter dissatisfaction may be the most important force pushing both parties away from established policy orthodoxies. A frustrated electorate could push both parties toward more populist, interventionist and less predictable approaches to business." "Technological disruption could reshape the political agenda as profoundly as traditional partisan conflict. AI and related technologies are becoming a political variable — not merely a sector-specific policy issue." "Generational turnover will weaken established political assumptions even where ideology remains unchanged. The next generation of leaders may inherit existing parties without inheriting their relationships, orthodoxies or governing style." The bottom line: "Divided government does not necessarily mean lower political/legislative risk," FGS writes. "It may mean that policy/political conflict moves in less predictable ways." Get the 16-page FGS report .

Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will. Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon . —Robin George Andrews This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. events.title: Trump privately expresses doubts about livestreaming execution
events.summary: President Trump has privately shared misgivings about livestreaming the firing-squad execution of a former Army major who murdered 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas, according to four people who have spoken with the president. Why it matters: Trump has been deluged with "negative input" about the idea from a bipartisan chorus of lawmakers as well as advisers inside and outside of his White House, a senior administration official said. A livestream of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan's execution on Dec. 3 "might not happen," Trump told one confidant, who doesn't work in the administration and shared the comment with Axios. "He didn't sound particularly enthusiastic" about webcasting the execution, the source said. "That's why he's calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think." Zoom in: Hasan faces a firing squad at Fort Hood, where he went on his murderous shooting rampage 17 years ago. He would be the first person in the U.S. whose execution would be livestreamed. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the norm-shattering idea Thursday on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it — that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. Zoom out: The idea was roundly condemned domestically and internationally . In the ensuing days, Trump started to publicly shift his positions: At first, Trump was full-throated in his support. "Absolutely, I approve," Trump told reporters early Friday evening. Later that night, Trump was more nuanced : "They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision." On Saturday, Trump took control by telling reporters he would have the final say: "There are two thoughts: Don't show it and show it. 'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we'll make a decision," the president told reporters at the White House. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance has signaled where he thinks the president is going with the decision, according to a source. "I don't know if that's actually going to happen," Vance, speaking off the cuff, told reporters Friday. He has privately repeated that to others. "I'm not going to be watching it," Vance said. Between the lines: Trump, Vance and everyone else in the administration is clear about supporting Hasan's execution. But the president is grappling with competing pressures. "The president wants the bastard to pay, and a public execution might be that extra humiliation [Hasan] deserves," another confidant who spoke with the president said. "At the same time, he doesn't want to make the guy a martyr." Said another: "This is an old dude in a wheelchair we're shooting. We want to livestream that?" (Hasan, 56, was permanently injured when he was shot during his capture.) Friction point: The divide in opinion over livestreaming the execution is another point of disagreement between Vance and Hegseth. They've been on opposite sides when it comes to the use of military force in Yemen and Iran , to the leadership of the Army . Advisers say the men have a good relationship. Context: Whether at the state or federal level, executions often are witnessed only by family members or select media. They haven't been livestreamed. Executions used to be viewed in public squares, but that practice was discontinued in the 1930s, according to NPR . Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh's 2001 execution was viewable to loved ones and bombing survivors via a private closed-circuit telecast. Flashback: Yelling "Allahu Akbar!" Hasan fatally shot 13 people — including a pregnant woman — and wounded 32 others on Nov. 5, 2009, when they lined up for medical checks at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center. The rampage was the worst terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11. A special Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee report criticized the military for "political correctness" that blinded authorities to the major's increasingly clear Islamist radicalization. The bottom line: Hasan will be executed unless something unexpected happens. The only real doubt is whether private citizens with no attachment to the case will be able to witness it. "If I had to bet, I would bet the president doesn't authorize this," said one administration official. "But I'm not gonna get ahead of the boss and try to predict what he'll do." "Hasan will be executed for his crimes," the official said, "and that's what matters."

events.summary: The Scene Israel has produced more tech unicorns per citizen than any country in the world, twice as many as the US. Ittai Ben-Zeev’s job is getting them to stay there. The CEO of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is tasked with convincing the next Wiz, Monday.com, and Fiverr, which all went public in New York or sold to US rivals, to list at home instead. He’s also courting global investors whose money will help boost trading and valuations. His biggest tailwind, he said, is the takeover of US markets by a handful of AI giants. Israeli startups worth a few billion dollars can’t get the attention of investors rhapsodizing about trillion-dollar IPOs from SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI. “New York is no longer an option,” said Ben-Zeev, the exchange’s CEO since 2016. After the Oct. 7 attacks, 7% of its workforce was called up for military service and the bear case for its stock market was obvious. Since Oct. 8, 2023, the TA-125 has beaten the S&P 500 by 50 percentage points and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite by 23. The country is on track this year for a record 30 IPOs . Foreign holdings of Israeli shares more than doubled from September 2023 to the beginning of this year. Ben-Zeev dismissed wartime nationalism as a reason for Israeli founders to list at home, or for Israeli investors to buy their shares. “Israelis will be patriotic about certain issues, but that’s not the way they view the exchange,” he said. But he said the Jewish diaspora has increased its investments. Bill Ackman and his Israeli-born wife, Neri Oxman, bought 4.9% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange in 2024 after a 45-minute meeting with management, Ackman said in an interview. “Owning a stock exchange is the purest way to bet on a country,” he said, taking a minute to run the numbers: His $23 million investment is worth $230 million today. He said AI’s productivity-enhancing potential will overcome Israel’s economic weakness, its small population. “There will be a trillion-dollar company coming out of Israel, and that value will be shared among a tiny country.” The war also gave TASE cover to move its Sunday-to-Thursday trading to Monday through Friday. It wasn’t an easy pitch in a country that takes Shabbat seriously, but a way “to signal the world that we are part of it” and gain entry into global indexes that have long snubbed it, Ben-Zeev said. Anti-Israel sentiment and antisemitism are fueling campaigns at many US institutions to divest from Israel. Politicians will politick, he said, but “investors, at the end of the day, want to make a return.” Q&A Liz Hoffman: Israel has produced more tech unicorns per capita than any other country in the world, but they all want to go public in New York. How do you hold onto them? Ittai Ben-Zeev: It used to be that a tech company with $100 million [in annual revenue] could IPO in New York. That’s no longer the case. The $100 million became $500 million. And because of the gigantic IPOs that are coming, for most Israeli tech companies, New York is no longer an option. Six or seven years ago, if an Israeli company couldn’t do an IPO on Nasdaq or NYSE, they were looking at Singapore, Toronto, Australia. We managed to change the perception. And I believe that in 2027, maybe before the end of 2026, we’ll start seeing global investment banks leading global IPO offerings on TASE, and only for TASE. I’m mindful, speaking to you the week of the anniversary of Oct. 7 — is patriotism part of the pitch? No. Post-Oct. 7, I see a genuine change in the way that Jewish people in the diaspora, especially in the States, want to invest in Israel, not only to make a return but also to get a broader connection to Israel. But that’s not the case with the Israeli entrepreneurs. Israelis, I have to tell you, will be patriotic about certain issues, but that’s not the way they view the exchange. Then what’s the pitch? You are Israeli. You don’t understand the American mentality. The American market can be brutal. You miss your estimates by one cent, your share price goes down, and then what? Start in the Israeli market and, once you’re ready, you can always do a dual listing. Think about TASE as a stop on the way to New York. You’ve also courted global companies to dual-list in Tel Aviv. Palo Alto Networks did that after buying [Israeli startup] CyberArk, but why would most companies bother? We have data that shows you get more liquidity and more demand for your shares. You can argue that it’s not significant enough, but it’s a free option. And not too many people are aware of it, but if you look at the amount of money Israelis have in cash deposits in Israeli banks and you compare it to GDP, we are No. 1 of any western society. That’s money that is just ready to be invested. You’re in New York this week, selling the Israeli economy to investors. But the Middle East is a volatile place to invest right now, and there are big anti-Israel divestment campaigns at some US institutions. In the old days, people would ask me: What will happen to Israel if something happens in Iran? I remember being in New York a couple of years ago, telling one of those American investors that if something happened in Iran, you should be more worried about your American portfolio than your Israeli portfolio. Israel is more well-positioned than it used to be, and I’m not sure that everybody fully understands it. In terms of BDS [the push for boycotts, divestment, and economic sanctions against Israel], there are politicians all over the world. Investors, at the end of the day, want to make a return. And the Israeli market is a good marketplace to make a return. Also, I think Israel can do a better job of PR. This is part of what we tell companies: You need to know how to sell the pitch. It’s not only about facts; it’s also about storytelling. As a country, this is something we need to do better. You shifted trading from Sunday to Thursday to Monday to Friday. Was that a hard sell? We were in the middle of a war. Everybody understood that it’s important for us to signal the world that we are part of it. We needed to get aligned to global standards, and this is what we did this year. What’s it like having Bill Ackman on your cap table? For sure it has helped change the perception. Israeli tech guys, they look to New York. When they will read what you’re writing, they will give it much more credit than what the Israeli newspaper writes. So a very successful businessman like Bill talking about the Israeli economy, putting faith in the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, helps my pitch.

events.title: Saudi Arabia’s resolve, and fears of a ‘forever war’
events.summary: The Scene Riyadh Season — the Saudi capital’s biggest suite of events that had been key to its tourism push — opens next week with concerts, UFC, the Epcot-esque Boulevard World, and the world’s top ranked tennis players set to compete at the Six Kings Slam. Since 2019, it has been the capital’s answer to anyone asking whether Riyadh is the place to be. After the Houthi strikes over the weekend, residents are asking themselves the same question. Traffic on King Fahd Road is lighter and some companies — mostly those based in the King Abdullah Financial District — told staff to work from home on Sunday. Schools in the city have moved to remote learning for the week, with no clear date yet on when students will return to class. When I ask Saudis — friends, relatives, and sources — how they are doing, most say: , thanks to God, the catchall for everything from the greatest blessings to the mantra mourners repeat when family members die. It’s the same expression they used in March when Iranian missiles first reached the capital, but the tone now is different after more than a dozen people were killed and hundreds wounded in attacks on King Khalid International Airport. Fear is breaking through. Social media and WhatsApp group chats have been filled with eulogies for Captain Hamoud Alkalthami, the Saudia Airlines pilot killed on Thursday, and for Saturday’s dead — eight of them foreign residents from countries including Bangladesh, Egypt, and Sudan. People are posting about and queuing to donate to blood banks. The crown prince himself did so last week, part of an annual campaign, and that image was used to spur urgently needed donations. The captain’s death in particular has become a symbol for many Saudis: The war now has a martyr, with a name and face that looks like theirs. Manal’s view Saudis broadly trust their government. When they wrap themselves in the flag, or share statements of solidarity after attacks (at least for those who use their real names), it’s genuine and reflects how people speak in private. But there has been a shift. Some are talking about leaving, which a few months ago would have been seen as a betrayal. Most are still confident and say the kingdom has come through worse. What’s pretty universal is the desire for the disruption to be over and to get back to living. While the conflict with Iran was clear — we have been told to be wary of the Islamic Republic from the time we understood what an enemy was — the confrontation with the Houthis is more complex. Riyadh has tried a mix of strikes and diplomacy for more than a decade, and the UN-brokered truce in 2022 held long enough for people to stop thinking about the issue. It’s clear now that it’s a forever war, and few people I speak to can describe what winning would look like. Without public polls, it’s impossible to gauge exactly what the Saudis think. Speaking to more than 25 people this weekend showed a split. One camp wants the Houthis finished for good, whatever that may meanOthers worry about the toll on Yemenis, our poorer neighbors, who make up the kingdom’s largest foreign community and share ties of kinship and history with Saudis. Over the past six months, those who lived through the 1991 Gulf War used it to explain why they weren’t worried. Those six weeks of Iraqi strikes had one Saudi business leader “ more frightened of the uncertainty of the Scud than anything else. ” Uncertainty is again, 35 years later, the greatest fear. Notable The strikes sharply raise the risk of Saudi Arabia being drawn into a wider war, after a decade in which Riyadh worked to contain the Yemen conflict rather than escalate it , Bloomberg reported. Eulogies for the 12 killed in Saturday’s strike filled Saudi social media, among them a Flynas flight attendant killed on duty and a university student in her final year , Arab News reported.

events.title: Two U.S. professors win Nobel prize in economics
events.summary: Stanford University's Robert E. Hall and Columbia University's Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in economics for research on how policymakers can stabilize economies , the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday. Why it matters: Their work helped shape how central banks set interest rates and communicate policy. The win comes as those institutions fight energy-driven inflation and risks to economic growth. Zoom out: For decades, policymakers relied on economic models that linked higher inflation with lower unemployment. But that framework broke down during the 1970s stagflation when both prices and joblessness surged at the same time. "The solution by Robert Hall and Michael Woodford was to build a new framework ground up," Timo Boppart, a member of the Nobel economics prize committee, said on Monday. What they're saying: Woodford, who called into Monday's press conference hosted by the committee, said he was "elated" by the win. " It's a tremendous honor. It's a surprise — but I'm feeling very good about it," Woodford said. The intrigue : Asked by a reporter about the threat to the global economy, Woodford said the Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets and driven price changes with consequences far beyond the region. He pointed to the 2008 financial crisis as a key test of his research, when central banks cut interest rates to near zero but struggled to revive economic activity. His framework helped explain how other tools, including forward guidance and asset purchases, could support the economy. Zoom in: In research culminating in a landmark 2003 book, Woodford developed a framework linking businesses' pricing decisions to inflation and monetary policy. Hall — a Stanford professor who chaired the committee that dates U.S. recessions for 46 years — showed in a 1978 paper how consumers' spending decisions reflect expectations about future income. Of note: The prize comes with an award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), up from 11 million kronor last year, to be divided between the two winners. Flashback: Recent economics Nobels have recognized research on technological progress, economic prosperity and labor markets. Last year's prize went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for their work explaining how innovation drives economic growth. In 2024, Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won for their research on how institutions shape economic prosperity. Harvard economist Claudia Goldin won in 2023 for research that advanced the world's understanding of women's labor market outcomes.

events.title: US says Hormuz oil flows recover to 14 million bpd despite Saudi attacks
events.summary: Up to 14 million barrels of oil a day are moving through the Strait of Hormuz , with Gulf crude flows recovering to between 80 and 90 per cent of prewar levels, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said. Additional supplies from the Gulf are also being transported through pipelines bypassing Hormuz, Mr Wright said on Monday, addressing the 25th WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh remotely. "The crude problem we talked a lot about – it's still there but it's mostly handled," he said, offering a more optimistic assessment than ship-tracking data suggests. Figures from analytics firm Kpler show oil exports through Hormuz averaged slightly under nine million bpd in September, the highest monthly level since the war began, but only about 44 per cent of the 20.6 million bpd recorded in February. About 22 vessels crossed the strait daily in the 30 days to October 12, about two thirds of them tankers, according to Kpler. The data is provisional and subject to revision as tracking information is updated, reflecting movements registered by 2pm UAE time on October 12. Laden crude tankers leaving the Gulf carried about 8.9 million bpd over the past month, mostly from Saudi Arabia and Iraq. The figures are not directly comparable with Mr Wright's broader recovery estimate, which includes supplies transported through bypass pipelines. Kpler's September data nevertheless suggests lower volumes through Hormuz than those cited by the US official. Mr Wright's comments came after an attack on Riyadh airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured about 300, underscoring the security risks facing the world's biggest oil-exporting region. "I want to start out by strongly condemning the cowardly attacks by the Houthis on the people of Saudi Arabia, on civilian infrastructure," Mr Wright said in addressing the energy congress on Monday. He reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the kingdom as energy ministers and industry executives gathered in Riyadh despite heightened security concerns. "We are here as your partners," he said, reiterating the US's "unwavering support for Saudi Arabia". Mr Wright warned the recovery in crude supplies had yet to ease pressure on fuel markets, with diesel prices remaining "very high", and jet fuel and petrol prices also elevated. "The challenge is still here and the challenge is still ahead of us," he said.

events.title: UAE wealth set to hit $6 trillion in 2030 despite short-term war volatility
events.summary: Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East , a new report has found. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group said. The sharp projected increase, driven by a rise in real assets and financial wealth, “points to the UAE's long-term wealth creation potential”, BCG said in its Global Wealth Report 2026: The Great Reordering report on Monday. Last year alone, net wealth in the Arab world’s second-largest economy grew by almost 13 per cent on an annual basis to reach $3.6 trillion. Real, or physical, assets with intrinsic value such as property portfolios reached $2.4 trillion in 2025, jumping from $2.2 trillion at the end of the previous year. Financial wealth grew to $1.4 trillion in 2025, rising from $1.2 trillion a year earlier, while liabilities for the same period rose from $210 billion to $220 billion. The report estimates liabilities to rise to $340 billion by 2030. The Iran war has introduced “short-term volatility across Middle Eastern markets, with investor sentiment shaped by geopolitical uncertainty and oil-price movements”, said Lukasz Rey, managing director and partner at BCG. “While we anticipate slightly lower growth over the next one to two years, a rebound is expected towards the latter part of the decade.” Sovereign wealth strength, economic diversification agendas, family-business liquidity events and private capital activity will all help drive wealth creation in the country, Mr Rey said. Caution to prevail BCG, he said, expects wealth managers to remain cautious in the near term. However, “the region's wealth development story remains structurally resilient over the five-year projection horizon”, Mr Rey added. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased economic uncertainty across the Middle East. Despite a halt in all-out hostilities since early April, several attempts to reach a permanent deal to end the conflict have failed. The World Bank last week said Gulf economies would contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downwards revision of 5.7 percentage points from its forecast in April. The International Monetary Fund also expects economies in the region to contract this year but anticipates a sharp expansion next year once the conflict settles, managing director Kristalina Georgieva said. Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country remains a magnet for the ultra-wealthy , as well as global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers. A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices and institutional partners. Concentration of wealth The UAE’s financial wealth remains concentrated among high-net-worth individuals, with “the composition of wealth expected to evolve by 2030 as more wealth accumulates within the lower high-net-worth segment”, the BCG report said. The country had about 500 ultra-high-net-worth individuals – those with assets in excess of $100 million – in 2025. That number is expected to jump to about 800 by the end of the decade, while their share of total financial wealth will rise marginally from 26.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The upper high-net-worth segment, featuring people with assets of $20 million to $100 million, is forecast to grow from about 2,700 to 4,200 individuals, with their share of wealth broadly stable, rising from 7.4 per cent in 2025 to 7.6 per cent in 2030. Meanwhile, the group of 200,000 lower high-net-worth individuals, with an asset range of $1 million to $20 million, are estimated to increase their share of financial wealth from 29.3 per cent in 2025 to 31.5 per cent in 2030. The affluent segment with assets worth $1 million is expected to expand from about 500,000 to 600,000 individuals in 2030. However, its share of wealth will decline from 15.5 per cent to 14.6 per cent, BCG data found. Centre of choice The UAE also continues to strengthen its position as a global wealth booking centre, with cross-border wealth belonging to international clients and booked in the country jumping more than 11 per cent to $721 billion last year. Currency and deposits, valued at $471.8 billion in 2025, are projected to rise more than 10 per cent annually to $778.9 billion by 2030. Bonds are estimated to grow almost 12 per cent on an annual basis to $27.8 billion, while equities are expected to reach jump to $591.9 billion by 2030, from $419.4 billion last year, BCG found.

events.title: American professors Hall and Woodford win Nobel economics prize
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Americans Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel memorial prize in economics Robert E Hall (left) and Michael Woodford shared the economics award. ( Reuters: Anders Wiklund ) American professors Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford have won the Nobel memorial prize in economics. They were honoured for their groundbreaking work on the micro-economic foundations of macro-economic stabilisation. The will receive around $900,000 each for winning an award that began in 1968. American-born economists Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford have won the Nobel memorial prize in economics for their work on the micro-economic foundations of macro-economic stabilisation. Professor Hall, 83, is professor of economics with Stanford University in California, and 71-year-old Professor Woodford is the John Bates Clark Professor of Political Economy at Columbia University in New York. The award was announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm. "The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said. "With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume." Last year, three researchers who study business innovation won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare , even as they leave older companies in the dust. The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was first awarded in 1968. ( Reuters: Tom Little ) The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel prize, but it is always presented together with the others on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.8 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organisation, so they will receive around $900,000 each. Journalists in Stockholm were able to interview co-winner Michael Woodford on the telephone from the US. ( AFP: Jonathan Nackstrand ) "It's a surprise, but I'm feeling very good about it," Professor Woodford told reporters via phone during the announcement of the prize, saying he felt "elated" over receiving "a tremendous honour". The US imposes sanctions on the International Criminal Court hours after one of its former judges is given the Nobel Peace Prize. A concrete example of his work implemented in practice was when the 2008 financial crisis created a situation where "traditional tools of monetary policy were not really adequate to deal with the problem of restoring economic activity," he said, noting that interest rates were already lowered to zero in many countries. One of the new approaches employed by central banks was to start making "more explicit statements" on where they believed guiding interest rates were headed in the future, which continues to this day. The majority of previous economics laureates have been from the US. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States. Nobel prizes for the categories of medicine , physics , chemistry , literature and peace were announced last week.

events.title: HMV to close Oxford Street store after three years
events.summary: HMV says it is looking for a new site in London's West End HMV has said it will shut its flagship Oxford Street store three years after it reopened the site, blaming a proposed doubling of the rent for the closure. The entertainment chain said it would leave the shop in March 2027, in a move affecting more than 50 staff. It said it was looking for a new site in London's West End district for its flagship shop and said it planned to maintain a "significant presence" in the capital. Phil Halliday, managing director of HMV, said it was "frustrating" that the Oxford Street shop was "commercially unviable". He said: "This is a special store, it's where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history. "We are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for HMV in 2027." HMV shut its Oxford Street store in 2019 after it went into administration The group said its landlords had proposed doubling the rent on the site at 363 Oxford Street, and it was also facing a bill for "substantial" renovation works at the store, which together would make the shop "commercially unsustainable". HMV said it would look to transfer affected workers to its two other London stores and head office while it looked for a new site. The chain reopened its historic Oxford Street store in November 2023 after a four-year absence following a deal secured with landlords. It first opened the Oxford Street site in 1921. HMV has 113 stores across the UK, including six sites under the Fopp brand, as well as another eight in Europe. The group said it remained committed to high street stores. events.title: Tanzania seeks investment to tackle youth job pressure
events.summary: The News Tanzania is counting on increased investment to accelerate industrialization and create jobs for its young population, the prime minister said. The government has targeted $15 billion in annual foreign direct investment, roughly triple last year’s figure, as part of its long-term economic plans . Mwigulu Nchemba, speaking on the sidelines of an investment forum in London, said the government had put money into rail and port infrastructure, as well as expanding power generation to create an industrial base. This was on top of cutting the cost of doing business, and strengthening supply chains. Nchemba said increased industrialization would boost local processing of natural resources leading to more employment opportunities. Tanzania, like many African countries, has a rapidly expanding population. The UN estimates 42% of people are aged 14 or under . The prime minister said the path to creating work for all the country’s school leavers rests on developing the private sector through investment. “There is no way you can absorb all those graduates,” the prime minister told reporters. “The only way you can solve the issue of job creation is by empowering the private sector to create those vacancies for our youth.” Know More Tanzania has large offshore gas resources and deposits of minerals needed for the energy transition and digital infrastructure — such as copper, lithium, and cobalt — as well as precious metals and stones, including gold and diamonds. In August, the country commissioned a 2,115 MW hydropower plant that more than doubled its electricity generation capacity and ​created a surplus that officials said could support power exports and industrial growth. Tanzania, like governments across the continent, is looking for ways to add value locally instead of raw minerals exports. In neighboring Kenya, President William Ruto has focused on job creation through industrialization as a key plank in his campaign to secure a second term in next year’s election. Notable Liquefied natural gas development offers Tanzania its most obvious means of monetizing its giant gas reserves after the wars in Ukraine and Iran upended global energy markets, wrote Neil Ford in African Business.

events.title: Sheng Siong, OCBC, SGX receive analysts’ downgrades
events.summary: New challenges are emerging for Sheng Siong, while its previous competitive advantage might be fading, says an analyst. SINGAPORE – A few Singapore stocks received downgrades by analysts recently, including OCBC, Sheng Siong and the Singapore Exchange (SGX). Maybank analyst Hussaini Saifee downgraded the supermarket’s stock to “hold”, leading to the stock sliding more than 2% on Oct 12. Hussaini said Sheng Siong remains a high-quality operator, but its “strong share price re-rating now prices in much of it”. He added that Sheng Siong has benefited from resilient consumption, market share gains and targeted vouchers that channelled spending directly to supermarkets, but that support is weakening as assistance is shifting to GST vouchers and cash payments. “Supermarket growth has already eased to low single digits,” he said, adding that growth will track underlying income and population trends, instead of repeating the “unusually favourable” conditions of recent years. He added that new challenges are emerging for the supermarket brand, while its previous competitive advantage might be fading. Previously, Sheng Siong captured displaced demand when Giant and Cold Storage shut some stores. Hussaini also noted that people may be crossing the border into Malaysia to shop, given the upcoming Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link, or going online to get groceries, which might pose challenges to Sheng Siong. “While neither appears disruptive enough to reshape the industry in the near term, both point to a less favourable backdrop than in recent years,” he added. He downgraded the target price to $3.12, from the $3.22 he previously aimed for. Meanwhile, Citi analyst Tan Yong Hong downgraded OCBC to “sell” and reiterated his call to sell UOB. However, he kept DBS at a “buy” call. He said analysts see downside earnings risks to the third-quarter forecasted results, based on “market misplaced optimism on Singapore dollar rates and after an exceptional first-half wealth-related income”. This is particularly the case with OCBC, which he said is trading at the tightest dividend yield spread over bond yield, followed by UOB and DBS. This means that the market is pricing in most aggressive growth, he noted. “Singapore banks have enjoyed a three-year re-rating cycle from 2024, starting from capital management hopes from 2024, wealth management growth from 2025, and recently crowding positionings amid the Equity Market Development Programme and ‘anti-AI’ trade,” Tan said. The programme refers to a $6.5 billion initiative launched by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to boost the liquidity and vibrancy of the local equities market. Tan also said there are risks that forecasters have been mispricing net interest income upside by assuming higher rates because of the resurgence in loans growth. Higher Singapore dollar funding costs is a key risk to that, alongside fixed-rate loans repricing lower, he noted. However, JP Morgan analysts recommended trimming OCBC and DBS, while relatively preferring UOB. They noted that banks in the region may be impacted by the ongoing sharp increase in long bond yields. All three banks saw share price gains on Oct 12 despite the downgrades. DBS rose 0.8% to hit $73.94 on Oct 12, while OCBC rose 0.2% to $29.06. UOB gained 1.4% to close at $40.50. Separately, SGX was also downgraded by Macquarie analysts a week ago. It was labelled as “underperform”, down from “neutral”, as analysts noted its monthly statistics were starting to wane. Citi analysts noted that the SGX acts as a proxy to the Singapore market. If there is an improved economic outlook, SGX will see upsides. But if there is news of a slowdown, it could imply downside risks for the exchange. The analysts also noted that turnover of securities and derivatives on the local bourse has been volatile, among other factors. SGX closed 3% higher at $21.35 on Oct 12. Sue-Ann Tan is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, covering capital markets and sustainable finance.

events.title: Dangote's Kenya refinery triggers political battle
events.summary: The News The $16 billion project to build Aliko Dangote’s refinery on the Kenyan coast is at the center of a high-stakes political battle ahead of elections in 10 months. President William Ruto is hinging his second-term bid on a series of major infrastructure developments. He has argued that the refinery could raise Kenya’s annual gross domestic product by 12%. Additional expected benefits include 500MW added to the national grid and thousands of new jobs. But mounting litigation, some initiated by his political rivals, is threatening to delay its construction, scheduled to be completed by 2030. Groups behind the legal action allege that the project is only the latest in a series of “secretive deals” signed by Ruto and his administration. The government’s refusal to make public key agreements related to the refinery has been criticized by opposition leaders, including one of Ruto’s main challengers, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has launched a bid in parliament for the documents, including the refinery contract, to be released. Unanswered questions remain over the impact on the environment, the community living near the refinery, and taxpayers. The president and his allies have warned that legal hurdles and uncertainty affecting key projects could dampen investor confidence. Ruto’s government is no stranger to court challenges to its financial deals. Its plan to privatize the country’s fuel pipeline company was eventually approved after various cases were dismissed. Last month, the $1.6 billion sale of a government stake in telecoms company Safaricom to UK’s Vodafone was declared illegal by the courts — the administration has launched an appeal. Both deals are meant to fund Ruto’s infrastructure push, according to government documents. Know More Ekuru Aukot, leader of the opposition Thirdway Alliance,told Semafor he would “definitely file a suit” if the government failed to meet an Oct. 23 deadline in his access to information request seeking more details about the refinery including the names of those who stand to benefit. “We are not opposed to investment. What we are saying is follow the law, follow the constitution,” he said. “The era of secretive deals negotiated in the dark will end when we kick this current regime out and return our country back to the rule of law,” Sifuna said on social media , adding that Ruto was frustrating his parliamentary push for more details. He insisted that the disclosure was “a constitutional imperative.” The threat of protracted litigation also looms over a suit launched by more than 100 Lamu residents arguing that the site of the refinery is part of their ancestral lands, with a court halting construction until the matter is heard. In addition, campaign groups have raised the alarm over the government’s failure to publish the environmental impact report, with Greenpeace threatening legal action . Last year, its five-year effort to block the construction of a $2 billion coal plant in Lamu ended in success for the activists. Despite the legal cases, Dangote and Ruto, who broke ground on the refinery project on Sept. 30, have expressed confidence that the project will overcome the legal hurdles. Step Back Seen as the candidate for the young and downtrodden in the last election, Ruto’s popularity has waned especially among the youth after the deadly 2024 Gen Z-led protests in which dozens of demonstrators were killed by police. Instead, Ruto is now leaning heavily on his infrastructure plans and the promised opportunities to shore up support for his re-election campaign. He has promised to move Kenya “from third world to first world” within 10 years, and unveiled a $38 billion infrastructure fund meant to finance various projects. The View From Nigeria Dangote is taking the objections in his stride. Speaking to investors in Nairobi ahead of the groundbreaking ceremony, Dangote said legal challenges were “normal for us in Africa. In fact, this is small.” He drew parallels with concerns over his cement plant in Senegal , which faced delays over land-related legal disputes. “They stopped our factory for one year. We went up to the Supreme Court to get a judgment,” he said. Notable Kenya’s Capital Markets Authority approved the Dangote IPO , enabling local investors to participate on the Nairobi Securities Exchange.

events.title: Why Trump’s Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire may offer oil markets little relief
events.summary: US President Donald Trump's declaration of an " energy ceasefire " between Russia and Ukraine has raised questions over its validity, after Moscow offered no confirmation about the truce and Russian strikes hit Ukrainian power plants within hours of the announcement. The move sent oil and diesel prices into decline early on Monday, but analysts cautioned that even a sustained halt to attacks on energy infrastructure would offer limited relief to global fuel markets, with much of Russia's refining capacity offline after months of Ukrainian drone strikes. Brent fell 1.3 per cent to $103.35 a barrel in early trading, while West Texas Intermediate declined 1.4 per cent to $90.55 a barrel. ICE gas oil futures, a benchmark for diesel, dropped about 3 per cent. The oil benchmarks pared losses by midday, with Brent trading 1.10 per cent higher at $105.87 a barrel by 1.55pm UAE time, while WTI was up 1.13 per cent at $92.89 a barrel. “Effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv supported a ceasefire but was awaiting details from Washington. A similar announcement by Mr Trump in September failed to produce a lasting halt to strikes. “Only time will tell how durable it proves to be,” said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at Swiss bank UBS. “We have seen similar commitments in the past that ultimately failed to hold.” Diesel squeeze The announcement follows a US Treasury decision on October 9 to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel transactions until April 7, 2027, after Mr Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release additional fuel into global markets. But the volumes are modest relative to the scale of the disruption. The proposed 300,000 tonnes for the rest of this month equates to about 100,000 barrels a day, Mr Staunovo said. That “would only partially offset the decline in seaborne diesel exports, which in September were around 1.3 million barrels per day below the levels seen at the start of the year”, he said. Francesco Sassi, assistant professor of energy geopolitics at the University of Oslo, said Washington's decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel for six months marked a significant shift in energy geopolitics that threatened to undermine western unity against Moscow. He described the move as the clearest failure yet of efforts to isolate Russia through energy sanctions. “What remains unsaid regarding the guarantees that Russia had from the US for supplying diesel is far more important than the few details we know so far about the energy ceasefire,” Mr Sassi said. Ukraine's response would also be a test of its relationship with Washington, potentially increasing pressure on the European Union to sustain support for Kyiv without US backing, he added. Russia's capacity to deliver the additional fuel is also in doubt. Its diesel exports fell from about 706,000 bpd in January to 47,000 bpd in August and almost nothing last month, according to Kpler data, as Ukrainian drone attacks damaged refineries and curtailed fuel production. Total Russian oil exports declined to about 6.8 million bpd in September from 8 million bpd in May. Shipments to India , Russia's biggest buyer, have more than halved since June to 1.2 million bpd, the data showed. The drop highlights the difficulty of restoring Russian fuel supplies without first repairing damaged infrastructure, a process that could take months even if attacks cease. S&P Global Commodity Insights said the announcement could weigh on diesel refining margins but only if Russian exports increase. “We see the immediate market impact as limited,” analysts James Bambino and Richard Joswick said. Additional Russian shipments would cover only about 10 per cent of the global shortfall in diesel exports, assuming they represent new supply rather than cargoes diverted from existing buyers, S&P Global said. About half of Russia's refining capacity is offline and repairs could take months, limiting the scope for a rapid recovery. Any additional cargoes are likely to remain in the Atlantic Basin, potentially reaching the US East Coast or Brazil and freeing up US Gulf Coast supplies for Europe. That could put downwards pressure on diesel margins in north-west Europe and the US but only “as long as a ceasefire holds”, the analysts said. Middle East risks persist Even if Russian fuel exports recover, the broader oil market remains exposed to disruption in the Middle East, where the Iran war has restricted supplies and forced major changes to established shipping routes. Crude has largely remained above $100 a barrel in recent weeks as attacks on infrastructure and shipping continue to threaten supplies from the Gulf. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 a barrel from $85, saying Gulf supply disruption was likely to ease more slowly than previously expected. The bank estimates geopolitical tension is adding slightly more than $20 a barrel to prices and does not assume a quick resolution to the US-Iran conflict. “Potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk,” the bank's analysts said.

events.title: AI set to continue growing, but how it unlocks value is the question: TikTok, Broadcom, Intel CEOs
events.summary: TikTok chief executive officer Chew Shou Zi speaking at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. AI will keep growing and may beat some human skills, but leaders said its real value depends on human judgement, creativity and safe use. TikTok’s Chew Shou Zi warned about alignment and cybersecurity risks, and said people still value authenticity as AI-made content remains low. Broadcom and Intel CEOs said AI demand for compute will stay strong for three to five years, but growth depends on supply, ROI, costs and talent. SINGAPORE – Artificial intelligence is set to continue its growth and may even surpass some human capabilities, but what matters is how it can unlock value for businesses and society, said the chief executives of three major tech companies. TikTok CEO Chew Shou Zi said there is a “non-zero chance” that AI could surpass humans in certain ways in the future, but he also noted the importance of human judgment and creativity even as AI becomes more widely used . Meanwhile, in response to a question by DBS CEO Tan Su Shan on whether the world is “overbuilding” AI infrastructure , Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Intel CEO Tan Lip-Bu said the demand for AI infrastructure will continue to grow in the next three to five years, limited mainly by supply constraints. They were speaking on panels at the inaugural DBS Asia Future Forward Conference held at Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. Organised by DBS, the new flagship event brings together global leaders across technology, business and investment to examine the forces shaping the region’s future. Chew said AI models might currently be unable to do certain things that humans can, such as rapid visual learning or long-term memory retrieval. But he added: “The technology is evolving, (and) you can see a world where silicon is just superior to carbon. “You can see a world where it will last longer. It’s more scalable. It finds it easier to connect information together than us human beings.” But Chew also said there is a place for human judgment in AI usage. He noted that there are some extreme examples of how machines can behave without human alignment, such as the “paper clip analogy”, where a machine is asked to produce paperclips and goes completely overweight on paperclip production at the expense of everything else. “My view is that in the next two to three years, we’re going to have a real scientific breakthrough: physics, biotech, chemistry, material science, because of AI. It’s very, very, very possible,” he said. “And if that happens, then you know the question will be: How do you align the models? How do you align the machines to be doing things that are obvious to us as human beings?” These include moral and ethical boundaries that humans recognise, but AI models may not. “I don’t think we have an answer, to be honest, at this moment in time. I think it really is a very complex issue, but it will matter in the age of AI,” Chew said. Human creativity is also a very relevant question, especially for TikTok, he added. He noted that AI -generated content has not totally taken off yet, with views in the low single-digit percentages. “I think people still value authenticity when they see a video and it’s very obviously... artificially generated. I think there’s still a little bit of pushback in terms of consumption. So I agree that human creativity will continue to be important,” he said. Chew added that in the long term, AI agents might be able to do more things autonomously, especially as the trust and guard rails are built. But in the short term, referring to the next two to three years, Chew said that what matters is developing skills to be able to use AI effectively. “I think that’s probably the most important thing for us internally. We are encouraging not just our engineers, but also our lawyers and people working in corporate functions to have more first-hand experience,” he said. “If you don’t use these products yourself, you cannot figure out exactly what it can or cannot do just by reading about it.” He added that users should be curious and hands-on while understanding the boundaries of this technology. Education is also important, Chew said, especially as AI also poses cybersecurity risks . This is particularly the case when users give agents permission to do things for them, like making purchases using credit cards , without fully understanding what the technology does. events.title: Obama cuts ad in Mississippi Senate race
events.summary: Former President Barack Obama has cut an ad for Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, the latest sign of Democrats putting real effort behind boosting their candidate in the deep red state as they eye a potential upset next month. The Colom campaign will run the 30-second spot on digital and radio statewide in Mississippi as part of a seven-figure media buy in Mississippi, according to details shared first with Semafor. In the ad, Obama tells voters: “Mississippi, it’s time for a change.” “You need to send Scott Colom to the US Senate,” Obama continues in the ad . “Scott made his community safer, prosecuting violent crimes as a district attorney and fighting corruption.” Colom is running against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a conservative GOP senator who blocked Colom’s nomination to a federal judgeship under then-President Joe Biden. Colom currently serves as a district attorney in Mississippi. The race to defeat Hyde-Smith is not a must-win for Democrats to retake the Senate and Colom remains an underdog in deep red Mississippi. But national Democrats have been eying the race for months due to the state’s large Black population, and Obama’s ad is a clear effort to juice turnout. Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., will appear with Colom on Wednesday in Jackson and Democratic Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, and Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware have also previously campaigned with the Democratic candidate.Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has also listed Mississippi as a target for Democrats. Democrats tried to beat Hyde-Smith in the past and failed. She defeated former Democratic Rep. Mike Espy by 7 points in 2018 and a wider margin in a 2020 rematch. But most Senate Democrats think Colom, a young father, is a stronger candidate in a tough environment for Republicans.

events.title: Few Hong Kong investors take interest in listing by Africa’s top phone maker Transsion
events.summary: Shenzhen Transsion’s US$428 million offering oversubscribed just 3.5 times, sources say, as sharp decline in listing sentiment continues Shenzhen Transsion Holdings drew a lukewarm response for its HK$3.36 billion (US$428 million) Hong Kong share offering, heightening worries over market sentiment for new listings in the fourth quarter. The maker of Africa’s bestselling phones closed its bookbuilding on Monday, with preliminary figures showing the offering attracted about 14,000 applications and was oversubscribed roughly 3.5 times, according to people familiar with the matter. Retail participation in Hong Kong initial public offerings (IPOs) has dropped sharply since September. Out of 12 listings last month, only two – Camsense Technologies and Mech-Mind Robotics Technologies – drew more than 100,000 retail applicants, while Red Avenue New Materials Group recorded the lowest demand with just 12,645, according to the companies’ allotment results. In contrast, 11 out of 19 listings across July and August topped 100,000 applicants, with Momenta and Basic Semiconductor each surpassing 200,000.

events.title: Learning to Play Like a Pro: Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking for Humanoid Robots
events.summary: This White Paper provides roboticists and control engineers with a comprehensive overview of how motion planning and motion tracking can be decoupled to preserve professional athletic style in humanoid robots, and why adaptive, speed-aware control is essential for closing the gap between simulation and real-world deployment. What you will learn about: Why combining a professional athlete’s motion style with reliable task performance remains an open challenge in humanoid ball-sports robotics, and how separating a high-level planner from a low-level tracker addresses this trade-off. How motion data extracted from broadcast video and motion-capture recordings can be reconstructed, retargeted, and physically corrected into reference motions a humanoid robot can safely track. Why the sim-to-real transition introduces compounding tracking errors, and how training a tracker on randomized execution speeds, paired with a learned motion-speed adapter in the planner, improves robustness on physical hardware. How this adaptive framework was validated across two humanoid platforms, including full-size, in-the-wild serving performed without any motion-capture system. Download this free whitepaper now!

events.title: UAE approves 2027-2029 budget with Dh292.5bn in spending
events.summary: The UAE Cabinet has approved its federal budget for 2027 to 2029 with spending of Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion). The allocation marks an increase of 28.3 per cent compared to the previous three years, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai said on Monday. The Cabinet also approved the 2027 budget with expenditure of Dh90.1 billion. Main sectors covered by the new federal budget include community protection and safety, the economy of the future, future-orientated education, employment and empowerment, health and quality of life, leadership, government affairs and international relations, the UAE Government Media Office said in a statement. The budget will also focus on industry, technology, energy, infrastructure, culture, media and sports. “Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged … Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen,” Sheikh Mohammed said in a post on X. The UAE last year launched its 2027-2029 budget cycle , focusing on sustainability, artificial intelligence and efficiency. It followed four consecutive cycles during which the total federal budget reached about Dh900 billion ($245 billion), officials said in July last year, adding that the cycle focuses on sectors such as education, health care, social welfare and core government services. Mohammed bin Rashid: Today, we approved the UAE Federal Government’s general budget for 2027 to 2029, with total expenditure of AED 292.5 billion, up 28.3% compared with the previous 3 years. We also approved the 2027 budget, with total expenditure of AED 90.1 billion. Our… pic.twitter.com/0vkaH0AljA — Dubai Media Office (@DXBMediaOffice) October 12, 2026 The UAE's economy grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to the country's gross domestic product during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said last week. The Iran war has tipped the Middle East into one of its worst geopolitical crises in decades. The conflict, which began on February 28, led to Iranian strikes on its Arab neighbours and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, continues to grow despite the conflict. Ratings agency Fitch said on Monday that the UAE non-oil growth model is broadly resilient to the war baseline. The non-oil growth model of the UAE has leveraged a role as a hub between Asia and Europe “backed by a favourable operating environment, supportive government policy, and the ability to attract and retain foreign labour and visitors”, it said in a report. It added that it expects further measures to “improve the operating environment along with a smoothing of administrative procedures” for corporates and residents, backed by higher spending and other sources of financial support at the sovereign and government-related entity level. “Fitch sees structural strengths that will support the resilience of the non-oil economy. However, a persistent period of regional insecurity will call into question logistical advantages and perceptions of the country as a commercial and financial centre and tourism destination,” said Paul Gamble, senior director at Fitch Ratings. The approval of the budget confirms the UAE government’s “keenness to achieve a balance between current development requirements and investment in future opportunities, and to establish a government financial system characterised by flexibility, efficiency and sustainability”, the media office said on Monday. It enhances the UAE’s position among the most advanced and prosperous countries in the world, it added.
