events.title: Roofing scammers con homeowners out of thousands of pounds
events.summary: Scammers pretending to be legitimate workmen are charging homeowners thousands of pounds for roofing work that is not completed, done badly or not necessary, according to Citizens Advice. The consumer advice charity says one in 10 of all the scams it recorded over the past year were related to roofing, making it the most common type of scam brought to them. It can leave victims like Crystal, from the Midlands, thousands of pounds out of pocket. The 68-year-old was frightened and found it hard to sleep after a rogue builder left her roof with dislodged bricks and blocked gutters. She said she felt pressured into agreeing to having her roof re-done and paid a total of £5,500, only for the original contractor to send his son instead, who left work in the eaves incomplete. "We had heavy rain a couple of weeks after he did the job, and it ended up like a waterfall coming down the wall," she said. Her neighbour's house was also damaged. "They took the lead off my neighbour's side of the chimney, which caused bricks to fall into his attic and the rain to go into his house," she told the BBC. The experience still haunts her: "I can't sleep. I don't eat properly." In the year to August the Citizens Advice Consumer Service received 9,000 complaints about roofing work, including problems with construction, repairs and weatherproofing. Of those 2,205, or about one in four complaints, were suspected scams, up from 2,098 the year before. Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice, urged consumers to carry out thorough checks on traders before agreeing to hire them. "Scammers exploit the fact that roofs are out of sight and reach, knowing most people can't easily inspect the work themselves," she said. Victims also reported aggressive and intimidating behaviour, with three quarters of fraudsters using "doorstep" sales tactics. Citizens Advice cited the case of Charlotte, 65, who lives alone in north eastern England. Tradesmen she found online initially offered to fix her leaking gutter for £250. The two men then said there was further work that needed to be done, that would cost £2,500. "An hour later they said it was sorted, but they'd found another problem," she said. It was dark and Charlotte felt afraid. "They knew I was alone, I didn't feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500," she said. But the next day she could see no sign of any work having been done, she said. To avoid falling victim to roofing scams, Citizens Advice suggests: Be alert: Always ask for references and for everything to be in writing. Be wary of unsolicited doorknockers and callers Gather evidence: If a trader causes problems, be sure to take photos and gather the necessary paperwork and receipts Know your rights: Traders must give you the information about your right to cancel in writing. If the job is not done with "reasonable care and skill," the Consumer Rights Act 2015 also entitles you to ask for the problem to be fixed or a refund Lord Bichard, chair of National Trading Standards, said rogue traders were "criminals deliberately preying on people in their own homes". He described roofing fraud as "particularly cruel", and said Trading Standards would pursue fraudsters through legal routes. "Victims can lose life savings in a matter of hours and be left with damaged homes, financial hardship and a profound sense of vulnerability long after the criminals have gone," he said. events.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
events.summary: Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices. Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments. That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago. The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws. As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that. This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended". It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen. A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course". "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said. They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine". The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden. Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent Published 1 day ago Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Published 3 days ago Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 3 days ago Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products. Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong. Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel. The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress. Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain. The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market. The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September. Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers. The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption. It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war. Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

events.title: UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety efforts
events.summary: Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers Companies building the most advanced AI systems must increase safety efforts, the UK’s AI minister will say, as he announces a strengthening of Britain’s cyber defences. Kanishka Narayan will call on companies developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. He will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models and will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure. Narayan’s speech in west London will be the first since Andy Burnham made AI a cabinet-level brief. It comes as Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which tests the most powerful AI models, raised fears enemy states could steal unreleased cutting-edge models. Amid increasing global concern at dangers posed by AI, Irving told the Guardian: “The AI companies do not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models.” He cited a recent incident at OpenAI where it was “hacked” by cybersecurity researchers, who said “the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge”. The attack was carried out under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers testing its systems. OpenAI says it has multiple protections against theft of its models, including encryption and continuous monitoring. Irving, a former employee at OpenAI and Google DeepMind who now runs an AI safety research body , has warned there is a “50% chance” of humanity being wiped out by superintelligent AIs and the only answer, for now, is to stop development of advanced systems as soon as possible. Irving is concerned by the rate of progress in alarming attributes shown by models, which could lead to them becoming highly advanced in traits such as concealing their actions and manipulating humans. “It is possible we [will] get superintelligence in less than 12 months, on the current path,” he said. Narayan’s speech will be watched closely for signs the UK may join a call for international governments to coordinate common safety standards for AIs, which has been signed by leaders of nations including Finland, France, Germany, Australia, Singapore, the UAE and Ireland, but not the UK and the US, where Donald Trump has said he wants the leading AI companies to “self-police”. The international alliance calling for strict rules comes after a wave of recent incidents with misaligned advanced AIs hacking into private and government systems. In one of the latest cases, Anthropic on Friday revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model the AI contacted police claiming it could help solve a murder. It had landed on a page containing a police department tip form and a mention of an unsolved homicide. It wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Although Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, its instructions did not rule out form submissions. Last week UK intelligence leaders from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ briefed the cabinet on AI’s threat to national security, according to the Sunday Times. The warning from the spy chiefs is being seen by some as encouragement for Burnham to grip the AI safety issue more firmly. The prime minister told the UN last month that Britain would use its G20 presidency next year to champion agreement on AI safety with “a single set of global principles and standards”. But safety experts are calling for faster action to avert the most serious risks, which range from advanced AIs being used to mount a cyber-attack on essential infrastructure to the creation of novel bioweapons. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Meanwhile, Satya Nadella, the chair and chief executive of Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is an OpenAI shareholder, on Saturday called for AI models to be designed with an “emergency brake”. He said people needed to start from the principle of assuming advanced AI models posed an insider risk. “We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.” The best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. events.title: China, EU reach agreement to reduce Chinese hybrid vehicle imports
events.summary: The EU and China reached a deal Friday to reduce China’s shipments of hybrid vehicles to Europe by half, forestalling a damaging trade war but doing little to address Brussels’ broader complaints. The agreement slashes Chinese imports by millions of cars over four years, the EU’s trade commissioner said, calling it “ only a first step .” The deal leaves untouched the vast majority of Brussels’ $1 billion-a-day trade deficit with Beijing. Chinese brands accounted for one in four European hybrid sales in August, swamping Europe’s legacy automakers. Volkswagen recently announced 100,000 job cuts . events.title: Environmental watchdog to review new Kimberley gas project
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Buru Energy sends gas project for EPA approval, saying it could power northern WA by 2029 Buru Energy's proposed Rafael conventional gas project in the Canning Basin. ( Suplied: Buru Energy ) Buru Energy has referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority for assessment. Environmentalists claim it could be a "Trojan horse for fracking" — something the company rejects. Buru expects a decision from the EPA by the end of the year. The company behind a proposed gas project in Western Australia's Kimberley says it could meet the region's power demands with locally produced energy for the first time. Buru Energy referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) for review in early October. The proposal involves developing a facility at the project site, located in the Kimberley's Canning Basin about 85 kilometres south of Derby, to process conventional gas from two co-located production wells. Conventional gas is natural gas extracted using simple drilling and pumping methods, as opposed to unconventional extraction methods like hydraulic fracturing, or fracking. Well testing underway at Buru Energy's Rafael conventional gas project. ( Supplied: Buru Energy ) Buru executive chairman David Maxwell said the Rafael project was the only proven conventional gas and liquids resource in the greater Kimberley region. "At the moment, the Kimberley relies on imported energy … from Karratha, Perth, Darwin, and Asia," he said. He said the Rafael project would improve energy security and be cost-effective, with reduced road traffic another potential benefit. Up to 300 tonnes of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) would be produced at the Rafael plant per day — the equivalent of about 16 or 17 terajoules of energy — alongside LPG and condensate. Mr Maxwell said the Kimberley used between six and 13 terajoules per day for power generation, with the amount varying based on the time of year. "We'll also supply beyond the Kimberley into, for example, the northern Pilbara. "In the case of LPG, we would be supplying in the order of a quarter to a third of the Kimberley's LPG demand." The West Australian government has banned fracking in over 98 per cent of the state, but this does not include parts of the Kimberley including the Canning Basin. Earlier this year, WA's EPA recommended a fracking proposal by Black Mountain Energy subsidiary Bennett Resources go ahead subject to conditions. The Valhalla Gas Exploration and Appraisal Program would see up to 20 exploration and appraisal wells drilled in the basin. A record 8,000 appeals were lodged against the project. Community members gather in Broome to protest the Valhalla fracking proposal. ( ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic ) When asked about the fracking proposal in Broome this month, WA Mines Minister Daniel Pastorelli said the method had drawn varied perspectives. "I understand everyone has differing views on these types of things and I respect that completely," he said. "Obviously our policy and our approach is based on science, and that is what we're doing when it comes to hydraulic fracturing." Daniel Pastorelli acknowledges fracking is a controversial topic. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) Environmentalists have expressed concern Buru's Rafael project, although a conventional gas project, could pave the way for fracking to occur in the future. Environs Kimberley executive director Martin Pritchard said Rafael "could be a Trojan horse for fracking". "They (Buru) might be saying right now that they're not intending on fracking, but their statements to the ASX clearly say that they want to undertake fracking in the future," he said. Buru's David Maxwell rejected the accusation. "It's got nothing to do with fracking at all," he said. "And if there was any fracking involved — and I stress there is not — that would be a separate [EPA] referral, a separate application and a separate approval process and we're not in that process at all." Buru Energy's Yulleroo 2 wellhead 60 kilometres east of Broome was fracked in 2010. ( ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins ) The company previously used the hydraulic fracturing technique at its Yulleroo gas field also in the Canning Basin, but Mr Maxwell said it no longer did so. "We do not currently practice hydraulic fracturing," he said. "In the past Buru has, but Buru has put that on the shelf, and at the moment we have no plans for fracture stimulation." Mr Pritchard said solar and batteries, rather than gas fields, were the way forward for cheaper and cleaner electricity in the Kimberley.

events.title: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
events.summary: A bipartisan group of six senators are calling on President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.” Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Man attacked by tiger after entering enclosure at England wildlife park Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says “The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS's “Face the Nation.” He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month. “This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said. Energy experts say the Russia deal is unlikely to make a dent in high prices at the pump. Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, noted that the total amount of diesel appears to be less than what the U.S. uses in a day. Nephew argued that Iran and Russia might benefit more than the U.S. “The Iranians are probably very excited because it shows that there’s a lot of pressure still on the U.S. And the Russians are excited because it puts a big hole in the sanctions regime,” he said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices. Associated Press writer Mae Anderson in New York contributed to this report. events.title: Buttigieg gambles on a different path for 2028
events.summary: Pete Buttigieg has been able to campaign for Democrats across the country more than many of his potential 2028 rivals this past year. One reason: He doesn't have a job. That's by choice. Buttigieg said no when top Democrats urged him to run for governor or the U.S. Senate in Michigan this year. Why it matters: That decision is a gamble for Buttigieg's presidential ambitions. He's been able to build a national network over the last two years but hasn't added to his relatively thin resume as a former mayor of South Bend, Ind., and Joe Biden's transportation secretary. Buttigieg, 44, became a national political figure without following the typical path. He ran for president in 2020 as a small-town mayor and won the Iowa caucus by offering an optimistic vision and impressing voters with his communication skills — including in hostile environments. Driving the news: In early 2025, Democratic lawmakers and strategists including New York Sen. Chuck Schumer and former Michigan Sen. Debbie Stabenow urged Buttigieg — who had moved to Michigan — to run for office in his new state. Winning such an office, they argued, would help Buttigieg build his resume for a future White House run and give him a chance to distance himself from the unpopular Biden administration. Buttigieg passed, citing both a desire to stay home more with his husband and young twins, and figuring that he could still get his message out without being in the Senate. Instead, he set about building a larger national network among Democrats — particularly with Black voters in the South, where he had struggled in the 2020 Democratic primary. Buttigieg has traveled to 37 states since he left the Biden administration, Politico reported last week. Democratic candidates in vital swing districts and states have welcomed him to campaign for them this year while resisting offers from other potential presidential candidates such as former Vice President Kamala Harris , New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. In Buttigieg, many Democrats see a surrogate who can draw attention and crowds without the degree of negative attention that other prominent Democrats attract. Buttigieg also will campaign in key races in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 election. He's scheduled to be in Michigan and Virginia — which happen to hold early contests in the 2028 presidential primary. Between the lines: Buttigieg has tried to position himself as a candidate of the next generation who also has enough experience in the executive branch to be able to deliver. He's betting that the traditional ladder of running for president — becoming a senator, governor, or vice president first — no longer applies, especially after the Trump era. What they're saying: Buttigieg "knows what no one else on the Democratic side does, which is what it's actually like to run for this office — the pacing, the pressures and imperatives," David Axelrod, a former senior aide to President Obama and an outside adviser to Buttigieg in the past, told Axios. "At a time when the party and country will be searching for youth and forward-looking vision, he has the capacity to articulate one in a powerful way," Axelrod added. Axelrod said that if Buttigieg runs, "it will be because he feels the timing is right for someone like him, and the big mission is more compelling than the statewide races on which he took a pass." A Buttigieg spokesperson said that "when Pete decided not to run for office in Michigan, he promised he would still get to work to help candidates everywhere. He's been doing just that."

events.title: Turning AI Ambition into Real-World Advantage
events.summary: As enterprises race to adopt AI, Amitabh Sarkar, argues that AI’s real test is on infrastructure, and durable transformation will depend on converging networks, cloud, security, governance and trust. When executives talk about artificial intelligence today, they often talk in absolutes: an existential threat, a historic opportunity, the next great productivity leap. For Amitabh Sarkar, Tata Communications’ Vice-President, Asia Pacific and Japan, the more important story lies beneath the rhetoric and inside the data centres, networks and operating models trying to empower corporate ambition to meet their targets. “In the last 20 to 30 years, technology has moved from supporting the business, to enabling the business, to increasingly becoming the business,” he says. That shift has transformed corporate technology leadership. Once, CIOs were judged largely on uptime, efficiency and cost control. Today, the question is whether an enterprise has the infrastructure to launch new digital services across markets in weeks rather than months. For Tata Communications, the evolution has also been internal. Long associated with global connectivity, the company is positioning itself as a digital infrastructure and intelligence partner. The story is no longer only about pipes and bandwidth, but about platforms, AI readiness, cybersecurity and measurable business outcomes. A decade ago, customers came to Tata Communications with a simple request: connect one location to another. “Ten or fifteen years back, the prime reason clients talked to us was: can you connect country A to country B, data centre A to data centre B?” Sarkar recalls. “Transactional connectivity and interconnected data centres are all still important, but it’s now just one part of the story.” Enterprises today operate across multiple clouds, legacy and modern applications, overlapping cybersecurity tools and fragmented data. What they need is not another layer of complexity, but a partner who can simplify and orchestrate it. Tata Communications has built its business around that shift. Today, it positions itself as a digital infrastructure and intelligence partner. Its network fabric still underpins global connectivity, but it now sits alongside cloud and edge capabilities, security services, digital platforms and customer experience tools. The aim is to help enterprises connect, secure and control complex environments end to end. The story is no longer only about pipes and bandwidth, but about platforms, AI readiness, cybersecurity and measurable business outcomes. That evolution has changed not just what the company offers, but whom it serves. “Yesterday it was just the chief network officer,” Sarkar says. “Today the buying centre has expanded to several functions - the CMO, CDO, CTO, CIO and line-of-business leaders. Decisions on customer experience don’t always sit with IT any more.” As a result, Tata Communications’ teams have moved from selling technology to selling outcomes: revenue growth, cost efficiency, customer experience, resilience and security. The question is no longer whether a network is fast, but whether the architecture can support the business model the organisation wants to build. Sarkar’s view of the future begins with a contradiction at the heart of the AI boom. Boardrooms are moving quickly, but enterprise infrastructure is often the least regarded vector in the equation. “There is a widening gap between AI ambition and AI readiness,” he says. “Boardroom ambitions have perhaps moved faster than the infrastructure required to support these ambitions.” The mistake, he argues, is treating transformation as a purchase, and buying the latest model, tool or cloud service to automatically deliver transformation. “Technology is the easy part to buy,” he says. “The harder questions are those that technology alone cannot answer. What business outcome are you actually trying to change? Can your operating model support it? Can your data move across the organisation? Will your people adopt it? And can your infrastructure scale it securely?” Many companies can build impressive AI demonstrations quickly. The challenge is turning pilots into production systems connected to real workflows, governed data and secure infrastructure. Without that foundation, AI risks becoming a boardroom showcase rather than an operating advantage. The rise of AI agents will make those questions more urgent. Sarkar believes organisations may soon manage more digital agents than human employees. “You and I walk into an office with an ID card. Agents don’t,” he says. “How do you identify, govern and securely manage them? What are they allowed to access? What actions can they take? Can we trace why they made a decision and pivot quickly if it’s not the right move?” His conclusion is clear: the real AI story is increasingly an infrastructure story, not simply one about models and GPUs. Hybrid cloud is where many of the stress fractures are already visible.

events.title: Aaron Sorkin’s ‘The Social Reckoning’ is off to a weak start
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. “The Social Reckoning,” Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network,” is on track to make only $5.5 million at the domestic box office this weekend, according to Sunday estimates. That’s below the already underwhelming $7 million to $8 million the studio had projected, and it means Sorkin’s new movie is unlikely to become a “Social Network”-sized hit. The earlier film had a $22 million opening weekend and made a total of $97 million domestically (and that’s at 2010 ticket prices). It also won Sorkin an Oscar and became one of most influential on-screen depictions of Silicon Valley and startup culture. Beyond the fate of a single film, the weekend box office could also offer hints about audience excitement, or lack thereof, as we kick off a fall full of movies starring villainous, real-world tech CEOs . There’s Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” (which also opened this weekend), Nathan Fielder’s apparently uncategorizable Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” (coming next weekend!), and the OpenAI boardroom drama “Artificial” (which has a new distributor after being dropped by Amazon). Outside of theaters, Netflix also has a series called “The Altruists” coming in November , telling the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the collapse of FTX. As for “The Social Reckoning,” while “The Social Network” was a notable success, the theatrical landscape has changed significantly in the last 16 years. And where the first film focused on the excitement and drama of Facebook’s early days, the sequel is darker and heavier — it’s all about whistleblower Frances Haugen’s decision to leak what became known as the Facebook files. So maybe a movie about Senate hearings and algorithm changes was never going to be a big hit. Or maybe the real audience is among older moviegoers who have only returned sporadically to theaters . And I wonder if critiquing Facebook feels a bit less urgent to audiences who are more likely to be losing sleep over AI. Maybe just as importantly, the new movie’s reviews just aren’t very good . (For what it’s worth, I enjoyed “The Social Reckoning” but will fully admit that it’s overloaded with Sorkin’s trademark speechifying. And I couldn’t help dreaming about a version directed — like the original — by David Fincher, with a score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross.) “Musk,” meanwhile, made $69,000 during its opening weekend in four theaters. It will roll out more broadly in the coming weeks, but given its length and subject matter, the documentary will probably reach many more viewers once it starts streaming on HBO Max. events.title: Mildura and South Australia connected by bus service after six-year hiatus
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts New bus service re-establishes link between Mildura and South Australia The Monty Express can drop Mildura residents off in South Australia, and SA residents off in Mildura. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The Monty Express coach will re-establish a direct road transport link between Mildura, Renmark and Adelaide. The route has not been serviced in almost six years. The service will make its first interstate journey on October 12. A new bus service has launched connecting Mildura in Victoria's north-west to South Australia. From this week, a bus named The Monty Express will be travelling the Sturt Highway between Sunraysia and Adelaide via Renmark. It has been nearly six years since the route was serviced, with Greyhound Australia canning its Mildura to Adelaide coaches in 2016 , and another bus company ceasing its operations in 2020, in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. The lone direct flight between Mildura and Adelaide also no longer exists, with Rex Airlines terminating the service in May 2023. Ever since, getting into the festival state from Mildura involved detours via Ouyen, Horsham or Broken Hill, or at greater cost, flying to Adelaide via Melbourne or Sydney. The Monty Express will start taking passengers from October 12. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) Former Sunraysia resident Stuart Saunders ran a survey six months ago to gauge interest in restoring a Mildura to Adelaide bus service. He said support was overwhelming, and he soon prepared to pivot from his information technology career to become a bus driver. He purchased a 36-seat bus, which he named The Monty Express after the family's pet Cavoodle, Monty. "There's very much a sense of community in the coach industry," he said. Stuart Saunders and his family in front of their new business venture. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The Mildura–Renmark–Adelaide service begins today. It will initially run twice a week, departing Adelaide on Mondays and Thursdays and returning on Tuesdays and Fridays. It will run as an express service with pick-ups at Mildura, Renmark, Adelaide Airport and the Adelaide Central Bus Station. Under a service agreement with the SA government, The Monty Express cannot pick up South Australian residents unless they go to Mildura. Stuart Saunders with his children, Matilda and Gabriel, wife, Melody and dog, Monty. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The agreement exists to avoid impacting passenger numbers on the existing Stateliner coach service route between the Riverland and Adelaide. Mildura man Steven Haby describes himself as a transport enthusiast. The former Melburnian is a member of the Bus and Coach Society of Victoria and the Australian Timetable Association. He will be travelling from Mildura to Adelaide to experience the first service of The Monty Express on Monday. Steven Haby has booked his ticket on The Monty Express. ( Supplied: Steven Haby ) "I'm very much an advocate and supporter of public transport," Mr Haby says. "I thought this was a really good opportunity to support the service going forward and be one of the first passengers on the run. "You can have a sustainable public transport network in a city like Mildura … making it frequent, reliable, cheap, and to places where people want to go." Mr Saunders hopes The Monty Express will not only benefit Mildura residents, but will connect people in the Riverland with Sunraysia's V/Line bus services and flights. "Not only are we trying to give an express service into Adelaide from Mildura, but the challenges for the Riverland people trying to get into Mildura, I'm hoping we can solve some of their problems as well," he said. Tamille Hunter is a resident of Cobdogla, a South Australian town less than two hours from Mildura by car. Ms Hunter is unable to drive and has occasionally used existing transport options to get to Mildura. The journey she took involved catching a bus to Adelaide, a flight to Melbourne, a train to Swan Hill and a bus to Mildura. The Monty Express can seat as many as 36 passengers. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) "At the moment, for us to go to Mildura it takes us 24 hours and over $600," Ms Hunter said. She said getting The Monty Express to Mildura would open up lots of opportunities for her. "From there, I could visit my family and friends in Melbourne on the V/Line," she said.

events.title: Ongoing Birdsville Track closure hits outback businesses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Birdsville Track's long-term closure hurting outback businesses Cooper Creek over the Birdsville Track, in June 2025. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) The Birdsville Track has been closed for 400 days of the past two years. The road is a major freight and tourism route cutting through outback South Australia and Queensland. Part of the track is expected to reopen next week, while northern sections could remain closed for many months. One of Australia's most iconic outback roads has been closed for 400 days out of the past two years due to rain damage, with remote businesses feeling the pinch. Stretching more than 500 kilometres, the Birdsville Track connects Birdsville in south-west Queensland, to Marree in far-north South Australia. It provides access to local pastoral properties to move cattle, allows stock to flow to the South Australian market and has become increasingly popular with outback tourists. The track is largely unsealed, meaning flooding and heavy rain have periodically closed the track over the years — but never for this long. Despite the challenges, Lyall Oldfield is "very happy" living in the outback. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) Marree Roadhouse owner Lyall Oldfield said his business was "probably one third of what it normally is". "It's just dreadful what's happening with the roads. It's not even a joke." Business at the Marree Roadhouse is one third of what it normally is. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) About 230km north of Marree is the Mungerannie Hotel, which was taken over by new owners in 2023. Three years later, the business has not opened all year, with road closures stopping the daily water deliveries it relies on. Cattle coming off Clifton Hills Station on the Birdsville Track in South Australia after flooding. ( Supplied: Pete Nunn ) Co-owner Andrew Norman said it was a similar tale in 2025, when there was "no sort of season whatsoever". Mr Norman said the closure north of Mungeranie is having the biggest impact, deterring tourists from making the trip. The Birdsville Track has sustained significant damage from rain events. ( Supplied: Department for Infrastructure and Transport ) Mungerannie Hotel secures water source The owners of the Mungerannie Hotel on the Birdsville Track will now truck 13,000 litres of water to the pub each day, after being told they can no longer use a nearby bore. "Nobody's really coming up to Mungeranie to turn around and go back," Mr Norman said. "If they can get that road open just north of us and get the Birdsville Track open, next year should be fine. "If the track is open, we'll be open. But without a track, we're not open." The SA Department for Infrastructure and Transport hoped to reopen the 200km section between Marree and Mungeranie "next week", but the route north of Mungeranie is expected to remain closed for some time. Large parts of the Birdsville Track remain underwater. ( Supplied: Department of Infrastructure and Transport ) Regional north and outback road maintenance manager Juanita Chester said with some northern parts of the Birdsville Track still underwater, it would be "several more months before [the department] can even consider reopening". While the construction of a single-lane access route has been considered, Ms Chester said the local pits where materials are sourced have flooded too. The track has sustained damage from several significant rain events in the past 24 months. ( Supplied: Department for Infrastructure and Transport ) "They're like a dam when it rains, they fill with water," she said. "If we can't get in there to get material, there's very little we can do short of carting material from a long, long way away, which then impacts the roads." The department is assessing the scope and price of the remaining work, which will then require approval before it can begin, and Ms Chester said this would be unlikely in the next two months.

events.title: Trump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump's announcement Sunday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official said. The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next. Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants. Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries. "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said. "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready." Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media. What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me." State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices. White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia. "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said. Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin. A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.

events.title: Can the AI industry persuade data center opponents by getting rid of NDAs?
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebecca Bellan, and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco , which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York . I believe it’s a one-year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms of how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried.

events.title: Trump sticks with tariffs even as US voters turn against them before the midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump shows no signs of budging from a trade policy that many Americans don't like as the midterm elections loom NEW YORK -- Maybe President Donald Trump really does believe that “tariff” is the most beautiful word in the dictionary . Despite higher prices, criticism from trade experts and displeasure among voters, Trump holds fast to his belief that imposing the highest import duties on U.S. trading partners since the Great Depression is a winner . A recent poll suggests that is a big gamble with less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterms. Most U.S. adults disapprove of his trade policies, with more than 64% saying he has gone too far with his latest tariffs, compared with 58% in January. A look at the political, legal and economic challenges to the Republican president's approach to trade. The United States has set taxes on imports from most countries in the low double digits, although the rates have gone up and down because of legal setbacks as well as Trump's habit of changing them seemingly on a whim . In the biggest round last year, Trump levied what he called “reciprocal” tariffs and other duties on dozens of countries. He cited a 1977 law that he said allowed him to act without congressional approval in an economic emergency. After the Supreme Court struck that down in February, Trump turned to an array of other trade laws to accomplish his goals. The primary one he is using now, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 , allows him to impose tariffs on countries that he believes are engaging in unfair trade practices, such as not adequately enforcing a ban on forced labor. The new duties range from 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 economies, including big U.S. trading partners such as the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico. Trump is taking a sledgehammer to a relatively open global trading system that many mainstream economists think has benefited the U.S. enormously. It has helped boost growth, keep prices low and make U.S. businesses more competitive and often dominant in global industries. The U.S. is the second-largest exporter in the world, after China. It exported $3.4 trillion in goods and services last year, far ahead of third place Germany’s $2.3 trillion. Although Trump claims foreign exporters are paying tariffs, it is mostly Americans who are footing the bill. Studies, including ones from New York Fed and Harvard , have shown that overseas companies have largely not lowered their prices to offset the tariffs that U.S. businesses pay at the border. Those businesses are absorbing the added costs or passing them along to consumers through higher prices. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer The White House responds that the factory boom is already underway and points to statistics showing that manufacturing jobs, after falling last year, are on the upswing and work in certain nonresidential construction trades is rising, too. “Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online,” said White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers. In the four years after China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, nearly 3 million U.S. manufacturing jobs were lost, accelerating a shift away from factory work. Even global trade enthusiasts recognize the damage. Many U.S. companies struggled to compete with an influx of discounted products from China, which has suppressed consumption to encourage exports It also is true that some countries have higher tariffs than the U.S., manipulate their currencies lower to ensure to make their exports to the U.S. cheaper and help industries with subsidies. But tariffs among U.S. major trading partners are low, often comparable to U.S. rates and sometimes lower. Before the trade war, the U.S. rate averaged 1.47% for goods from the European Union, slightly above the average 1.35% imposed by the EU on American products , according to the Brussels think tank Bruegel. Europeans are big buyers of what America wants to sell. About 30% of European imports are from U.S.-owned companies, according to the European Central Bank. The relationship with Canada, America's big trading partner to the north, was also similar before trade talks broke down this summer. Canada's effective tariff rate on U.S. imports was about 2.4%, less than half the 5% that the U.S. had on Canadian imports, according to calculations by Oxford Economics. Now the countries are mired in a tit-for-tat dispute, with both countries escalating tariffs on each other. Self-driving truck companies Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI received a federal exemption this week that removes a massive barrier to commercialization. Under federal regulations, if a traditional big rig runs into trouble, the human driver must pull over, activate the hazard lights, and then physically place reflective warning triangles on the road within 10 minutes to alert other road users. But if a mechanical problem forces a self-driving truck to pull over, there’s no human driver to deploy those warning devices. It was a big enough hurdle that Aurora took federal safety regulators to court over the requirement. After the court denied its request for an exemption, the company escalated the fight to the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. (Companies did have a temporary waiver as it awaited a decision.) Now Aurora and other self-driving truck developers have been given the green light from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration . The agency has granted a five-year exemption allowing companies to replace roadside warning devices, such as reflective warning triangles, with cab-mounted warning beacons. Check out Aurora’s first responders page to see how it works. Daniel Goff , vice president of external affairs at Kodiak AI, said the exemption will help the industry “usher in an autonomous era of freight movement on U.S. roads, one that can save lives and improve the efficiency of goods delivery.” Gerardo Interiano , Aurora’s head of government relations and public affairs, echoed that sentiment, saying the decision underscores the government’s recognition of the economic and community benefits of autonomous trucking. He described the high-visibility, cab-mounted warning beacons as a “critical, 21st-century solution that enhances roadside safety by immediately alerting other road users without ever needing to put a person in harm’s way.” One question I’m left with: Could these cab-mounted warning beacons eventually become standard equipment across the entire trucking industry? events.title: Dawn Myers is making it easier to style, detangle, and care for curly hair
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Normally, Dawn Myers wears her hair up in a big old afro, and anyone with an afro can attest that wash days — the routine of washing and styling textured hair — are often tedious. They take a lot of detangling, product, styling, and, well, time. “I was watching ‘Shark Tank,’ and there was another curly girl idea,” she recalled of a day around eight years ago, when a pitch for a hair product aired. She started thinking about all the hair tools on the market, like blow dryers and curling irons, “things that straighten and change the chemistry of our naturally curly hair,” she told TechCrunch, adding that it takes around an hour and 20 minutes to wash and style her own hair. None of those tools help with that, and for Myers, it highlighted a gap that has always existed in the beauty hardware space — a lack of tooling for textured hair. It’s a space that’s complex, expensive, and just overlooked . “If you think back to slavery, we were mandated to cover our hair. That’s where do-rags come from. You had to cover your hair. Why? Because our hair was seen as ugly and unkempt and unacceptable,” she said. Later came hot combs, chemical relaxers, and flat irons, all of which straighten textured hair. “It’s only been the past 15 years or so where women of color and Black women in particular and, quite frankly, white women as well have really felt comfortable exposing their naturally curly hair and really just embracing it.” Soon after that episode aired, she whipped out a legal pad and sketched out a business idea, then went to Ace Hardware and CVS and put together a “Frankenstein-looking prototype.” Her idea eventually became the company Richualist , which is known for its product Mint, a hair tool that helps detangle, condition, gel, and style in a single stroke using refillable product pods. It even has warming technology to gently heat the product before it’s applied. “We get that styling time down to about seven to 10 minutes,” she said. “It’s a massive game changer for the customer really stressed out by wash day.” She said her product, which also comes in travel size, helps make hair a bit healthier, reducing shedding and breakage by up to 70% since people no longer need to tug endlessly on their strands as they wash and style. She built it with the materials science company Dow, after an early prototype caught the company’s attention during a startup accelerator program. “It just so happens that Dow had identified this white space recently as well, and they were starting a textured hair care unit,” she said. “So they ended up collaborating with us and giving us a lot of engineering help and manufacturing guidance.” Even though she eventually became one of the first 100 Black women to raise more than $1 million in venture funding, the early days were rough. “It’s really impossible to get hardware funded,” she continued. “It’s even more impossible to get it funded when we’re talking about such a niche problem.” She recalled the early meetings with executives in the beauty industry. “There are no people who look like me in those R&D suites.” In fact, she said, when she described wash days, “these people didn’t know what a wash day was. They didn’t understand that there’s this whole process that their customers have to go through.” She would tell them how painful and arduous the process is. “And the powers that be, up until this point, did not know,” she continued. “Even the bonds in our hair are totally different than other technology types. We really do need bespoke technology.” Myers sold her home and liquidated her 401(k) retirement account to fund the initial development of this product. “That was a crazy bet, but it paid off,” she said. “We were able to get about $1.4 million in the door to commercialize the product and just validate it.” Overall, it took about five years of development to get the product to “a place where it made sense to the customer,” she said, adding that her team also had to conduct their own research in the space since what they needed — like how much product the average person with textured hair uses — didn’t yet exist. Then, in 2022, just as she was about to expand and go to market, she was diagnosed with stage three colorectal cancer. “We ended up closing our round while I was still going through treatment,” she recalled, saying the round took “forever” to close. She remembers sitting in the chemo chair at Johns Hopkins, on her laptop, trying to close deals. She applied to “Shark Tank” in 2023 and appeared on the show later that year, though the episode aired in 2024. “I was still wearing a binder around my abdomen [a compression wrap] under the dress I wore for my ‘Shark Tank’ experience,” she said.

events.title: Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say
events.summary: Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries Trump announces partial ceasefire but Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’ Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted. The US president infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran. The package announced by Trump involves 300,000 tonnes of diesel released immediately “to the American and global marketplace” followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1m tonnes after that. The 300,000 figure equates to about three-quarters of what the US would use in a day, according to calculations using figures from the US Energy Information Administration . “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted. However, experts suggested that the quantities involved – and the time it will take for the supplies to arrive in the US – is “too little, too late” to affect current high diesel prices, which observers have linked to challenging Republican party polling numbers before next month’s midterm elections. US prices have surged by almost 70% since the start of the Iran war, to about $6.30 a gallon , according to American Automobile Association. In the UK, the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre earlier in October, and sat just below that mark on Friday. Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst with the investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “It is not going to have any impact on prices. The first amount [due to be shipped to the US] is so small. “They are going to have to charter vessels, load them and transport the cargo to the US. That will take about three weeks – so we are pretty much at the end of the month and about a week before the midterms.” The US Treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, said on Sunday: “This is ​good ‌for the ​American ​people … bringing these diesel prices down.” However, Kelty said the diesel shipments would also cause complications in a global supply chain, including multinational companies having to work out which of its supplies originated from Russia and therefore might breach sanctions in other jurisdictions, including Europe . The US Treasury suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, while keeping in place other sanctions on Russian products. Zelenskyy described Trump’s deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to keep attacking Ukraine, but Trump then blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for rising fuel prices. Trump said Ukraine neeeded “a new leader” . On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia curbed its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Trump later posted on Truth Social: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine . Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Maximilian Hess, the founder of the political risk consultancy Enmetena Advisory and a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said: “It will not have any meaningful domestic US effect or international effect given its full terms are highly unlikely to be met as a result of the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining which have limited its diesel output. “The whole point of the deal for Putin is that it fails, which he can blame on Ukraine and thus stoke tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Indeed, it’s already working.”

Sepsis, an acute inflammation triggered by infection, is a leading cause of childhood mortality, claiming roughly 3 million children under the age of five annually. Efferon , a startup selected as one of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026’s Startup Battlefield 200 , is on a mission to drastically lower that number. The company has developed a medical device that it says lowers organ failure rates and significantly accelerates recovery in children. When standard treatments like antibiotics cannot stop the immune system’s overreaction, a patient’s blood must be filtered to remove deadly toxins. That is where Efferon’s devices, of absorbers of dangerous cytokines and toxins, step in to make a critical difference. Dima Romashin, Efferon’s co-founder and CEO, compares what happens in the body during sepsis to a fire, where an immune response overwhelms the body rapidly. “In a fire, there are two things: the flame itself and smoke that it produces,” he told TechCrunch. In sepsis, endotoxins are the flames and cytokines are the smoke. Efferon, unlike other devices on the market, has developed a mechanism that can absorb both at once, according to Romashin. Although Efferon makes absorbers for adults, Efferon NEO, its pediatric device developed specifically for young kids, is proving especially effective. Since children have a significantly lower circulating blood volume, they require medical devices engineered specifically for their physiology, according to Romashin. In April, Efferon NEO received a CE mark , Europe’s equivalent to FDA approval, making it the first multimodal blood-purification device specifically engineered for pediatric sepsis. Efferon NEO is used in intensive care units across 30 countries, including European hospitals, Saudi Arabia, and Thailand. The company is now preparing to file for FDA approval and is on track to hit $2 million in annualized revenue by the end of 2026. The startup’s technology was originally developed by scientists at Moscow State University, including co-founder Ivan Bessonov. Recognizing its potential, Romashin, a serial entrepreneur, stepped in earlier this year as CEO to help commercialize it. Although Romashin admits that Efferon isn’t growing at the breakneck pace of today’s AI startups, true success for the company is measured by something else entirely: every child who gets to go home. Earlier this year, the streaming and entertainment industry witnessed one of its most high-stakes megadeals ever, stunning industry observers. Not only is it historic in its size, but it is also predicted to disrupt Hollywood and the media business as we know it. After years of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) struggling under the weight of billions of dollars in debt, compounded by declining cable viewership and fierce competition from streaming platforms, the company has been considering major strategic changes, including selling its entertainment assets to one of its rivals. Several major players saw the potential in acquiring the media giant, and in December, Netflix announced it would acquire WBD’s studios and streaming for $82.7 billion. But in a surprise eleventh-hour move in late February, the David Ellison-run Paramount became the winner of this bidding war, offering $111 billion to acquire all of WBD’s assets, including its studios, HBO, streaming platforms, games, and TV networks such as CNN and HGTV. Paramount was recently acquired by Ellison with significant support from his father, Larry Ellison — the Oracle chairman, world’s sixth-richest person, and major Trump donor. Paramount’s offer was approved by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) in June. A federal judge then paused the deal after a lawsuit was filed on July 13 by a coalition of 12 state attorneys general. However, a judge approved it in late September, with the acquisition finally official as of October 6 . Let’s break down exactly what happened and what could come next. ​This all started back in October 2025 when Warner Bros. Discovery revealed it was exploring a potential sale after receiving unsolicited interest from several major players in the industry. ​The bidding process quickly became competitive, and Paramount and Comcast emerged as serious contenders, with Paramount initially viewed as the frontrunner. However, WBD’s board eventually determined that an offer from the streaming giant Netflix was the most attractive. Netflix offered $82.7 billion for just Warner’s film, television, and streaming assets. Thus began the bidding war. Paramount believed its bid of approximately $108 billion for all of Warner’s assets was superior to Netflix’s offer that focused on just the studios and streaming. To sweeten its deal, Netflix amended its agreement in January to an all-cash offer at $27.75 per share of Warner Bros. Discovery, further reassuring investors and paving the way for the deal to proceed. ​Paramount persisted in its attempts to acquire WBD . Still, the Warner board repeatedly rejected its offers, citing concerns about Paramount’s heavy debt load and the increased risk associated with its proposal, including concern over the suite of investors bankrolling Paramount’s bid, which includes Saudi, Qatari, and Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth funds. The board noted that Paramount’s offer would have left the combined company burdened with $87 billion in debt, a risk they were unwilling to take at the time. In January, Paramount filed a lawsuit seeking more information about the Netflix deal. A month later, the company sought to sweeten its deal by announcing it would offer a $0.25 per share “ticking fee” to WBD shareholders for each quarter the deal fails to close by December 31, 2026. It also said it would pay the $2.8 billion breakup fee if Warner backs out of its deal with Netflix. Then, in a final attempt to secure a deal, Paramount increased its offer to $31 per share in February. This prompted the WBD board to prolong discussions with Paramount regarding a potential agreement, considering it as a superior offer. Netflix declined to increase its bid and withdrew from the negotiations. “The transaction we negotiated would have created shareholder value with a clear path to regulatory approval,” Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters said in a statement on February 26. “However, we’ve always been disciplined, and at the price required to match Paramount Skydance’s latest offer, the deal is no longer financially attractive, so we are declining to match the Paramount Skydance bid.” In addition to the billions Paramount already holds in debt, the company is also set to assume the approximately $33 billion in debt Warner Bros. Discovery holds under the agreement . The deal will be backed by a $54 billion debt commitment from Bank of America, Merrill Lynch, Citi, and Apollo Global Management, as well as $45.7 billion in equity from Larry Ellison. Regulatory hurdles and other concerns In addition to the assumption of substantial debt posing a significant financial burden, Paramount faced several other hurdles in its deal with WBD. For one, Ellison has warned about significant job reductions that are expected in the near future.

events.title: These execs think voice AI hasn’t reached its ChatGPT moment yet
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The theory of voice being the next big interface has picked up strong momentum, with investors pouring billions of dollars into voice AI startups working on areas ranging from model makers to enterprise customer service providers, and from meeting note-takers to AI-powered dictation. Every week there is a new model or a tool release that claims to sound human and converse like one. However, in reality, that might not be the case. Enterprise voice AI platform PolyAI’s CTO Shawn Wen thinks that despite the release of full-duplex models — which can speak while listening to you — voice AI hasn’t had its “ChatGPT moment” yet. “We have reached the milestone of developing full-duplex models. The next challenge is to make reasoning very fast, so that the models can fetch answers quickly and the conversation feels natural,” he told me onstage at the HumanX conference last month. He also said that AI agents in customer service should not sound robotic and should give callers enough confidence that they can solve problems. “I think the next stage will be slightly different because once the voice is good enough, like, and the customer is willing to engage with them for the first two or three turns, they start to build confidence, and over time, they will feel like I probably don’t have to talk to a human if the agent can solve my problem,” he said. Alex Gay, CMO for meeting note-taker Otter, opined that speaker identification, intent capture, and typing that up with organizational knowledge is a key step for enabling automation. The company is also working on digital twins that might represent people in meetings. For that technology, he said it’s paramount that the output voice gives the same emotive expressions of talking to a human in a meeting. “If you think about the meetings that you’re in right now, the best conversations that you have are where you can have debate, and strategic discussions, and when you feel like there’s a relationship that underpins it. If you aren’t able to have that with an avatar, then it’s just a Q and A chatbot,” Gay noted. Voice AI’s understanding and transparency While voice AI models have improved, AI assistants often don’t understand users, or your meeting note-taker shows the wrong transcript or a summary. Wen thinks that ASR (automatic speech recognition) models often miss important keywords, and that creates an issue in capturing the whole context. Otter’s Gay agreed with this, adding that the company keeps working on improving transcription. He also said that language is one area where voice models need to improve. “For Otter, you know, transcription was never the end point. It was just the layer that we could start to drive some of the productivity gains on the back of. But if your original transcription didn’t have the accuracy that you needed, all the follow-up actions that you have become flawed. And the minute that starts to take action, that is wrong. You lose trust in the platform. It is critical for us to continue to improve that ASR model because all of the downstream impacts are significant,” he said. With the new voice tools, there is also a question of transparency. Tools should declare to customers that they are being recorded or talking to AI. Otter said that it wants to instill trust in people who are in a meeting, so even for a meeting where the bot is not present, it wants to try methods like notifying everyone in the chat that the meeting is being recorded.
